stem: Pakistan's population at the 2023 census was about 241.5 million and had grown by about 2.55% a year since 2017.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Assume the population keeps growing at 2.55% a year. Calculate the population after 10 years, using population × 1.0255¹⁰. Give your answer in millions to one decimal place.
parts.working: M1 correct use of 1.0255¹⁰ (≈ 1.286); A1 310.7 million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems that this growth would create for providing food and water. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Food demand would rise by about 70 million more people, but farmland is limited and much is affected by waterlogging and salinity, so more wheat and pulses may have to be imported; water per person would fall further because river flows do not increase, causing shortages for farms and cities.
parts.working: 1 mark for each problem + 1 for development. Problems: more food needed from limited land; import bills; falling water per person; pressure on groundwater; loss of farmland to housing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the real figure may turn out lower than your answer.
parts.answer: The growth rate is likely to fall as fertility declines (education, urbanisation, family planning), so the population will grow by less than 2.55% each year.
parts.working: 1 mark: growth rate will not stay constant / will fall; 1 mark: reason, e.g. falling fertility, emigration.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why large families are still valued by many rural households in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Children help with farm work and livestock; sons are expected to support parents in old age.
parts.working: 1 mark each: farm/household labour; old-age security; social status/tradition; religious beliefs; to replace children who may die.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read the two views below.
View A: The best way to slow population growth in Pakistan is to educate girls.
View B: The best way to slow population growth in Pakistan is to expand family-planning services.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: A balanced answer, e.g. View A: educated girls marry later, understand health care, often work, and want fewer, healthier children; the effect lasts for generations. View B: many women already want fewer children but cannot get contraceptives, especially in villages, so services such as Lady Health Workers give quick results. Judgement: both are needed; education changes demand while services meet it, but education has the longer-lasting effect.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both views, with Pakistani examples, and a clear supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points only. Points A: later marriage; awareness of health/contraception; jobs for women; smaller family ideal. Points B: unmet need for contraception; Lady Health Workers/clinics reach rural women; faster results; but cultural resistance/supply problems.

stem: A survey of a village in Punjab found 1,200 people of working age. Of these, 780 were in the labour force, and 690 of them had jobs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by the labour force?
parts.answer: All the people of working age who are either in work or actively looking for work.
parts.working: B1 employed + unemployed people of working age.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the unemployment rate, using unemployed ÷ labour force × 100. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the working-age population that is in the labour force.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why many working-age people in the village are not in the labour force.
parts.answer: Many women do unpaid housework and childcare and are not counted as looking for paid work; some young people are still students.
parts.working: 1 mark each: women in unpaid household/farm work; students; disabled or ill; discouraged workers; elderly within the age range; living on remittances.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two types of work in Pakistan where child labour is often found.
parts.answer: Brick kilns; carpet weaving.
parts.working: 1 mark each: brick kilns; carpet weaving; agriculture/cotton picking; car/motorbike workshops; domestic work; hotels/tea stalls; football stitching (in the past).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why child labour continues in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Poor families need the child's income to survive, so they take the child out of school; some families are in debt to employers (for example at brick kilns), so the whole family, including children, must work; schools may be far away or of poor quality, so parents see little value in education; laws are not always enforced.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: poverty; debt bondage; poor access to/quality of schools; weak law enforcement; employers want cheap labour; cultural acceptance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two machines that have reduced the number of workers needed on farms in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Tractor; combine harvester.
parts.working: 1 mark each: tractor; combine harvester; thresher; tube well (replacing Persian wheel); seed drill; reaper.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects of farm mechanisation on rural employment. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Fewer labourers are needed for ploughing and harvesting, so landless workers lose seasonal jobs and may migrate to towns; some new jobs appear in repairing and driving machines, but these need skills, so the poorest workers may not benefit.
parts.working: 1 mark for each effect + 1 for development. Effects: loss of jobs for landless labourers; rural–urban migration; seasonal unemployment rises; new skilled jobs (mechanics, drivers); higher output may create jobs in processing/transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two examples of tertiary jobs that have grown in Pakistan's large cities in recent years.
parts.answer: Software development or IT freelancing; banking and call-centre work.
parts.working: 1 mark each: IT/software/freelancing; call centres; banking/finance; telecoms; online delivery riders; private education; health care; retail in shopping malls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the number of tertiary jobs is growing faster in Lahore, Karachi and Islamabad than in smaller towns. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: These cities have universities producing graduates with the skills that IT and finance firms need; they have reliable internet, offices and airports, so firms can serve customers at home and abroad; large populations with higher incomes create demand for shops, restaurants and services.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: skilled/educated workforce; better infrastructure (internet, power, transport); large market; head offices of firms and government; foreign investment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one problem faced by freelancers who work online from Pakistan.
parts.answer: Power cuts or slow internet interrupt work.
parts.working: B1: load-shedding; internet speed/outages; difficulty receiving payments from abroad; no job security or benefits.

stem:
Average monthly wages in a district in central Punjab (hypothetical figures, rupees):
Farm labourer 26,000
Factory worker 37,000
Construction worker 34,000
Shop assistant 30,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean monthly wage of the four jobs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much more a factory worker earns than a farm labourer in one year.
parts.working: M1 difference × 12; A1 Rs 132,000.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons, other than higher wages, why young men leave farm work for jobs in towns. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Farm work is seasonal, so labourers have no income for parts of the year, while factory jobs pay every month; towns offer better schools, hospitals and entertainment for families; mechanisation has reduced the number of farm jobs available.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: seasonal/irregular farm work; fewer farm jobs (mechanisation, small farms); services in towns; status/lifestyle; family contacts already in towns.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A technical training institute in a town in Sindh trained 640 young people in one year. Six months later, 416 of them had found work.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of graduates who found work within six months.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which technical and vocational training can reduce unemployment in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: It gives young people practical skills such as welding, electrical work or IT that employers need, so they are more likely to be hired; it lets people start their own small businesses, such as repair shops or tailoring units, creating jobs for others; trained workers can find skilled jobs abroad and send remittances.
parts.working: 1 mark for each way + 1 for development. Ways: matches skills to employers' needs; self-employment/small businesses; overseas employment as skilled workers; raises productivity attracting investment; women's home-based enterprise.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why some graduates of the institute did not find work.
parts.answer: There are few factories or workshops in the area to employ them; the courses may not match the skills local employers want.
parts.working: 1 mark each: lack of local jobs; mismatch of courses with demand; lack of experience; women unable to travel to work; poor quality training; lack of contacts.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Employment structure of three countries (illustrative, % of workers in primary, secondary and tertiary activities):
Country X: 62, 12, 26
Country Y: 37, 25, 38
Country Z: 3, 19, 78

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the percentage of workers in services in Country Z and in Country X.
parts.answer: 78 − 26 = 52 percentage points

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rank the three countries from least developed to most developed. Give a reason for your order.
parts.answer: X, then Y, then Z. As countries develop, the share of workers in primary activities falls and the share in services rises; X has the most farm workers and Z the most service workers.
parts.working: 1 mark correct order X, Y, Z; 1 mark reason linking falling primary/rising tertiary to development.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Pakistan's structure is closest to Country Y. Explain two reasons why the share of workers in industry in Pakistan has not risen as fast as in some East Asian countries. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Energy shortages and high electricity prices raise factory costs, so investors choose other countries; low levels of technical education mean fewer skilled workers, so high-value industries do not develop; political instability and security problems discourage foreign investment.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: power shortages/costs; skills gap; low investment/instability; reliance on a few industries (textiles); poor infrastructure; competition from imports.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two examples of new kinds of tertiary work that have grown with the spread of mobile phones in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Mobile phone repair shops; mobile money (branchless banking) agents.
parts.working: 1 mark each: phone repair/sales; mobile-money agents; ride-hailing drivers; food delivery riders; online selling; app-based freelancing; call centres.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read the two views below.
View A: Agriculture will remain the most important source of jobs in Pakistan for many years.
View B: Services will soon become the most important source of jobs in Pakistan.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: View A: agriculture still employs well over a third of all workers, about as many as all services together, most people live in rural areas, and many have few skills for other work; cash crops and livestock remain vital. View B: services already employ a large and growing share, urbanisation is rapid, and IT, trade, transport and retail are expanding; mechanisation is reducing farm jobs. Judgement, e.g. services are overtaking agriculture in total jobs, but agriculture will stay important in rural areas.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both views with Pakistani evidence and a supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple statements. A: large rural population; low skills; food security; livestock. B: urbanisation; IT/telecoms; trade/transport; mechanisation; young people prefer town jobs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the difference between internal migration and international migration?
parts.answer: Internal migration is moving to live in another place within the same country; international migration is moving to live in another country.
parts.working: 1 mark each definition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of internal migration in Pakistan.
parts.answer: People moving from villages in southern Punjab to Karachi to find work.
parts.working: B1 any named movement within Pakistan, e.g. rural Sindh → Karachi; KP → Karachi/Lahore; northern areas → Islamabad.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two pull factors that attract migrants to Karachi. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Karachi is Pakistan's main port and industrial city, so there are many jobs in factories, the docks and trade; it has more schools, colleges and hospitals than most rural areas; relatives or people from the same village already live there and help newcomers find work and housing.
parts.working: 1 mark for each pull factor + 1 for development. Pull factors: jobs (port, industry, services); higher wages; education/health services; family networks; perceived better lifestyle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In which year did a very large movement of people take place between the new states of India and Pakistan?
parts.working: B1 1947 (Partition).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which this migration changed the population of Karachi. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Hundreds of thousands of refugees from India settled in Karachi, so its population grew very quickly and many lived in temporary camps; as the first capital it attracted government workers and traders, so new housing colonies had to be built; the language and culture of the city changed, with Urdu-speaking migrants becoming a large group.
parts.working: 1 mark for each change + 1 for development. Changes: rapid growth; refugee camps/new colonies; change in language/ethnic mix; new businesses and skills; pressure on services.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one problem the new arrivals faced.
parts.answer: Shortage of housing, so many lived in tents or makeshift shelters.
parts.working: B1 lack of housing; lack of jobs; poor sanitation/disease; loss of property; separation from family.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by the term 'environmental refugees'?
parts.answer: People forced to leave their homes because of a natural hazard or environmental change, such as floods or drought.
parts.working: B1 movement forced by natural disaster/environmental change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why some families displaced by floods in Sindh do not return to their villages. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Their houses and fields may stay under water for months, so there is nothing to return to; they may have found work in the town where they sheltered, so staying is safer than restarting farming; their animals and savings may have been lost, so they cannot afford to rebuild.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: land still flooded/damaged; homes destroyed; loss of livestock/assets; jobs found elsewhere; fear of future floods; services better in towns.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which the government can help displaced families to return.
parts.answer: Give cash or materials to rebuild houses.
parts.working: B1 rebuilding grants; seeds/fertiliser for the next crop; repairing roads and embankments; draining water; restoring schools/clinics.

stem: A student asked 50 migrants in Lahore why they had moved to the city. Reasons given: jobs 26, education 9, marriage 8, joining family 5, other 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the migrants who moved for jobs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage who moved for education or marriage together.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why marriage is a common reason for migration among women in Pakistan.
parts.answer: In most families a woman moves to live with her husband's family after marriage, which is often in another village or town.
parts.working: 1 mark: women move to husband's home; 1 mark: development, e.g. joint family system / husbands working in cities.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of using a sample of only 50 migrants.
parts.answer: A small sample may not represent all migrants to Lahore, so the percentages could be misleading.
parts.working: 1 mark: may not be representative; 1 mark: development, e.g. chance results/bias in where they were interviewed.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, 340 men from a village in the Jhelum district work in the Gulf states. On average each sends home Rs 450,000 a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total amount sent to the village in one year.
parts.working: B1 Rs 153,000,000 (Rs 153 million).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which return migrants can change their home villages. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: They often build larger brick houses with savings, which creates work for local builders; some start businesses such as shops, transport services or tube wells, creating jobs; they bring new ideas, for example about education for daughters or modern farming.
parts.working: 1 mark for each way + 1 for development. Ways: new houses/construction; businesses and jobs; new skills/ideas; investment in land/tube wells; rising land prices; inequality between families.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one problem for a village that depends heavily on money sent from abroad.
parts.answer: If the workers lose their jobs, for example when Gulf economies slow down, the village income falls sharply.
parts.working: 1 mark problem + 1 development: vulnerable to job losses abroad; spending on consumption not productive investment; inflation of land prices; inequality.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which the lives of women change when many men migrate from a village.
parts.answer: Women take on more farm work and look after livestock; they take more household decisions, such as spending money and children's schooling.
parts.working: 1 mark each: more farm/livestock work; more decision-making; heavier workload; more contact with markets/banks; loneliness/stress.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the migration of young men can affect farming in the village. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: There are fewer workers at busy times such as wheat harvesting, so farmers must hire labour or machines; remittances may be used to buy tractors or tube wells, raising output; some land may be rented out or left uncultivated because no one is available to farm it.
parts.working: 1 mark for each effect + 1 for development. Effects: labour shortage; more mechanisation; investment from remittances; land left idle or rented out; change to less labour-intensive crops.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two types of work done by many Pakistani migrant workers in the Gulf states.
parts.answer: Construction labourers; drivers.
parts.working: 1 mark each: construction; driving/transport; domestic or hotel work; shop work; oil and gas industry; security.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems that Pakistani migrant workers can face in the Gulf states. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Under the sponsorship (kafala) system their visa is tied to one employer, so it is hard to leave a bad job; some pay large fees to recruiting agents and start their jobs in debt; wages may be low or paid late and living conditions in labour camps can be crowded; they are separated from their families for years.
parts.working: 1 mark for each problem + 1 for development. Problems: sponsorship system; recruitment fees/debt; low or unpaid wages; poor housing; extreme heat; separation from family; loss of jobs when projects end.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way in which the government of Pakistan could protect its workers abroad.
parts.answer: Register and control recruiting agents so that workers are not cheated.
parts.working: B1 regulate recruiters; pre-departure training; agreements with host governments; help desks at embassies; skills training for better-paid work.

stem:
Migration data for a rural district in one year (hypothetical figures):
In-migrants 48,000
Out-migrants 63,500
Population 1,250,000

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net migration for the district.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express the net migration as a percentage of the district's population. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two consequences for the district if this pattern continues for many years. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Most out-migrants are young adults, so the district is left with more children and old people and fewer workers; fewer skilled people stay, so it becomes harder to attract businesses; remittances from those who have left may support families and fund new houses.
parts.working: 1 mark for each consequence + 1 for development. Consequences: ageing/dependent population; labour shortage; brain drain; less investment; remittances; lower political weight; services close.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one reason why net migration figures for districts are hard to collect accurately.
parts.answer: Many people move without officially registering a change of address.
parts.working: B1 unregistered moves; seasonal/temporary movers; people counted where they are on census day; informal settlements.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by step migration?
parts.answer: Migration that takes place in stages, for example from a village to a small town, then to a large city.
parts.working: 1 mark: migration in stages; 1 mark: example or idea of moving up the urban hierarchy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Rural–urban migration does more good than harm to Pakistan.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: Good: migrants fill jobs in factories, construction and services; remittances sent home support rural families; cities give access to education and health care; it reduces pressure on farmland. Harm: cities grow faster than housing and services, so katchi abadis, traffic and pollution increase; villages lose young workers; unemployment in cities. Judgement: benefits are real but depend on planning for urban growth.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points on both sides with Pakistani examples and a supported judgement on the extent. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) on one side or simple points on both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points.

stem:
Remittances received by a country as a percentage of its GDP (illustrative figures):
Year 1: 5.1  Year 2: 6.4  Year 3: 7.0  Year 4: 6.2  Year 5: 8.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean of the five figures, to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase from Year 1 to Year 5. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why it is risky for a country to rely heavily on remittances. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Remittances depend on economic conditions abroad, so a fall in oil prices that cuts Gulf jobs can reduce them sharply; host countries may change visa rules or give jobs to their own citizens; much of the money is spent on consumption and imported goods rather than productive investment, so it does not build industry at home.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: dependence on foreign economies/oil prices; host-country policy changes; spent on consumption/imports; brain drain; currency and informal (hawala) channels; may reduce effort to create jobs at home.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by urban sprawl?
parts.answer: The spread of a city's built-up area outwards into the surrounding countryside.
parts.working: B1 unplanned/rapid outward growth of a city into rural land.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects of urban sprawl on the land around a city such as Lahore. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Fertile farmland is turned into housing schemes, so less food and vegetables are grown near the city; orchards and trees are cleared, which raises temperatures and reduces green space; new roads and drains are needed over a larger area, which is costly and often left incomplete.
parts.working: 1 mark for each effect + 1 for development. Effects: loss of farmland; loss of trees/green space; longer journeys/traffic; higher cost of services; rising land prices; flooding from sealed surfaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three basic services that are often lacking in poor areas of large cities in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Piped clean water; sewerage/drainage; regular rubbish collection.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: piped water; sewerage; waste collection; electricity/gas connections; schools; clinics; paved roads; street lighting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why city governments struggle to provide these services. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The population grows faster than the city can build pipes and drains, because many new settlements are unplanned and the city has limited money from taxes.
parts.working: 1 mark reason + 1 development: rapid growth; lack of funds; unplanned/illegal settlements; corruption/poor management; unclear land ownership.

stem:
Population (millions) of three provinces (illustrative figures):
Sindh: total 55.7, urban 29.9
Punjab: total 127.7, urban 51.9
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: total 40.9, urban 6.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the population that is urban in each province. Give your answers to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: Sindh 54%; Punjab 41%; Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 15%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why Sindh has the highest percentage of urban population.
parts.answer: Karachi, Pakistan's largest city and port, is in Sindh, so a large share of the province's people live in one huge city.
parts.working: 1 mark: Karachi/Hyderabad; 1 mark: development, e.g. port and industry attract migrants from all over Pakistan.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, a city of 4 million people produces about 0.5 kg of solid waste per person per day. Only 60% of it is collected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of solid waste the city produces each day, in tonnes.
parts.working: B1 2,000 tonnes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many tonnes of waste are not collected each day.
parts.working: B1 800 tonnes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two problems caused by waste that is not collected. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Rubbish blocks drains and nullahs, so streets flood after heavy rain; rotting waste attracts flies, rats and mosquitoes, spreading diseases such as diarrhoea and dengue; waste is often burnt in the open, adding smoke to the city's air pollution.
parts.working: 1 mark for each problem + 1 for development. Problems: blocked drains/flooding; disease; air pollution from burning; smell/ugly environment; water pollution; harm to animals.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, the number of registered vehicles in a large city rose from 1.8 million to 6.3 million in 15 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in registered vehicles. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which mass-transit systems, such as the Metro Bus or the Orange Line in Lahore, help to reduce urban problems. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: One bus or train carries many more passengers than cars or rickshaws, so traffic congestion falls on main roads; fewer vehicles mean less exhaust, reducing smog and air pollution; cheap, fast journeys let poorer workers reach jobs across the city.
parts.working: 1 mark for each way + 1 for development. Ways: less congestion; less air pollution/fuel use; affordable access to jobs/education; safer travel for women; shorter journey times.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why many people still use private vehicles.
parts.answer: The mass-transit routes do not reach their homes or workplaces.
parts.working: B1 limited network coverage; convenience; crowding; status; carrying goods/families.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Islamabad was built as a planned capital in the 1960s. Describe two features of its planning.
parts.answer: The city is divided into sectors, each with its own market, schools and green areas; wide roads in a grid pattern and green belts separate the sectors.
parts.working: 1 mark each: sector system; markaz (commercial centre) in each sector; grid of wide roads; green belts/parks; separate zones for government, housing and industry; Margalla Hills protected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why informal settlements (katchi abadis) have still developed in Islamabad. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The city needs many low-paid workers such as cleaners, drivers and builders, but planned housing is too expensive for them, so they build homes on empty land; rapid migration from other parts of Pakistan has been faster than the building of cheap housing; some settlements began as camps for construction workers and became permanent.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: high cost of planned housing; demand for low-paid labour; rapid migration; construction-worker camps; empty government land; weak enforcement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the large informal area in Karachi where a community-led sanitation project began in 1980.
parts.answer: Orangi (Orangi Town).
parts.working: B1 Orangi.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the residents improved sanitation in their lanes.
parts.answer: Residents of each lane organised themselves, paid for and laid their own underground sewer pipes with technical advice from the project, while the government built the larger main sewers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: lane groups organised; residents paid costs; residents did the work themselves; technical advice/training given; low-cost design; government provided main/trunk sewers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two benefits of this kind of community-led approach. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Costs were much lower than a government contract, so more lanes could be served; residents felt ownership and maintained the drains themselves; health improved because sewage no longer flowed in open lanes, reducing diarrhoea.
parts.working: 1 mark for each benefit + 1 for development. Benefits: low cost; ownership and maintenance; improved health; skills learnt; could be copied in other cities.

stem:
Survey of two areas of a city (hypothetical figures):
Area A (planned housing scheme): 1,250 households, 1,050 connected to sewers
Area B (katchi abadi): 980 households, 245 connected to sewers

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of households connected to sewers in each area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the lack of sewers in Area B is likely to affect the health of residents. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Waste water collects in open drains and pools where mosquitoes breed, spreading malaria and dengue; sewage can leak into shallow water pipes or wells, causing diarrhoea, typhoid and hepatitis, especially among children.
parts.working: 1 mark for each effect + 1 for development. Effects: water-borne diseases; mosquito-borne diseases; flies spreading infection; child illness/missed school; flooding with sewage in monsoon.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Populations of the four largest cities in a country (illustrative, millions): City 1: 20.4, City 2: 13.0, City 3: 3.7, City 4: 3.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times larger City 1 is than City 3. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the combined population of City 1 and City 2 as a percentage of the total of the four cities. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two advantages of developing smaller cities rather than allowing the largest cities to keep growing. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Jobs in smaller cities would reduce migration to the largest cities, easing their housing shortages and traffic; regional development would spread income more evenly, so more people could find work near their home villages; land and services are cheaper to provide in smaller cities.
parts.working: 1 mark for each advantage + 1 for development. Advantages: less pressure on mega-cities; balanced regional development; cheaper land/services; reduced commuting/pollution; more opportunities near rural areas.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why katchi abadis often grow along railway lines and beside nullahs (storm-water channels).
parts.answer: The land usually belongs to the government and is left empty, so people can build without buying it; it is close to jobs in the city centre.
parts.working: 1 mark each: unused public land; free/cheap; close to work; others already settled there; not wanted by developers because of risk.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read the two views below.
View A: Katchi abadis should be cleared and their residents moved to new housing on the edge of the city.
View B: Katchi abadis should be upgraded where they are, by adding services and giving residents ownership of their plots.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: View A: some settlements are on dangerous land (nullah banks that flood, railway lines), new housing can be properly planned with services. But moving people far from jobs increases travel costs and breaks communities. View B: upgrading is cheaper, keeps people near work and social networks; ownership encourages residents to improve homes (examples such as Orangi). But it may leave people in unsafe locations. Judgement: upgrade where safe, relocate only from hazardous sites with fair compensation.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both views with examples and a supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points.

stem: An area of 1 km² (1,000,000 m²) on the edge of a city receives 80 mm of rain in a monsoon storm. Before building, about 20% of the rain ran off the surface. After it is covered with houses and roads, about 70% runs off.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of runoff from the area after it is built over, and before. Give both answers in m³.
parts.working: M1 80,000 m³ of rain; A1 56,000 m³ and 16,000 m³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which rapid urban growth increases the risk of flooding in cities such as Karachi. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Roads and roofs are impermeable, so rain runs off quickly instead of soaking in, and drains overflow; houses have been built on or beside nullahs, narrowing them, so they cannot carry storm water; rubbish dumped in drains blocks the flow.
parts.working: 1 mark for each way + 1 for development. Ways: impermeable surfaces; encroachment on nullahs; blocked drains; loss of green space; drains designed for smaller population.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way to reduce this risk.
parts.answer: Clear encroachments and rubbish from the nullahs before the monsoon.
parts.working: B1 clearing nullahs; parks/green areas; permeable paving; larger drains; ban building in flood channels; rainwater storage.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two areas of Pakistan that are sparsely populated.
parts.answer: The Cholistan Desert; the Chagai/Kharan desert areas of western Balochistan.
parts.working: 1 mark each: Cholistan; Thar; Kharan/Chagai; much of Balochistan plateau; high northern mountains (e.g. Karakoram); Makran coast.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why one of these areas is sparsely populated. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Rainfall is very low and unreliable, so crops cannot be grown without irrigation and there is little drinking water; there are few roads, so it is hard to reach markets, schools and hospitals; very high summer temperatures make life difficult.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development, referring to the named area. Reasons: low rainfall/no water; poor soils; extreme temperatures; rugged relief; poor communications; few jobs.

stem:
Approximate figures:
Islamabad Capital Territory: population 2,360,000, area 906 km²
Sindh: population 55,700,000, area 140,914 km²

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the population density of Islamabad Capital Territory and of Sindh. Give your answers to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why Islamabad Capital Territory has a much higher density than Sindh as a whole.
parts.answer: Islamabad is almost all city, with government offices and many jobs; Sindh includes large, thinly populated desert areas such as the Thar and Kohistan.
parts.working: 1 mark each: ICT small and mostly urban; jobs/services in capital; Sindh contains deserts/dry hills; Sindh has large rural areas.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two human factors that can attract large numbers of people to an area.
parts.answer: Availability of jobs; good transport links.
parts.working: 1 mark each: jobs/industry; transport; services (schools, hospitals); government/administration; trade/markets; security.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two human reasons why the area around Faisalabad has a high population density. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Faisalabad is a major textile city, so its many factories provide jobs that attract workers; it lies on main roads, a motorway and railway lines, so goods and people move easily; the surrounding canal colonies were settled by planned irrigation, creating many farming villages.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: industry (textiles) and jobs; transport links; markets/trade; canal colony settlement; services and education.

stem: A description of a map of part of Sindh: the River Indus runs from north to south. Villages lie close together along both banks of the river and along the main canals. East of the canals is a sandy desert with very few settlements; west of the river are dry hills with almost no settlements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pattern of settlement shown in the description.
parts.answer: Settlements are linear: villages lie in a narrow belt along the river and canals, with very few people away from the water.
parts.working: 1 mark: concentrated along river/canals; 1 mark: linear pattern / few people in surrounding areas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why people in Sindh live close to the Indus and its canals. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Rainfall is very low, so the river and canals are the only reliable source of water for drinking and irrigation; the floodplain has fertile alluvial soil, so crops such as wheat, cotton and rice can be grown; roads, railways and towns developed along the river valley.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: water supply; irrigation; fertile alluvium; flat land; transport routes along the valley; fishing.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A district on the edge of the Thar Desert (hypothetical figures): total area 5,000 km², cultivated (irrigated) land 1,200 km², population 1.8 million.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the population density of the district using its total area.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of people per km² of cultivated land.
parts.answer: 1,800,000 ÷ 1,200 = 1,500 people per km² of cultivated land

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the figure in (b) gives a better picture of the pressure on land in this district than the figure in (a). You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Most of the district is desert that cannot support people, so dividing by total area hides how crowded the irrigated land really is.
parts.working: 1 mark: much of the land is unusable desert; 1 mark: (b) shows people per unit of productive land / real pressure.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two problems caused by high pressure on the cultivated land.
parts.answer: Farms are divided into very small plots between heirs; land is over-used, so soils lose fertility.
parts.working: 1 mark each: farm fragmentation; overuse/soil exhaustion; overuse of groundwater; landlessness/migration; low incomes.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the distribution of population along Pakistan's coastline.
parts.answer: Population is concentrated in Karachi in the east; most of the Makran coast of Balochistan is thinly populated, with small towns such as Gwadar, Pasni and Ormara.
parts.working: 1 mark: concentration at Karachi; 1 mark: sparse Makran coast with a few small fishing towns.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the Makran coast is much more thinly populated than the Karachi area. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Rainfall is very low and there are no large rivers, so fresh water for drinking and farming is scarce; it is far from the main cities and was poorly connected by road until recently, so few industries have developed; the hills behind the coast leave little flat land.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: water shortage; aridity/heat; remoteness and poor transport; few jobs other than fishing; rugged land; lack of services.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the population of Gwadar may increase in future.
parts.answer: The development of the deep-sea port is creating jobs and attracting investment.
parts.working: B1 port development/CPEC; new roads; industry/free zone; airport.

stem: In an illustrative example, a small town next to a new motorway interchange in Punjab grew from 18,000 to 41,000 people in 12 years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the town's population. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a new motorway interchange can attract people to live near it. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Factories and warehouses are built near the interchange because goods can be moved quickly to cities and ports, creating jobs; journeys to the nearest large city become faster, so people can live in the town and commute; service businesses such as petrol stations, restaurants and repair shops open to serve travellers.
parts.working: 1 mark for each way + 1 for development. Ways: industry/logistics jobs; commuting possible; roadside services; land/housing development; better access to markets for farmers.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Population and area of three districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (hypothetical figures):
District A: population 4.2 million, area 1,250 km²
District B: population 0.45 million, area 14,850 km²
District C: population 2.0 million, area 2,150 km²

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the population density of each district. Give your answers to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: District A is in the Peshawar valley and District B is in the high mountains of Chitral. Explain two reasons for the difference in their densities. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The Peshawar valley is flat, with fertile soils irrigated from the Kabul and Swat rivers, so it can support many farmers; Chitral is steep and cold, with long snowy winters and little flat land, so only narrow valley floors can be farmed; Peshawar is a large city with jobs and good transport links, while Chitral is remote.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: relief/flat land; climate (cold winters/short growing season); soils and irrigation; jobs and city; accessibility/transport.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A grid of 12 squares, each 1 km², shows population density (people per km²) over part of southern Punjab. Rows run north to south and columns west to east:
Row 1 (north): 120, 95, 4, 2
Row 2: 210, 160, 6, 0
Row 3 (south): 340, 180, 12, 3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean population density of the 12 squares. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Total = 1132; 1132 ÷ 12 = 94.3 people per km²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the data only, describe the pattern of population density across the area.
parts.answer: Densities are high in columns 1 and 2 (95–340 per km²) and very low in columns 3 and 4 (0–12 per km²); density increases from north to south in the western columns, with the highest value (340) in the south-west square.
parts.working: 1 mark: west dense / east sparse; 1 mark: north–south increase in west; 1 mark: use of figures (e.g. 340 maximum, 0 minimum).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The western half of the area is irrigated plain and the eastern half is desert. Suggest why the densities in the eastern squares are not all zero.
parts.answer: A few people live at wells or small oases, keeping livestock such as camels, goats and sheep, which can graze on sparse desert vegetation.
parts.working: 1 mark: water sources/wells/tobas; 1 mark: pastoral herding/livestock.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two cities in Pakistan whose growth is mainly due to human factors such as government, industry or trade.
parts.answer: Islamabad (government); Karachi (port and industry).
parts.working: 1 mark each for named city with a human reason implied, e.g. Islamabad, Karachi, Faisalabad, Gwadar, Sialkot.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Physical factors are more important than human factors in explaining the distribution of population in Pakistan.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: Physical: the Indus plain's flat land, fertile alluvium and river water explain the dense rural population of Punjab and Sindh, while deserts (Thar, Kharan) and high mountains are sparse. Human: cities such as Karachi, Lahore, Faisalabad and Islamabad have huge densities because of jobs, trade, government and transport; canal colonies were created by people, not nature. Judgement: physical factors set the broad pattern, but human factors now explain the highest densities and recent change.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed physical and human points with named Pakistani places and a supported judgement on the extent. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) on one side or simple points on both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points.

stem:
Share of Pakistan's population and area (illustrative, rounded, %):
Punjab: population 53, area 26
Balochistan: population 6, area 44

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each province, divide its share of the population by its share of the area. Give your answers to two decimal places.
parts.answer: Punjab: 53 ÷ 26 = 2.04; Balochistan: 6 ÷ 44 = 0.14.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what these results show about how population is distributed between the two provinces.
parts.answer: Punjab has about twice as many people as its area would suggest, while Balochistan has only about one-seventh, so population is crowded into Punjab and spread very thinly in Balochistan.
parts.working: 1 mark: Punjab ratio > 1 means more people than its share of land; 1 mark: Balochistan very low ratio = sparse/uneven distribution.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two difficulties of providing services such as schools and hospitals in Balochistan because of this distribution. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Villages are small and far apart, so each school or clinic serves only a few people and the cost per person is high; long distances over poor roads mean that teachers and doctors are unwilling to work in remote places and patients cannot reach hospitals quickly.
parts.working: 1 mark for each difficulty + 1 for development. Difficulties: high cost per person; long travel distances; staff unwilling to work in remote areas; poor roads; scattered/nomadic population; fewer votes/less political attention.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two diseases that childhood vaccination programmes in Pakistan protect against.
parts.answer: Polio; measles.
parts.working: 1 mark each: polio; measles; tuberculosis; diphtheria; tetanus; whooping cough; hepatitis B; pneumonia (pneumococcal); typhoid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two difficulties of vaccinating every child in remote areas of Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Villages are scattered in mountains and deserts, so teams must travel long distances, often on foot; vaccines must be kept cold, which is hard where there is no reliable electricity; some parents refuse because of rumours or mistrust; insecurity in some areas puts vaccination teams at risk.
parts.working: 1 mark for each difficulty + 1 for development. Difficulties: distance/terrain; cold chain; refusals and misinformation; insecurity; shortage of female health workers; nomadic/migrant families.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why many children in rural Pakistan leave school before finishing primary education.
parts.answer: They are needed to work on the farm or earn money; the nearest school is too far away.
parts.working: 1 mark each: poverty/child labour; distance; poor teaching/absent teachers; lack of girls' schools or female teachers; early marriage; cost of books/uniform.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the government could increase the number of children who complete primary school. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Give cash stipends to poor families whose children attend regularly, so the loss of a child's earnings is replaced; build more schools within walking distance, especially girls' schools with female teachers, so parents feel safe sending daughters; provide free books and meals to make attendance cheaper.
parts.working: 1 mark for each way + 1 for development. Ways: stipends/conditional cash transfers; more schools nearer villages; female teachers; free books/meals; better teacher training/attendance checks; enforcing compulsory education laws.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Human Development Index (HDI) combines three measures. State the three.
parts.answer: Life expectancy (health); education (years of schooling); income per person (GNI per capita).
parts.working: 1 mark each: life expectancy/health; education/schooling; income per head.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why income per person alone is not a good measure of a country's development. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: It is an average, so it hides inequality between rich and poor, and it does not show whether people are healthy or educated.
parts.working: 1 mark: hides inequality / average only; 1 mark: ignores health, education or quality of life.

stem: A primary school in a village in Balochistan has 186 boys and 124 girls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of pupils who are girls.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which more girls in the village could be encouraged to attend school.
parts.answer: Appoint female teachers; provide a boundary wall and toilets at the school.
parts.working: 1 mark each: female teachers; separate girls' school nearby; toilets/boundary wall; stipends for girls; transport; community awareness.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one benefit to a family when a daughter completes her education. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: She is more likely to understand health and nutrition, so her own children will be healthier.
parts.working: 1 mark benefit + 1 development: healthier children; can earn income; later marriage/smaller family; helps siblings learn.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two services provided by a Basic Health Unit (BHU) in rural Pakistan.
parts.answer: Vaccination of children; treatment of common illnesses.
parts.working: 1 mark each: vaccinations; treatment of minor illness; mother and child care; family planning advice; first aid; referral to hospitals.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which Lady Health Workers help to reduce deaths of mothers and babies. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: They visit women at home during pregnancy, check their health and encourage them to give birth with a trained attendant, so dangerous problems are spotted early; they teach mothers about breastfeeding, clean water and oral rehydration salts, which reduces deaths from diarrhoea in babies.
parts.working: 1 mark for each way + 1 for development. Ways: home visits/antenatal care; referral to skilled birth attendants; health education (hygiene, ORS, breastfeeding); family planning; vaccination support.

stem:
Life expectancy (years) and adult literacy rate (%) for four districts (hypothetical figures):
District P: 68, 72
District Q: 64, 55
District R: 61, 38
District S: 66, 63

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean life expectancy and the mean literacy rate of the four districts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship between life expectancy and literacy shown by the data.
parts.answer: As literacy rises, life expectancy also rises (a positive relationship): R has the lowest of both (38%, 61 years) and P the highest of both (72%, 68 years).
parts.working: 1 mark: positive relationship; 1 mark: data used in support.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why higher literacy can lead to longer life expectancy. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Literate people can read health advice and medicine labels and are more likely to seek treatment early, so fewer die from preventable illnesses.
parts.working: 1 mark reason + 1 development: understanding health information; better jobs/income; better child care by educated mothers; use of clinics.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, a village health centre recorded 420 cases of diarrhoea in the year before a water filtration plant was installed and 150 cases in the year after.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in cases of diarrhoea. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why clean water improves the health and development of a village. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Fewer people catch water-borne diseases such as diarrhoea and typhoid, so children grow better and miss less school; women and girls spend less time fetching water, so girls can attend school and women can earn money; families spend less on medicines and doctors.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: fewer diseases; better school attendance; time saved fetching water; lower health costs; higher productivity of workers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the number of cases did not fall to zero.
parts.answer: Some families still drink from the canal or other unsafe sources.
parts.working: B1 unsafe sources still used; poor sanitation/hygiene; contaminated food; storage containers dirty; plant not maintained.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative survey, 152 of 400 children under five in a district were found to be stunted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by stunting?
parts.answer: When a child is too short for his or her age because of long-term poor nutrition.
parts.working: B1 low height for age due to chronic undernutrition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the children who were stunted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two causes of child malnutrition in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Poor families cannot afford a varied diet with enough milk, eggs, meat and vegetables; repeated diarrhoea from unsafe water stops children absorbing food; mothers may be malnourished themselves, so babies are born small; lack of knowledge about breastfeeding and weaning foods.
parts.working: 1 mark for each cause + 1 for development. Causes: poverty/food prices; unsafe water and disease; maternal malnutrition; poor feeding practices; large families; food insecurity after floods/drought.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A development index (from 0 to 1) for four regions of a country (illustrative figures):
W: 0.70  X: 0.66  Y: 0.61  Z: 0.48

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the highest and lowest index values, and express the lowest as a percentage of the highest. Give the percentage to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Region Z is a large, thinly populated province with a dry climate. Explain two reasons why its development index is low. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Villages are scattered over a huge area, so schools and hospitals are far apart and expensive to provide; the dry climate limits farming, so many people have low incomes; poor roads make it hard to reach markets and services; insecurity has discouraged investment.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: scattered population/distance; aridity and limited farming; poor infrastructure; few industries/jobs; insecurity; shortage of teachers and doctors.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions that could reduce the gap between region Z and the other regions.
parts.answer: Build roads to connect remote areas; give extra funding for schools and clinics in the region.
parts.working: 1 mark each: infrastructure; extra funds/NFC share; mobile clinics/schools; local recruitment of teachers/health workers; develop mineral or port industries with local jobs.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two examples of primary health care.
parts.answer: Vaccination; clean water and sanitation education.
parts.working: 1 mark each: vaccinations; health education; mother and child care; family planning; basic treatment at BHUs; clean water/sanitation; nutrition programmes.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read the two views below.
View A: The government should spend more on large hospitals in cities.
View B: The government should spend more on primary health care in villages.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: View A: large hospitals provide specialist care (surgery, cancer, heart treatment) and train doctors; cities have large populations. But they are far from most rural people and costly. View B: most deaths of children and mothers are from preventable causes (diarrhoea, pneumonia, childbirth complications) that cheap local care can prevent; a majority of Pakistanis live in rural areas; Lady Health Workers and BHUs reach many people at low cost. Judgement, e.g. B gives more health gain per rupee, but referral hospitals are still needed.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both views with Pakistani examples and a supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one view or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points.

stem: A rural district (hypothetical figures) has 54,000 children of primary-school age, 1,080 primary teachers and 240 primary schools.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of children per teacher and the number of children per school.
parts.answer: 54,000 ÷ 1,080 = 50 children per teacher; 54,000 ÷ 240 = 225 children per school.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why building more schools may not, on its own, raise literacy in this district. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: If there are not enough trained teachers, classes stay very large or teachers are absent, so children learn little even in a new building; poor families may still keep children at home to work, so enrolment does not rise; without books, electricity or toilets, especially for girls, attendance remains low.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: shortage/quality of teachers; poverty/child labour; lack of facilities; cultural barriers to girls' education; language of teaching; 'ghost schools'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one measure, other than building schools, that would improve learning in the district.
parts.answer: Train and recruit more teachers, especially women from the local area, so that class sizes fall and girls attend.
parts.working: 1 mark measure + 1 development: teacher training/recruitment; stipends; adult literacy centres; free books; monitoring of teacher attendance; mother-tongue teaching.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Average number of children per woman by mother's level of education (illustrative figures):
No education 4.2  Primary 3.6  Secondary 3.0  Higher 2.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how much lower, as a percentage, the fertility rate of women with higher education is than that of women with no education. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown by the data.
parts.answer: The more education a woman has, the fewer children she has on average (a negative relationship).
parts.working: B1 inverse/negative relationship.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons for this relationship. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Women who stay in education longer marry later, so they have fewer years in which to have children; educated women are more likely to work and to know about and use family planning; they understand child health, so their children survive and they do not need many births.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: later marriage; knowledge/use of contraception; paid work/career; better child survival; more say in family decisions; urban residence.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why these data alone do not prove that education causes lower fertility.
parts.answer: Educated women are also more likely to live in cities and be richer, and these factors also reduce fertility.
parts.working: B1 other factors (income, urban residence) linked to both; correlation is not causation.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by fog?
parts.answer: A cloud of tiny water droplets at ground level that reduces visibility to less than 1 km.
parts.working: B1 water droplets/cloud near the ground reducing visibility.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the months when dense fog is most common in the plains of Punjab.
parts.answer: December and January (the cold season).
parts.working: B1 December–January (allow mid-November to February).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which dense winter fog affects transport in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Visibility falls to a few metres, so sections of motorways are closed and journeys are delayed; road accidents and multi-vehicle collisions increase when drivers cannot see; flights at Lahore and other airports are delayed or cancelled; trains run slowly and late.
parts.working: 1 mark for each effect + 1 for development. Effects: motorway closures; accidents; flight delays/cancellations; train delays; goods delivered late, raising costs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by a flash flood?
parts.answer: A sudden, short-lived flood that rises very quickly after intense rain, usually in a small, steep catchment.
parts.working: B1 sudden/rapid flood after heavy rain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why hill torrents flowing from the Koh-e-Suleman range often cause flash floods in the Dera Ghazi Khan area. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Monsoon storms bring very heavy rain in a short time over the hills; the slopes are steep and rocky with little vegetation or soil, so water runs off instead of soaking in and reaches the plain within hours; the torrents spread out over flat land where villages and fields lie.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: intense monsoon rain; steep slopes; bare rock/thin soils/little vegetation; deforestation/overgrazing; flat plain below with settlements; no storage dams.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which the water of hill torrents is used by farmers.
parts.answer: It is diverted into embanked fields to irrigate crops (rod kohi farming).
parts.working: B1 rod kohi/spate irrigation of fields; filling ponds for livestock.

stem:
Average number of days a year with a maximum temperature above 45 °C at a station in upper Sindh (illustrative figures):
1990s: 12   2000s: 15   2010s: 19   2020–24: 23

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the average number of very hot days from the 1990s to 2020–24. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the trend shown by the data.
parts.answer: The number of very hot days has increased steadily in every period, from 12 to 23 a year.
parts.working: B1 steady increase with figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two effects of more frequent extreme heat on farming in the area. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Wheat ripens too early in very hot spring weather, so grains are small and yields fall; livestock suffer heat stress, so milk production falls and some animals die; crops need more irrigation water because evaporation is higher, increasing pressure on canals and groundwater.
parts.working: 1 mark for each effect + 1 for development. Effects: lower crop yields/early ripening; heat stress in livestock/poultry; more water needed; farm workers cannot work in the heat; crop failure.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how heavy rain or rapid snowmelt can trigger landslides on the slopes beside the Karakoram Highway. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Rain or meltwater soaks into loose rock and soil, making it heavier and reducing the friction holding it on the steep slope, so it slides; water flowing over the surface washes away material at the foot of slopes that were already cut back for the road, so the slope above collapses.
parts.working: 1 mark for each process point + 1 for development, for two. Points: saturation adds weight; water lubricates/reduces friction; undercutting by rivers or road cutting; weak, loose rock and steep slopes; earthquakes in the region add to instability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways of reducing the danger of landslides to traffic on mountain roads.
parts.answer: Build retaining walls and nets on the most dangerous slopes; close the road and warn travellers during very heavy rain.
parts.working: 1 mark each: retaining walls; rock netting/rock bolts; drainage channels on slopes; planting trees; tunnels/realignment; warning systems and road closures; rapid clearance teams.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one economic effect of the highway being blocked by a landslide for several days.
parts.answer: Trade with China and the movement of goods to and from Gilgit-Baltistan are delayed, raising costs.
parts.working: B1 trade delays; tourists stranded/cancel trips; food and fuel shortages in valleys; perishable produce spoils.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an illustrative example, 38% of the 2.4 million people of a district were affected by a flood. Calculate the number of people affected.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read the two views below.
View A: The best way to reduce deaths from floods and other climate hazards in Pakistan is to improve early warning systems.
View B: The best way to reduce deaths from floods and other climate hazards in Pakistan is to build stronger defences, such as embankments and flood-resistant buildings.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: View A: forecasts and warnings by radio, mobile phone and mosques give time to evacuate people and animals, are relatively cheap and work for many hazards (floods, cyclones, heatwaves); but warnings fail if people have nowhere to go or do not trust them. View B: embankments, raised houses and shelters protect property as well as lives, and are vital where warning time is short (flash floods); but they are expensive, can fail in extreme floods and need maintenance. Judgement: warnings save most lives quickly, but defences and shelters are needed for warnings to work.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both sides/views, Pakistani examples and a clear, supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one side or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points only.

stem:
Climate data for a station in lower Sindh (rounded, illustrative figures):
Mean temperature (°C): Jan 17, Feb 20, Mar 25, Apr 30, May 33, Jun 33, Jul 31, Aug 30, Sep 30, Oct 28, Nov 23, Dec 18
Rainfall (mm): Jan 3, Feb 4, Mar 4, Apr 2, May 3, Jun 10, Jul 55, Aug 60, Sep 20, Oct 3, Nov 2, Dec 3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the wettest month.
parts.answer: August (60 mm)
parts.working: B1 August.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total annual rainfall.
parts.answer: 169 mm
parts.working: M1 adding all twelve months; A1 169 mm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of months with less than 5 mm of rain.
parts.answer: 8 months (January–May and October–December)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain two ways in which this climate makes farming difficult without irrigation. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Annual rainfall is very low (169 mm), so there is not enough water for crops to grow; most months are almost dry, so there is no rain during the rabi season; very high temperatures (30 °C or more from April to September) cause rapid evaporation, drying the soil.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point + 1 for development, using the data. Points: low total rainfall; long dry season; rain concentrated in two months and unreliable; high temperatures/evaporation; salts left in soil.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each event, state the season of Pakistan's climate in which it usually happens:
(i) hot, dusty winds blow across the plains of Punjab
(ii) snow falls in the hills of northern Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
(iii) heavy thunderstorms flood the streets of Lahore
(iv) clear skies and falling temperatures after the rains have ended
parts.answer: (i) hot season (April–June, pre-monsoon); (ii) cold season (December–March); (iii) monsoon/rainy season (July–September); (iv) retreating monsoon / post-monsoon season (October–November).
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why skies are mostly clear across Pakistan in October and November. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The land cools and high pressure develops over the subcontinent, so dry winds blow outwards from the land and the moist monsoon air has withdrawn.
parts.working: 1 mark: monsoon winds retreat/withdraw; 1 mark: development, e.g. high pressure over cooling land, dry offshore winds, no moisture source.

stem:
Climate data for a valley-floor station at about 1,500 m in Gilgit-Baltistan (rounded, illustrative figures):
Mean temperature (°C): Jan 2, Feb 5, Mar 11, Apr 16, May 21, Jun 26, Jul 28, Aug 27, Sep 22, Oct 16, Nov 9, Dec 3
Precipitation (mm): Jan 4, Feb 7, Mar 18, Apr 22, May 20, Jun 8, Jul 12, Aug 15, Sep 8, Oct 6, Nov 3, Dec 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual range of temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total annual rainfall and the percentage that falls in March, April and May. Give the percentage to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why this valley floor receives so little rain, although it is surrounded by high mountains. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The valley lies in a rain shadow: moist air is forced to rise and drop its rain on the outer ranges and southern slopes before it reaches the valley, so the air descending into the valley is dry; it is far from the sea and the monsoon winds are weak by the time they reach the far north; descending air warms and clouds evaporate.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: rain shadow of surrounding ranges; distance from the sea/monsoon barely reaches; descending dry air; depressions lose moisture over mountains to the west.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Data for a hill station at about 2,250 m in the Galiyat and for a city on the Punjab plains (rounded, illustrative figures):
Hill station: June mean temperature 20 °C, annual rainfall 1,600 mm
Plains city: June mean temperature 35 °C, annual rainfall 190 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how much cooler the hill station is than the plains city in June.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more rain the hill station receives than the plains city. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the climate of hill stations such as those in the Galiyat attracts visitors from the plains. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: In June the hill station is about 15 °C cooler, so families escape the extreme heat of the plains during school holidays; monsoon rain and cool air keep forests green and the scenery attractive; winter snowfall attracts visitors who rarely see snow.
parts.working: 1 mark for each way + 1 for development, ideally using the data. Ways: cool summers; escape from heatwaves; green forests/scenery; winter snow; clean air.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one problem that the climate causes for the hill station in winter.
parts.answer: Heavy snowfall blocks roads, so the town can be cut off and visitors may become stranded.
parts.working: 1 mark problem + 1 development: blocked roads; landslides; cold/fuel demand causing deforestation; burst pipes; fewer visitors and income.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Monthly precipitation (mm) at a station in Pakistan (rounded, illustrative figures):
Jan 60, Feb 75, Mar 80, Apr 45, May 25, Jun 15, Jul 50, Aug 45, Sep 15, Oct 10, Nov 15, Dec 35

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the annual precipitation that falls (i) from December to March and (ii) from July to September. Give your answers to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using your answers, suggest in which part of Pakistan this station is located. Give a reason.
parts.answer: The north-west (for example the Peshawar valley or northern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa), because more than half of the precipitation comes in winter and early spring from western depressions, while the monsoon contributes less than a quarter.
parts.working: 1 mark: north-west/KP/northern Balochistan; 1 mark: reason linked to winter maximum from western depressions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the monsoon brings less rain to this station than to places in north-eastern Punjab. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The monsoon winds come from the east and south-east and lose much of their moisture over the plains and the foothills of the Himalayas before reaching the north-west.
parts.working: 1 mark: monsoon arrives from the east/Bay of Bengal; 1 mark: moisture lost on the way/distance from source.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two features of the climate of the arid (desert) region of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Very low and unreliable rainfall, usually under 250 mm a year; very hot summers with maximum temperatures above 45 °C and a large daily range of temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark each: low/unreliable rainfall; very hot summers; mild/cool winters; large daily range; dust storms; low humidity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'The highland climate region of northern Pakistan is more difficult for people to live in than the arid region of southern Pakistan.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: Highland: long, very cold winters with heavy snow, short growing season so often only one crop a year, roads blocked by snow and landslides, risk of avalanches and GLOFs; but there is plentiful water from snowmelt and glaciers, and cool summers. Arid: extreme heat, droughts and very little water for drinking and crops, so people depend on wells, canals or seasonal migration; but winters are mild and where canals reach, farming is possible all year. Judgement on the extent, e.g. the arid region is harder because water shortage is more limiting, or the highlands are harder because winter isolation is severe.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both sides/views, Pakistani examples and a clear, supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one side or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two seas or bays from which most of the moisture of Pakistan's summer monsoon comes.
parts.answer: The Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how differences in heating between land and sea cause the summer monsoon winds to blow towards Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: In summer the land heats up much faster than the sea, so the air over the land rises and an area of low pressure forms over the plains of Pakistan and northern India; the sea stays cooler, with higher pressure over it, so moist air is drawn in from the sea towards the low pressure over the land, bringing rain.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point + 1 for development, for two. Points: land heats faster than sea; low pressure over land (rising air); higher pressure over sea; wind blows from high to low pressure; air is moist from crossing the sea.

stem:
Average rainfall from December to March at three places (rounded, illustrative figures):
Place A (northern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa): 210 mm
Place B (central Punjab): 95 mm
Place C (Sindh coast): 25 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more winter rain Place A receives than Place C. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the direction from which western depressions enter Pakistan.
parts.answer: From the west (from Iran and Afghanistan, originating over the Mediterranean region).
parts.working: B1 west/north-west.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why winter rainfall decreases from Place A to Place C. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Western depressions enter Pakistan from the west and north-west, so the north-west receives them first while they still hold most of their moisture; the mountains of the north-west force the air to rise, giving extra relief rain and snow; the depressions weaken as they move south-east, and the southern coast is too far south of their usual track.
