parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: track of depressions across the north; moisture lost as they move; relief uplift in the north-west mountains; south lies outside the path of most depressions.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
A school in Sialkot recorded daily rainfall (mm) for one week in July:
Day 1: 0, Day 2: 12, Day 3: 34, Day 4: 0, Day 5: 6, Day 6: 51, Day 7: 9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the instrument used to measure rainfall.
parts.answer: A rain gauge.
parts.working: B1 rain gauge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total rainfall for the week and the mean daily rainfall. Give the mean to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Total = 112 mm; mean = 112 ÷ 7 = 16.0 mm per day

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two rules for placing the instrument in the school grounds so that readings are accurate.
parts.answer: Place it in an open space away from trees and buildings; set it into the ground with its rim about 30 cm above the surface so that rain does not splash in.
parts.working: 1 mark each: open site away from trees/buildings/overhangs; rim above ground level to avoid splash; on level ground; fixed firmly; read at the same time each day.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why rain on Day 6 may have been heavy but brief.
parts.answer: It came from a convectional thunderstorm in the afternoon after strong heating.
parts.working: B1 convectional storm/thunderstorm; monsoon downpour; cloudburst.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Number of days after 1 June on which the monsoon rains began at a station in Punjab in six years (illustrative figures):
28, 35, 31, 44, 26, 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean onset day. Give the date this represents.
parts.answer: (28 + 35 + 31 + 44 + 26 + 40) ÷ 6 = 34 days after 1 June, which is 5 July.
parts.working: B1 34; B1 5 July (allow 4/5 July).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the earliest and latest onset.
parts.working: B1 18 days.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a late start to the monsoon affects farmers in Punjab. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Rice seedlings need standing water for transplanting, so farmers must delay planting or pump expensive groundwater; cotton and other kharif crops suffer in the extreme heat of June without rain, lowering yields; reservoirs and canals receive less water, so supplies are cut; fodder for animals runs short.
parts.working: 1 mark for each effect + 1 for development. Effects: delayed sowing/transplanting; extra pumping costs; heat stress on crops; lower canal supplies; fodder shortage; later harvest delays rabi sowing.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Average annual precipitation at two places at similar heights on either side of a range in northern Pakistan (rounded, illustrative figures):
Windward (south-facing) slope: 1,400 mm
Valley on the far (northern) side: 140 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of rainfall on the windward slope to rainfall in the valley, in the form n : 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is meant by a rain shadow?
parts.answer: An area on the sheltered (leeward) side of mountains that receives little rain.
parts.working: B1 dry area on the leeward side of high ground.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a rain shadow forms on the far side of a mountain range. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Moist air is forced to rise over the windward side of the range, so it cools, water vapour condenses and most of the moisture falls as rain or snow on the windward slopes; the air then descends on the leeward side, warming as it sinks, so clouds evaporate and little rain falls.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point + 1 for development, for two stages. Points: air forced to rise; cooling and condensation; rain on windward slope; air descends and warms on leeward side; dry air gives little rain.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, 180 mm of rain fell on a part of Lahore in 6 hours during a monsoon storm. The drains there can carry away rain falling at up to 15 mm per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of rainfall in mm per hour.
parts.answer: 180 ÷ 6 = 30 mm per hour
parts.working: B1 30 mm per hour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater this rate is than the drainage capacity.
parts.answer: 30 ÷ 15 = 2 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons, apart from the amount of rain, why such downpours cause flooding in the streets of Lahore. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Most of the city is covered by concrete and tarmac, so rain cannot soak into the ground and runs straight into the streets; drains and nullahs are often blocked with rubbish and silt, so water backs up; low-lying areas and underpasses collect water; power cuts stop pumping stations.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: impermeable surfaces; blocked/undersized drains; encroachment on drains; low-lying areas/underpasses; pumping failures; loss of green space.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Monsoon rainfall at a station in Punjab as a percentage of the long-term normal, for eight years (illustrative figures):
Year 1: 112, Year 2: 78, Year 3: 95, Year 4: 61, Year 5: 130, Year 6: 88, Year 7: 70, Year 8: 105

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean of the eight values.
parts.answer: 739 ÷ 8 = 92.4% of normal

parts.label: b
parts.text: A year with less than 75% of normal monsoon rainfall is classed as a deficient year. State how many years were deficient.
parts.answer: 2 (Year 4: 61% and Year 7: 70%)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why monsoon rainfall in Pakistan varies so much from year to year. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Pakistan lies at the western, drier edge of the monsoon, so a small change in the path or strength of the monsoon winds makes a big difference to rainfall; the monsoon may arrive late or retreat early, shortening the rainy season; long breaks in the monsoon can occur when the rain-bearing systems stay further east; changes in sea temperatures far away (such as in the Pacific) can weaken or strengthen the monsoon.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: position at the edge of the monsoon; variable onset/withdrawal; breaks in the monsoon; strength/track of monsoon depressions; ocean temperature patterns (e.g. El Niño); climate change.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one reason why a deficient monsoon also affects people in cities.
parts.answer: Reservoirs such as Tarbela and Mangla fill less, so less hydroelectricity is generated and power cuts increase in cities.
parts.working: 1 mark effect + 1 development: less HEP/load-shedding; water supply shortages; higher food prices; more heat.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two rabi crops that benefit from winter rain in the rain-fed (barani) areas of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Wheat; gram (chickpea).
parts.working: 1 mark each: wheat; gram; barley; mustard/rapeseed; lentils.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Western depressions are more important than the monsoon for farming in Pakistan.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: For: winter rain from western depressions waters wheat, Pakistan's main food crop, in barani areas of Potwar and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; snowfall on the mountains melts in spring and summer to feed rivers and canals; it is gentler rain that soaks in. Against: the monsoon gives far more rain to most of the plains, fills Tarbela and Mangla, supports kharif crops such as rice, cotton and sugar cane and recharges groundwater; but it also brings floods. Judgement on the extent: the monsoon provides more water overall, but western depressions are vital for wheat and snowmelt.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both sides/views, Pakistani examples and a clear, supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one side or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Air near the ground is at 38 °C and cools by about 10 °C for every 1,000 m it rises. Clouds form when it has cooled to 24 °C. Calculate the height at which clouds begin to form.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why violent thunderstorms with strong winds and hail are common over the plains of Punjab in late spring and early summer. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The ground heats very strongly, so air near the surface becomes very warm and rises quickly in powerful convection currents; when moisture is present the rising air forms tall cumulonimbus clouds reaching high, very cold levels, where ice forms and grows into hailstones; strong downdrafts from the clouds cause gusty winds and dust storms.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point + 1 for development, for two. Points: intense surface heating; strong rising air/convection; tall cumulonimbus clouds; freezing upper levels produce hail; downdrafts give strong winds/dust storms; moist air arriving before the monsoon.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which such storms can damage crops.
parts.answer: Hail flattens and breaks ripening wheat, so grain is lost before harvest.
parts.working: B1 hail/strong winds flatten (lodge) crops; mango/fruit falls; heavy rain at harvest spoils grain.

stem: On a summer night in Karachi the temperature in the city centre was 31 °C, while in farmland 30 km outside the city it was 27 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the night-time temperatures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is meant by an urban heat island?
parts.answer: A city area that is warmer than the surrounding countryside, especially at night.
parts.working: B1 city warmer than surrounding rural areas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the city centre stays warmer at night. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Concrete, brick and tarmac absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night; traffic, air conditioners and factories give off extra heat; there are few trees and parks, so less water evaporates to cool the air; tall buildings trap heat and slow the wind.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: heat stored in building materials; waste heat from vehicles/ACs/industry; lack of vegetation/water; buildings reduce wind; pollution layer traps heat.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Approximate January mean temperatures (°C, rounded): Karachi 19, Lahore 13, Peshawar 11, Quetta 4, Gilgit 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the warmest and the coldest place in January.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two factors that help to explain the differences in the table.
parts.answer: Latitude; altitude.
parts.working: 1 mark each: latitude; altitude; distance from the sea.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why Karachi is warmer than Lahore in January. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Karachi is further south (closer to the Equator), so the winter sun is higher in the sky; it is on the coast, where the sea, which keeps its heat, warms the air in winter.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reason + 1 for development: lower latitude/higher sun angle; maritime influence of the warm sea; less exposed to cold northern air.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by the aspect of a slope?
parts.answer: The direction that a slope faces.
parts.working: B1 direction faced by a slope.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why south-facing slopes in the northern mountains of Pakistan are warmer than north-facing slopes. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: In the northern hemisphere the sun is in the southern part of the sky, so south-facing slopes receive the sun's rays more directly and for longer each day.
parts.working: 1 mark: sun in the south/receive more direct sunlight; 1 mark: more hours of sunshine/shade on north-facing slopes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which villagers in the northern mountains make use of warmer south-facing slopes. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: They build houses on sunny slopes, so homes stay warmer in the cold winters and less fuelwood is needed; they grow crops and fruit trees such as apricots there, because snow melts earlier and the growing season is longer.
parts.working: 1 mark for each use + 1 for development. Uses: settlements; crops/orchards; earlier snowmelt for grazing; drying fruit and fodder in the sun.

stem: A valley town in the northern mountains is at 1,500 m and has a mean July temperature of 25 °C. On the same days the mean temperature at a mountain pass above the town is 6.8 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using a fall of 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m, calculate the height of the pass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why temperatures in the high mountains can change greatly between day and night. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The air at high altitude is thin and dry, so it holds little heat and absorbs little of the outgoing radiation; by day strong sunshine quickly warms the ground, but at night the heat escapes rapidly to space through the clear, thin air, so temperatures fall sharply.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point + 1 for development, for two. Points: thin air; low water vapour/clear skies; intense daytime sunshine; rapid heat loss at night; little vegetation/bare rock.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Temperatures on the same day in May (rounded, illustrative figures):
A desert town in Cholistan: maximum 45 °C, minimum 25 °C
A coastal town in Sindh: maximum 34 °C, minimum 28 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the daily range of temperature at each place.
parts.answer: Desert town: 45 − 25 = 20 °C; coastal town: 34 − 28 = 6 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the daily range is much larger in the desert than on the coast. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The air in the desert is very dry and the skies are clear, so the ground heats strongly by day and loses heat quickly at night; sand and bare rock heat and cool quickly, while the sea heats and cools slowly and keeps the coastal air at a steady temperature; humid coastal air and sea breezes stop temperatures rising or falling as much.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: dry air/clear skies; sand heats and cools quickly; little vegetation; sea's moderating effect; humidity/cloud on the coast; sea breezes.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the hot, dry wind that raises temperatures on the plains in May and June.
parts.answer: The loo.
parts.working: B1 loo.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which winds or mountain barriers affect winter temperatures in Pakistan. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The high mountains of the north block much of the very cold air from Central Asia, so the plains have milder winters than places at similar latitudes further north; cold winds that do come down from the snow-covered mountains after western depressions cause cold spells in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Punjab; on the coast, winds from the sea keep winter temperatures mild.
parts.working: 1 mark for each way + 1 for development. Ways: mountain barrier against Central Asian cold air; cold northerly winds after depressions; cold air drainage into valleys; sea winds moderating coastal temperatures; dry winds raising temperatures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which sea breezes affect summer temperatures in Karachi.
parts.answer: They keep afternoon temperatures lower than inland.
parts.working: B1 cool/moderate afternoon temperatures; raise humidity.

stem: The angle of the noon sun above the horizon on 21 June can be found using 90 − (latitude − 23.5), and on 21 December using 90 − (latitude + 23.5). Pakistan stretches from about 24 °N to about 37 °N.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the noon sun angle on 21 June at 25 °N and at 36 °N.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the noon sun angle on 21 December at 36 °N.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a low sun angle gives lower temperatures. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: When the sun is low, the same amount of sunlight is spread over a larger area of ground, so each square metre receives less heat; the rays also pass through a greater thickness of atmosphere, so more energy is absorbed or reflected before reaching the ground; days are also shorter in winter.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point + 1 for development, for two. Points: energy spread over larger area; longer path through atmosphere; shorter days; more reflection.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Temperatures measured at different heights above a Punjab city at dawn on a calm, clear day in December (illustrative figures):
0 m: 6 °C
200 m: 9 °C
400 m: 8 °C
600 m: 6.5 °C
800 m: 5 °C

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the data, state the height range in which temperature increases with height.
parts.answer: Between the ground (0 m) and 200 m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate at which temperature falls between 200 m and 800 m, in °C per 1,000 m.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how a temperature inversion like this forms over the Punjab plains on calm, clear winter nights. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: With clear skies the ground loses heat rapidly by radiation at night, so the air in contact with it is chilled; with calm winds this cold, dense air stays near the ground beneath warmer air above, so temperature rises with height for the first few hundred metres.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point + 1 for development, for two. Points: clear skies → rapid radiation cooling; ground cools air above it; calm conditions/no mixing; cold dense air settles at the surface; long winter nights.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why inversions make smog worse in cities such as Lahore.
parts.answer: The warm layer above acts as a lid, so smoke and dust cannot rise and disperse and build up near the ground.
parts.working: B1 inversion traps pollutants near the ground.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In a valley in Gilgit-Baltistan, the valley floor is at 1,200 m and has a July mean temperature of 26 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A crop needs a July mean temperature of at least 18 °C. Using a fall of 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m, calculate the highest altitude at which it can be grown. Give your answer to the nearest 10 m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why farmers in the valley may grow the crop above your calculated height on some slopes.
parts.answer: South-facing slopes receive more direct sunshine, so they are warmer than the average temperature for their height.
parts.working: 1 mark: aspect/sunny slopes or sheltered sites; 1 mark: development – warmer than the lapse-rate estimate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two ways in which altitude limits farming in the northern mountains. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Temperatures fall with height, so the growing season is short and often only one crop can be grown a year; at high levels frost and snow cover the ground for many months, so only summer pastures can be used.
parts.working: 1 mark for each limit and 1 mark for development of either (max 3). Limits: short growing season; frost/snow; thin soils; steep slopes.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Mean temperatures (°C) for two stations (rounded, illustrative figures):
Station M (Balochistan plateau, about 1,600 m): coldest month 4, hottest month 26
Station N (Sindh coast): coldest month 19, hottest month 31

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual range of temperature at each station.
parts.answer: Station M: 26 − 4 = 22 °C; Station N: 31 − 19 = 12 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Altitude is the most important factor affecting temperatures in Pakistan.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: For: temperature falls by about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m, so the northern mountains and Balochistan plateau (e.g. Quetta, Gilgit) are far colder than the plains, with snow in winter and cool summers; hill stations are much cooler than nearby plains. Against: latitude makes the south warmer in winter; distance from the sea gives inland places such as Jacobabad and Station M large ranges, while the coast (Karachi) stays mild, as Station N shows; cloud, winds (loo), aspect and urban heat islands also matter. Judgement on the extent: altitude explains the biggest differences, but distance from the sea explains the ranges on the plains.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both sides/views, Pakistani examples and a clear, supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one side or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points only.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two diseases that can be caught from drinking contaminated water.
parts.answer: Cholera; typhoid.
parts.working: 1 mark each: diarrhoea; cholera; typhoid; hepatitis A or E; dysentery; polio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which households can make their drinking water safer. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Boiling water for several minutes kills bacteria and other germs; filtering through a cloth or ceramic filter removes dirt and some germs; adding chlorine tablets disinfects stored water; keeping water in clean, covered containers stops it being contaminated again.
parts.working: 1 mark for each method + 1 for development. Methods: boiling; filtering; chlorination; solar disinfection; clean covered storage; using a community filtration plant.

stem: In an illustrative example, a city uses 500 million litres of water a day. Industry produces waste water equal to 30% of this, and 90% of the industrial waste water is released without treatment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of industrial waste water produced each day, and the volume that is not treated.
parts.answer: Industrial: 500 × 30% = 150 million litres; untreated: 150 × 90% = 135 million litres
parts.working: B1 150 million litres; B1 135 million litres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects of untreated waste water from tanneries, such as those around Kasur, on the local area. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Tannery waste contains chromium and other chemicals, which seep into groundwater, so hand-pump water becomes unsafe and causes skin and stomach diseases; waste channels carry polluted water onto fields, so crops and soil are contaminated; drains and rivers become dark and smelly, killing fish.
parts.working: 1 mark for each effect + 1 for development. Effects: groundwater contamination (chromium); illness (skin, kidney, stomach); polluted crops/soils; fish deaths/river pollution; bad smell, lower quality of life.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways of reducing this pollution.
parts.answer: Build a combined effluent treatment plant for the tanneries; fine factories that release untreated waste.
parts.working: 1 mark each: treatment plants (individual or combined); enforce environmental laws/fines; cleaner tanning methods/chrome recovery; relocate tanneries to an industrial estate with treatment; monitoring.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, a coastal town in Balochistan needs 12 million gallons of water a day. A desalination plant supplies 5 million gallons a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by desalination?
parts.answer: Removing salt from seawater (or brackish water) to make fresh water.
parts.working: B1 removing salt from sea/brackish water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the town's daily needs met by the plant. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why desalination provides only a small part of Pakistan's water supply. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Desalination plants use large amounts of energy, and electricity in Pakistan is expensive and often in short supply, so the water is costly; the plants are expensive to build and maintain; they can only serve places near the sea, such as Karachi and Gwadar, and the very salty waste (brine) must be disposed of without harming marine life.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: high energy use/cost; high building and maintenance costs; only practical on the coast; brine disposal; breakdowns/lack of skilled staff.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, a town of 250,000 people receives 30 million litres of piped water a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average amount of water supplied per person per day.
parts.answer: 30,000,000 ÷ 250,000 = 120 litres per person per day

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Reducing water pollution is more important than increasing the amount of water supplied for improving health in Pakistan's cities.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: For: much illness in cities comes from contaminated water – sewage leaking into supply pipes, untreated industrial waste and polluted groundwater – so cleaning water and treating sewage would directly reduce diarrhoea, typhoid and hepatitis; more water that is still dirty would not help. Against: many poor areas get too little water, so people buy from tankers or use unsafe sources; enough water is needed for hygiene (washing hands, sanitation) which also prevents disease; supply and quality must be improved together. Judgement on the extent.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both sides/views, Pakistani examples and a clear, supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one side or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points only.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by barani farming?
parts.answer: Farming that depends on rainfall, without irrigation.
parts.working: B1 rain-fed farming.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how rod kohi (hill-torrent) irrigation works in areas such as Dera Ismail Khan and Dera Ghazi Khan.
parts.answer: When heavy rain falls in the hills, floodwater rushes down the torrent beds; farmers build earth embankments and channels to divert this water onto fields surrounded by bunds; the water soaks into the soil, which then stores enough moisture to grow a crop such as wheat or gram.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: depends on flash floods from the hills; water diverted by earth embankments/channels; fields enclosed by bunds; water soaks in/stored in the soil; crops sown afterwards; communal sharing of water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one disadvantage of rod kohi irrigation.
parts.answer: The supply is unreliable because it depends on irregular rainstorms.
parts.working: B1 unreliable/irregular floods; embankments washed away; too much or too little water; no control over timing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put these parts of the canal irrigation system in order, starting from the river: watercourse (khal), barrage, distributary, main canal, branch canal.
parts.answer: Barrage → main canal → branch canal → distributary → watercourse (khal)
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark with one pair reversed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is meant by warabandi?
parts.answer: A rotation system in which each farmer on a watercourse receives canal water for a fixed time on a fixed day, in proportion to the size of the land.
parts.working: 1 mark: rotation/turn system for sharing water; 1 mark: fixed time per farmer based on land area.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why farmers at the tail end of a watercourse often receive less water than they are entitled to. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Water seeps into the ground and evaporates along the earth channel, and farmers near the head may take extra water, so less is left by the time it reaches the tail.
parts.working: 1 mark reason + 1 development: seepage/evaporation losses; water theft/illegal outlets at the head; poorly maintained channels.

stem: In an illustrative example, a wheat field in Punjab used 1,050 mm of irrigation water in a season before it was laser levelled, and 800 mm after.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of water saved by laser levelling. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 1 mm of water over 1 hectare is 10 m³. Calculate the volume of water saved per hectare.
parts.answer: 250 mm × 10 = 2,500 m³ per hectare

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two benefits to farmers of laser levelling their fields. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Water spreads evenly across a level field, so less is needed and the tube-well pumping bill falls; all plants receive the same amount of water, so the crop grows evenly and yields rise; low patches no longer stay waterlogged, reducing salinity.
parts.working: 1 mark for each benefit + 1 for development. Benefits: water saving; lower fuel/electricity costs; even crop growth/higher yields; less waterlogging and salinity; faster irrigation; better fertiliser use.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, a diesel tube well uses 4 litres of diesel per hour. Diesel costs Rs 280 per litre and the pump runs for 600 hours in a season.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of diesel for one season.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages to farmers of changing to a solar-powered tube well. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: There is no fuel to buy after the panels are installed, so running costs are very low; the pump works during load-shedding because it does not depend on the grid; there is no diesel smoke and fewer engine repairs.
parts.working: 1 mark for each advantage + 1 for development. Advantages: low running costs; independent of grid/load-shedding; no fuel transport; clean/no pollution; less maintenance; reliable in sunny weather.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the spread of solar tube wells could make groundwater problems worse.
parts.answer: Because pumping is almost free, farmers may run pumps all day and take more water than is replaced by recharge, so the water table falls faster.
parts.working: 1 mark: very cheap pumping encourages over-pumping; 1 mark: water table falls / wells dry / saline water drawn in.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Illustrative figures for one hectare of land in central Punjab:
Rice: water used 12,000 m³, yield 3,000 kg
Wheat: water used 4,500 m³, yield 3,000 kg
(1 m³ = 1,000 litres)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the litres of water used to produce 1 kg of each crop.
parts.answer: Rice: 12,000 m³ ÷ 3,000 kg = 4 m³ = 4,000 litres per kg; wheat: 4,500 ÷ 3,000 = 1.5 m³ = 1,500 litres per kg.
parts.working: B1 4,000 litres; B1 1,500 litres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems of growing rice in an area where the water table is falling. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Rice needs standing water for months, so farmers pump large amounts of groundwater, making the water table fall faster; as it falls, wells must be deepened and pumping costs rise, so poorer farmers cannot afford to irrigate; deeper pumping may draw up saline water that damages soils.
parts.working: 1 mark for each problem + 1 for development. Problems: heavy groundwater use; rising pumping costs/deeper wells; small farmers lose access; saline water intrusion; less water for other crops or drinking.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which farmers could produce rice using less water.
parts.answer: Sow rice directly into the field instead of transplanting into flooded fields; alternate wetting and drying instead of keeping fields flooded all the time.
parts.working: 1 mark each: direct-seeded rice; alternate wetting and drying; laser levelling; growing rice on beds; shorter-duration varieties; switching some land to less thirsty crops.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two sources of power used to run tube wells in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Electricity from the grid; diesel engines.
parts.working: 1 mark each: grid electricity; diesel; solar; tractor PTO (power take-off).

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Tube wells have brought more benefits than problems to farming in Pakistan.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: Benefits: farmers can irrigate whenever they need, not only on their canal turn, so they can grow more crops a year and higher-value crops; tube wells help areas at the tail of canals and lowered the water table in waterlogged areas (SCARP). Problems: over-pumping has lowered the water table in many parts of Punjab and Balochistan (e.g. around Quetta), so wells must be deepened and costs rise; brackish water is drawn up, adding salt to soils; large farmers benefit more than small farmers. Judgement on the extent.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both sides/views, Pakistani examples and a clear, supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one side or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the river on which each of these is built: (i) Mangla Dam (ii) Kotri Barrage (iii) Khanpur Dam.
parts.answer: (i) Jhelum (ii) Indus (iii) Haro.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rawal Dam near Islamabad stores water in Rawal Lake. State two uses of this water.
parts.answer: Drinking water for Rawalpindi; irrigation of nearby farmland.
parts.working: 1 mark each: domestic water supply (Rawalpindi/Islamabad); irrigation; recreation/boating; fishing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the three western rivers whose waters were given to Pakistan by the Indus Waters Treaty of 1960.
parts.answer: Indus, Jhelum and Chenab.
parts.working: 2 marks all three; 1 mark for two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the international organisation that helped the two countries to agree the treaty.
parts.answer: The World Bank.
parts.working: B1 World Bank.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two large dams built in Pakistan as part of the Indus Basin works that followed the treaty.
parts.answer: Mangla Dam; Tarbela Dam.
parts.working: 1 mark each: Mangla; Tarbela.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how electricity is generated at a hydroelectric dam.
parts.answer: Water stored behind the dam flows down through large pipes (penstocks); the fast-moving water turns turbines; the turbines drive generators that produce electricity.
parts.working: 1 mark each: water stored at height/released through pipes; water turns turbines; turbines drive generators.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages of hydroelectricity compared with electricity from oil-fired power stations.
parts.answer: It uses a renewable source of energy; it does not need imported fuel, so it is cheaper to run.
parts.working: 1 mark each: renewable; no fuel cost/no imports; no air pollution/greenhouse gases; low running costs; can be switched on quickly to meet peak demand.

stem:
Water level (feet above sea level) in a large reservoir in northern Pakistan on the first day of each month (illustrative figures):
Jan 1,420, Feb 1,410, Mar 1,400, Apr 1,402, May 1,420, Jun 1,450, Jul 1,500, Aug 1,550, Sep 1,550, Oct 1,530, Nov 1,490, Dec 1,450

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the month with the lowest water level and calculate the range of water levels over the year.
parts.working: B1 March; B1 150 feet.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the reservoir is at its lowest in March and April. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Water is released through the winter to irrigate rabi crops such as wheat, while river inflow is low because snow and glaciers in the mountains are frozen and there is little rain.
parts.working: 1 mark: releases for rabi irrigation/power through winter; 1 mark: low inflow in winter (frozen snow/glaciers, little rain).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the level rises quickly from June to August. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Rising summer temperatures melt snow and glaciers in the Himalayas, Karakoram and Hindu Kush, greatly increasing river flow; monsoon rain adds more water; the reservoir is being filled for use in the following winter.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: snow and glacier melt; monsoon rainfall; policy of filling during high flows; heavy flows carry more water than is needed downstream.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the river on which the Mohmand Dam is being built.
parts.answer: The Swat River.
parts.working: B1 Swat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The Diamer-Bhasha Dam is being built on the Indus in the northern mountains. Explain two difficulties of building a large dam at such a site. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The site is remote and the only main road is the Karakoram Highway, so heavy machinery and materials are difficult and costly to bring in; the area lies in an earthquake zone, so the dam must be specially designed, raising costs; villages and parts of the highway will be flooded, so people must be resettled and roads rebuilt.
parts.working: 1 mark for each difficulty + 1 for development. Difficulties: remoteness/access; high cost/finance; earthquake risk; resettlement of people; relocating the Karakoram Highway; harsh winter climate; heavy sediment load.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two benefits Pakistan expects from new dams such as these.
parts.answer: More hydroelectricity; more water stored for irrigation.
parts.working: 1 mark each: HEP; water storage for irrigation; flood control; drinking water supply; replacing storage lost to silting in older reservoirs; jobs.

stem: Average hydroelectric power generated in Pakistan (illustrative figures): July 6,500 MW; January 2,100 MW.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more hydroelectricity was generated in July than in January. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why hydroelectric output is much lower in winter. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: River flow is low in winter because snow and ice in the mountains do not melt, so less water passes through the turbines; reservoir levels are low, so the water falls from a lower height and produces less power; water released is controlled to suit irrigation needs rather than electricity.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: low river flow (no snowmelt/little rain); low reservoir head; irrigation priorities; run-of-river plants depend on flow; ice in mountain streams.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way in which Pakistan meets the gap in electricity supply in winter.
parts.answer: By running more thermal power stations (gas, coal, oil) or nuclear plants.
parts.working: B1 thermal/nuclear generation; imports of fuel; load-shedding; solar.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Average annual flow of the Indus below Kotri Barrage (illustrative figures): 1950s: 82 km³; 2000s: 15 km³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in average annual flow. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects on the Indus Delta of the reduced flow of fresh water and silt. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Seawater moves further inland up the creeks, making groundwater and soils salty, so farming and drinking-water supplies are lost; mangrove forests, which need fresh water and silt, shrink, so breeding grounds for fish and shrimps are lost and coasts are less protected; with less silt the delta is eroded by the sea.
parts.working: 1 mark for each effect + 1 for development. Effects: seawater intrusion; loss of farmland/drinking water; mangrove decline; fewer fish/shrimps, fishermen lose income; coastal erosion; out-migration of delta people.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing these effects.
parts.answer: Guarantee a minimum release of water below Kotri Barrage every year, so that enough fresh water and silt reaches the delta.
parts.working: 1 mark measure + 1 development: minimum environmental flow; replanting mangroves; more efficient irrigation upstream to save water; protecting creeks.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two functions of a barrage (headworks).
parts.answer: It raises the water level of the river so that water can flow into canals; it controls the amount of water entering each canal.
parts.working: 1 mark each: raises river level; diverts water into canals; regulates flow; reduces flood peaks slightly; road/rail crossing of the river.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read the two views below.
View A: Barrages have done more than large dams for farming in Pakistan.
View B: Large dams have done more than barrages for farming in Pakistan.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: View A: barrages such as Sukkur, Guddu and Kotri feed the perennial canal system that irrigates most of the Indus plain; they were built first and made canal colonies possible. View B: dams such as Tarbela and Mangla store summer floods and release them in winter, which allows rabi crops to be grown and keeps canals flowing when rivers are low; they also generate HEP for tube wells. But barrages cannot store water, and dams depend on barrages to deliver water. Judgement: the two work together; dams add storage but barrages deliver the water.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both sides/views, Pakistani examples and a clear, supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one side or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points only.

stem: In an illustrative example, a planned reservoir will flood 100 km² of a valley where the average population density is 230 people per km².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of people who must be moved.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems faced by people who are resettled when a new reservoir floods their land. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Compensation may be too low or late, so families cannot buy land of the same quality; new sites may be far away with poorer soils, so farmers lose their livelihood; communities are split up and lose their mosques, graves and social ties.
parts.working: 1 mark for each problem + 1 for development. Problems: inadequate/late compensation; loss of fertile land; unemployment; break-up of communities; loss of cultural/religious sites; lack of services at new sites.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest three things a government should do to make resettlement fairer.
parts.answer: Consult the people before deciding; pay full compensation at market value before moving them; provide new villages with houses, water, schools and jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: consultation; fair, timely compensation; land for land; new villages with services; training/jobs at the dam; share of electricity or royalties.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by salinity?
parts.answer: The build-up of salts in the soil, making it less fertile.
parts.working: B1 accumulation of salt in soil.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two signs that a field is affected by salinity.
parts.answer: A white crust of salt on the surface; patchy, stunted crops.
parts.working: 1 mark each: white salt crust; bare patches; stunted/yellowing crops; low yields; salt-tolerant weeds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two plants that can be grown on salt-affected land.
parts.answer: Kallar grass; barley.
parts.working: 1 mark each: Kallar grass; barley; eucalyptus; tamarisk/frash; sesbania; date palm; sugar beet.

stem:
Depth (m) of the water table below the surface of a field beside a canal in Sindh, measured once a year (illustrative figures):
Year 1: 4.0, Year 2: 3.4, Year 3: 2.7, Year 4: 2.1, Year 5: 1.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average rise of the water table per year over the period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how seepage from an unlined canal raises the water table in nearby fields. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Water soaks through the earth bed and banks of the canal into the ground all year, adding to the groundwater faster than it can drain away; as the groundwater builds up, the water table rises towards the surface until the root zone of crops becomes saturated.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point + 1 for development, for two. Points: water seeps through unlined bed/banks; continuous recharge of groundwater; poor natural drainage on flat land; water table rises into root zone.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two causes of waterlogging, other than canal seepage.
parts.answer: Over-irrigation of fields; poor drainage on flat land.
parts.working: 1 mark each: over-irrigation; poor drainage/flat land; heavy monsoon rain; blocked natural drains by roads/embankments; rice cultivation with standing water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how lining canals with concrete or bricks helps to reduce waterlogging. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Lining stops water soaking through the canal bed, so less water reaches the groundwater and the water table stops rising.
parts.working: 1 mark: reduces seepage; 1 mark: less recharge so water table falls/stays down (or more water reaches fields).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one disadvantage of lining canals.
parts.answer: It is very expensive for long canals.
parts.working: B1 high cost; cracks need repair; less recharge for fresh groundwater used by tube wells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What does the Left Bank Outfall Drain (LBOD) in Sindh carry?
parts.answer: Saline drainage water from irrigated land, carried towards the sea.
parts.working: B1 saline/drainage water to the sea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is difficult to drain waterlogged land in lower Sindh. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The land is very flat and only a little above sea level, so water drains away very slowly by gravity.
parts.working: 1 mark: flat land/low gradient; 1 mark: near sea level so water cannot flow away easily / pumping needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two problems that a large drainage channel carrying salty water can cause.
parts.answer: Its banks may break in heavy rain or floods, spreading salty water over fields and villages; the salty water can damage wetlands and coastal areas where it reaches the sea.
parts.working: 1 mark each: bank breaches/flooding; damage to wetlands/lakes/fisheries; seawater flowing back in at high tide; cost of maintenance.

stem: In an illustrative example, an agricultural adviser recommends adding 5 tonnes of gypsum per hectare to reclaim salt-affected (sodic) soil on a 12-hectare farm in Punjab. Gypsum costs Rs 9,000 per tonne.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of gypsum needed and its cost.
parts.working: B1 60 tonnes; B1 Rs 540,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how leaching can be used to reclaim salt-affected soil. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Large amounts of good-quality water are applied to the field so that salts dissolve and are washed down below the root zone; drains are needed to carry the salty water away, otherwise the water table rises and brings the salts back.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point + 1 for development, for two. Points: flooding with fresh water; salts dissolved and washed down; need for drainage (tile/open drains); repeated over several seasons; gypsum added first for sodic soils.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why many small farmers do not reclaim their land.
parts.answer: They cannot afford the gypsum and extra water.
parts.working: B1 cost; lack of fresh water; no drainage; lack of knowledge; insecure tenancy.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Irrigated land affected by salinity in two districts (hypothetical figures):
District A: irrigated area 420,000 ha, affected 63,000 ha
District B: irrigated area 380,000 ha, affected 133,000 ha

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of irrigated land affected in each district.

parts.label: b
parts.text: District A is in northern Punjab and District B is in lower Sindh. Explain two reasons why the problem is worse in District B. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Lower Sindh is flatter and closer to sea level, so drainage is slower and the water table stays high; temperatures are higher and rainfall lower, so more water evaporates from the soil surface and leaves salt behind; much of the groundwater is naturally brackish, so it cannot be pumped for irrigation to lower the water table.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: flatter land/poor drainage; higher evaporation; less rain to flush salts; brackish groundwater; long canals with seepage; at the tail of the Indus system.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, canal water used on a farm contains 0.5 kg of dissolved salt in each m³. One hectare receives 8,000 m³ of irrigation water a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of salt added to one hectare in a year, in tonnes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why salts build up in the soil in hot, dry parts of the Indus plain. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Irrigation water and groundwater contain dissolved salts; in the hot, dry climate water evaporates rapidly from the soil surface, leaving the salts behind; when the water table is high, water rises to the surface by capillary action and evaporates, so salt collects in the top layer; low rainfall cannot wash the salts away.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point + 1 for development, for two. Points: dissolved salts in irrigation water; high evaporation; capillary rise from high water table; little rain to leach salts; poor drainage.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, a country has 16 million hectares of irrigated land, of which 25% is affected by waterlogging or salinity. Wheat yields on affected land are about 1.2 tonnes per hectare lower than on healthy land.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the area affected and the possible loss of wheat each year.
parts.answer: 16 × 25% = 4 million hectares; 4 × 1.2 = 4.8 million tonnes
parts.working: B1 4 million hectares; B1 4.8 million tonnes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which waterlogging and salinity affect Pakistan's economy as a whole. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Lower crop yields mean less wheat, cotton and rice, so Pakistan may have to import food and earns less from exports such as cotton textiles; farmers' incomes fall, increasing rural poverty and migration to cities; the government must spend large sums on drainage and reclamation schemes.
parts.working: 1 mark for each effect + 1 for development. Effects: lower farm output; food imports/trade deficit; reduced exports/raw materials for industry; rural poverty and migration; government spending on drainage; land values fall.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A SCARP tube well pumps groundwater at 0.08 m³ per second and runs for 20 hours a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of water the tube well pumps in a day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why SCARP tube wells did not solve the problem of waterlogging and salinity in many areas. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Where groundwater was salty, the pumped water could not be used for irrigation and there was no easy way to dispose of it, so it was put into drains or canals, spreading salt elsewhere; the tube wells were expensive to run and repair, and many stopped working when funds and electricity ran short; farmers still over-irrigated and canals still leaked, so recharge continued.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: saline water disposal; high running/maintenance costs; electricity shortages; poor maintenance after handover; continued seepage/over-irrigation; lowering water table too far in fresh areas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which farmers could reduce waterlogging on their own land without large government schemes.
parts.answer: Avoid over-irrigating by applying water only when crops need it; plant eucalyptus trees along field edges to draw up groundwater (biological drainage).
parts.working: 1 mark each: careful irrigation scheduling; laser levelling; bed-and-furrow planting; field drains; tree planting (biodrainage); growing less water-hungry crops.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two methods that farmers can use to grow crops successfully on salt-affected land.
parts.answer: Grow salt-tolerant crops such as barley; plant on ridges so that salt collects on the tops and seeds on the sides.
parts.working: 1 mark each: salt-tolerant crops/varieties; ridge or bed planting; adding gypsum/organic matter; leaching before sowing; mulching to reduce evaporation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Farmers themselves can solve the problems of waterlogging and salinity without help from the government.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: For: farmers can reduce over-irrigation, laser-level fields, add gypsum, plant salt-tolerant crops and trees (biodrainage) and use bed-and-furrow methods, all of which reduce the problem on their land. Against: the main causes – seepage from the huge canal network, high regional water tables and flat land with no outlet – need large drains (such as LBOD), canal lining and SCARP-type pumping that only the government can fund; small farmers cannot afford gypsum or machinery. Judgement on the extent: farmers can manage the symptoms, but lasting solutions need government drainage and canal works.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both sides/views, Pakistani examples and a clear, supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one side or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points only.

stem:
Yields (tonnes per hectare) of three crops on normal and on saline land on a farm in Punjab (illustrative figures):
Wheat: normal 3.2, saline 2.0
Cotton: normal 2.4, saline 1.8
Barley: normal 2.8, saline 2.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage loss in yield on saline land for each crop. Give your answers to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using your answers, state which crop is most tolerant of salt.
parts.answer: Barley, because its yield falls by the smallest percentage.
parts.working: B1 barley with reason.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A farmer with saline land decides to keep growing wheat rather than barley. Explain two reasons why he might make this choice, even though barley is more salt-tolerant. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Wheat is the family's staple food, so growing it means they do not have to buy flour; there is a guaranteed government procurement price and a large market for wheat, while barley sells for less and has fewer buyers; the farmer has the seed, machinery and experience for wheat.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: wheat is the staple food; higher/guaranteed price; larger market; tradition and experience; even reduced wheat yield may earn more than barley.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one main use of each of these minerals: (i) fireclay (ii) silica sand (iii) china clay (iv) gypsum.
parts.answer: (i) making firebricks to line furnaces and kilns; (ii) making glass; (iii) making crockery, ceramics and tiles; (iv) making cement (and plaster of Paris).
parts.working: B1 each. Also accept: china clay – paper/paint filler; gypsum – fertiliser/soil improver, plaster boards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one chemical made from rock salt in Pakistan's chemical industry.
parts.answer: Soda ash (sodium carbonate).
parts.working: B1 soda ash; caustic soda (sodium hydroxide); chlorine; hydrochloric acid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the province in which each of these mineral sites is found: (i) Khewra (rock salt) (ii) Lakhra (coal) (iii) Muslim Bagh (chromite) (iv) Shah Dheri (china clay).
parts.answer: (i) Punjab (ii) Sindh (iii) Balochistan (iv) Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why being close to a road or railway is important for a mine. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Most minerals are heavy and bulky, so they must be moved cheaply to factories or ports; without good transport the cost of moving them can be greater than the value of the mineral.
parts.working: 1 mark: minerals are heavy/bulky/low value per tonne; 1 mark: transport cost affects profit / access to markets or ports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three minerals from Pakistan that are used in the construction industry.
parts.answer: Limestone; gypsum; marble.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: limestone; gypsum; marble; granite; clay (bricks); silica sand; crushed stone/gravel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why demand for these minerals in Pakistan has grown. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Rapid urban growth means many new houses, roads and bridges are being built, so more cement and building stone are needed.
parts.working: 1 mark reason + 1 development: urbanisation/housing; infrastructure projects (motorways, dams, CPEC); population growth; exports of cement.

stem: Approximate figures often quoted: Pakistan has about 186 billion tonnes of coal reserves, of which about 175 billion tonnes are in the Thar coalfield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the Thar coalfield's share of Pakistan's coal reserves as a percentage. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of coal found at Thar.
parts.answer: Lignite (brown coal).
parts.working: B1 lignite.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why Thar coal was not developed for many years after it was discovered.
parts.answer: It lies deep under sand dunes in a remote desert with no roads, water or power lines.
parts.working: B1 deep/under sand; remote; no infrastructure; water shortage; low quality/high moisture; high cost/lack of investment.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Illustrative prices: rock salt exported in bulk earns about $40 a tonne; the same salt sold as packaged products and salt lamps earns about $400 a tonne.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the export value of 50,000 tonnes of salt sold as raw rock salt, and as processed products.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which Pakistan could earn more from its rock salt. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Process and package the salt in Pakistan (edible pink salt, lamps, bath salts) instead of exporting it in bulk, so more value stays in the country; develop a 'Made in Pakistan' brand and protect the origin of Himalayan pink salt, so buyers know where it comes from; invest in modern mining so less salt is wasted.
parts.working: 1 mark for each way + 1 for development. Ways: processing/value addition; branding/geographical origin; better packaging and marketing; modern extraction; new markets; using salt in local chemical industry.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why much rock salt is still exported in raw form.
parts.answer: Foreign buyers process and brand it themselves, and Pakistani firms lack the machinery and marketing contacts.
parts.working: B1 lack of processing industry/investment; buyers prefer bulk; low cost of selling raw; lack of branding.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Iron ore deposits have been found near Chiniot in Punjab. Name one other area of Pakistan where iron ore is found.
parts.answer: Kalabagh (or Nokkundi in Chagai).
parts.working: B1 Kalabagh; Nokkundi (Chagai).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two possible benefits to Pakistan of developing the iron ore near Chiniot. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Pakistan imports most of the iron ore used for steel, so a local supply could save foreign exchange; the deposit lies in central Punjab, close to industrial cities, roads and railways, so transport costs to steel works would be low; mining and steel-making would create jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark for each benefit + 1 for development. Benefits: reduce imports/save foreign exchange; near industrial centres and transport; jobs; growth of steel and engineering industries; government revenue.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the ore may be difficult to develop.
parts.answer: It lies deep underground, so mining is expensive.
parts.working: B1 depth/high cost; ore grade or quality; need for large investment; lack of local technology.

stem:
Index of mineral production in a country (Year 1 = 100; illustrative figures):
Year 1: 100, Year 2: 104, Year 3: 97, Year 4: 110, Year 5: 118

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean index value for the five years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage change in production between Year 3 and Year 5. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two factors that could cause mineral production to fall in a year such as Year 3. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: A slowdown in building and construction reduces demand for limestone, gypsum and marble, so quarries cut output; gas and electricity shortages stop machinery and processing plants; floods or heavy rain block roads and close mines; security problems or disputes over leases halt work in some areas.
parts.working: 1 mark for each factor + 1 for development. Factors: lower demand (construction, exports); energy shortages; floods/weather; security/law and order; policy or lease disputes; falling world prices.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, the copper-gold ore in a deposit in Chagai contains 0.5% copper and 0.3 grams of gold per tonne.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of copper (in tonnes) and of gold (in kg) in 1 million tonnes of this ore.
parts.working: B1 5,000 tonnes; B1 300 kg.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two uses of copper.
parts.answer: Electrical wires and cables; pipes and alloys such as brass.
parts.working: 1 mark each: electrical wiring/cables; motors and electronics; pipes; alloys (brass, bronze); coins.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why deposits such as those in Chagai are worth mining even though the ore contains so little copper. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The deposits are very large and also contain gold, and copper and gold have high values on world markets, so large-scale mining of huge tonnages is profitable.
parts.working: 1 mark: very large deposit/huge tonnage; 1 mark: high value of copper and gold (by-product gold adds value).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two minerals that Pakistan exports.
parts.answer: Rock salt; marble (and onyx).
parts.working: 1 mark each: rock salt; marble/onyx; chromite; gemstones; copper (from Saindak); gypsum; soapstone; coal (small amounts).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read the two views below.
View A: Pakistan should export its minerals as raw ores, because this earns money quickly.
View B: Pakistan should process its minerals at home before exporting them.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: View A: raw exports need little investment and technology, earn foreign exchange quickly and suit remote mines with no power or water for processing (e.g. chromite from Balochistan). View B: processing adds value – salt products, polished marble, refined copper earn many times more per tonne – and creates jobs and skills in Pakistan; but it needs energy, capital and skilled workers, which are in short supply. Judgement: process where energy and skills allow (salt, marble), while exporting some raw ore in the short term.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both sides/views, Pakistani examples and a clear, supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one side or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points only.

stem: In an illustrative example, a limestone reserve in the Salt Range is estimated at 600 million tonnes. Present production is 20 million tonnes a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many years the reserve would last at the present rate of production, and if production rose to 30 million tonnes a year.
parts.working: B1 30 years; B1 20 years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the estimated life of a mineral reserve can change. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: New surveys may discover extra deposits, increasing the reserve; new technology may make deeper or lower-grade ore worth mining; if the price rises, more of the deposit becomes profitable, but if it falls some deposits are no longer counted; faster or slower production changes how long it lasts.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: new discoveries; improved technology; price changes; rate of production; recycling/substitutes reducing demand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why minerals are described as non-renewable even though new reserves are sometimes found.
parts.answer: They take millions of years to form, so once used they cannot be replaced in a human lifetime; new discoveries only add to a fixed total stock.
parts.working: 1 mark: formed over geological time/cannot be replaced; 1 mark: finite stock will eventually be used up.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, a mine is 700 km by road from Karachi port. Road transport costs $0.05 per tonne per km. Values per tonne at the port: limestone $10, rock salt $40, marble blocks $120, chromite $200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of transporting one tonne of mineral from the mine to the port.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using your answer, calculate the value left per tonne for each mineral after transport, and state which minerals it would not be worth sending to the port.
parts.answer: Limestone 10 − 35 = −$25; rock salt 40 − 35 = $5; marble blocks 120 − 35 = $85; chromite 200 − 35 = $165. Limestone is not worth sending (it loses money), and rock salt leaves very little.
parts.working: B1 all four values correct; B1 limestone not worth sending; B1 rock salt hardly worth it / chromite and marble worth sending.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why some minerals can be profitably mined in remote areas such as Chagai while others cannot. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: High-value minerals such as copper, gold, chromite or onyx are worth much more per tonne than the cost of moving them, so they can bear long journeys to Karachi; low-value bulky minerals such as limestone or gravel cost more to transport than they are worth, so they are only used near where they are dug, for example by local cement or construction industries.
parts.working: 1 mark for each point + 1 for development, for two. Points: value per tonne compared with transport cost; high-value minerals can bear long transport; low-value bulky minerals used locally; processing on site reduces weight; poor roads/rail raise costs.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe drift mining.
parts.answer: A sloping or horizontal tunnel (adit) is dug into a hillside to reach a seam of coal or other mineral that comes to the surface on the slope.
parts.working: 1 mark: tunnel into a hillside; 1 mark: horizontal/gently sloping, following a seam that outcrops on the slope.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why drift mining is used in hilly coalfields such as those in Balochistan.
parts.answer: The coal seams are exposed on hillsides, so they can be reached by a tunnel without sinking a deep shaft.
parts.working: B1 seams outcrop on slopes; cheaper than shafts; little machinery needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two reasons why fresh air must be pumped into underground mines.
parts.answer: To remove dangerous gases such as methane; to give miners enough oxygen to breathe.
parts.working: 1 mark each: dilute/remove methane and other gases; supply oxygen; remove dust; reduce heat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two lung diseases suffered by workers exposed to mine or quarry dust.
parts.answer: Silicosis; pneumoconiosis (black lung).
parts.working: 1 mark each: silicosis; pneumoconiosis/black lung; tuberculosis (made worse by dust); asthma; chronic bronchitis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways of reducing the amount of dust breathed in by miners and quarry workers. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Spraying water on rock while it is drilled, cut or crushed keeps dust down so less gets into the air; giving workers proper dust masks filters out fine particles; good ventilation in mines carries dust away from working areas; using wet-cutting machines instead of dry cutting.
parts.working: 1 mark for each way + 1 for development. Ways: water sprays/wet drilling; masks/respirators; ventilation; enclosed crushers; health checks and rotation of workers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by overburden?
parts.answer: The soil and rock lying above a mineral deposit that must be removed before the mineral can be mined.
parts.working: B1 material above the deposit removed in open-cast mining.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is a spoil heap?
parts.answer: A pile of waste rock and soil dumped near a mine.
parts.working: B1 heap of waste material from mining.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe two ways in which open-cast mining changes the appearance of the landscape.
parts.answer: A large, deep pit is left where the ground has been removed; spoil heaps form new artificial hills of bare rock and sand.
parts.working: 1 mark each: large pits/holes; spoil heaps; removal of vegetation; dust over the area; new roads and buildings.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one use for spoil from mines.
parts.answer: Filling land or building road embankments.
parts.working: B1 road/embankment fill; landfill; refilling old pits; making bricks/blocks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which minerals are transported from mines to factories in Pakistan.
parts.answer: By lorry (truck) along roads; by railway.
parts.working: 1 mark each: lorries/trucks; railway; conveyor belts; pipelines (for slurry); donkeys/mules from small mines to the road.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of using railways rather than roads for transporting coal or limestone over long distances. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: One train carries as much as dozens of lorries, so the cost per tonne is lower and road traffic is reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark advantage + 1 development: cheaper for bulky goods; less road congestion/accidents/damage; less fuel and pollution per tonne.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why most minerals in Pakistan are still carried by road.
parts.answer: Many mines are far from a railway line, so lorries are needed anyway.
parts.working: B1 mines not near railways; rail is slow/unreliable; door-to-door service; shortage of wagons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two uses of sand and gravel dug from riverbeds.
parts.answer: Making concrete; building roads.
parts.working: 1 mark each: concrete; road building; plaster/mortar; bricks and blocks; filling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two problems caused by digging large amounts of sand and gravel from riverbeds. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The riverbed is lowered, so the river flows faster and erodes its banks, damaging farmland; foundations of bridges and embankments are undermined, so they may collapse during floods; habitats for fish are destroyed and water becomes muddy; the water table near the river can fall.
parts.working: 1 mark for each problem + 1 for development. Problems: bank erosion; damage to bridges/embankments; habitat loss; muddy water; lower water table; changes in river course.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why many coal miners working in Balochistan come from districts such as Swat and Shangla in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: There are few jobs in these mountain districts, where farms are small, so men must travel to earn money; mining is a tradition, and miners help relatives and neighbours to find work, so networks of workers from the same villages form; mine owners need experienced workers willing to do dangerous work.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: lack of local jobs/poverty; small farms; tradition and family networks; experience/skills; higher wages than farming.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two problems faced by the families of these miners.
parts.answer: The family loses its main earner if the miner is killed or disabled in an accident; men are away for months, leaving women to manage the household alone.
parts.working: 1 mark each: loss of earner through accidents; long absence of men; irregular income; little compensation; health costs of lung disease.

stem:
Two coal mines in Balochistan (illustrative figures):
Small mine using hand tools: 8 workers produce 12 tonnes per shift
Mechanised mine: 3 workers produce 30 tonnes per shift

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the output per worker per shift at each mine, and how many times more productive the mechanised mine is. Give the last answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: Small mine: 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 tonnes; mechanised mine: 30 ÷ 3 = 10 tonnes; 10 ÷ 1.5 = 6.7 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects on mining communities if mines in an area are mechanised. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Fewer workers are needed for each tonne, so many manual miners lose their jobs and may have to migrate; the remaining jobs need training to operate and repair machines, so wages for skilled workers rise; machines reduce the number of workers underground, so accidents and deaths may fall.
parts.working: 1 mark for each effect + 1 for development. Effects: job losses; migration; need for skills/training; higher wages for some; improved safety; higher output and profits.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, a copper mine in Chagai processes 12,000 tonnes of ore a day. The ore contains 0.4% copper and 85% of the copper is recovered.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of copper recovered each day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the main stages by which copper is obtained from ore at a mine such as Saindak.
parts.answer: The ore is blasted and dug from an open pit; it is crushed and ground into a powder; the copper minerals are separated into a concentrate; the concentrate is smelted to produce blister copper for export.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: open-pit extraction; crushing and grinding; concentration (flotation); smelting; blister copper exported.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two environmental problems caused by smelting.
parts.answer: Sulphur dioxide gas pollutes the air; waste slag is dumped.
parts.working: 1 mark each: sulphur dioxide/acid rain; smoke and dust; slag heaps; heavy water use; energy use/emissions.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how acid mine drainage forms. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Minerals containing sulphur (such as pyrite) in coal and waste rock react with air and water, forming sulphuric acid that drains from mines and spoil heaps.
parts.working: 1 mark: sulphur-bearing minerals exposed to air and water; 1 mark: produce acid that drains out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects of acid mine drainage on streams near coal mines. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The acidic water kills fish and other water life; it dissolves metals from rocks, so the water becomes poisonous for drinking and for animals; orange iron deposits coat the streambed, smothering plants and insects.
parts.working: 1 mark for each effect + 1 for development. Effects: acidity kills aquatic life; dissolved toxic metals; unsafe for drinking/irrigation; iron staining/smothering of streambed; damage to crops downstream.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing acid mine drainage.
parts.answer: Cover spoil heaps with soil and plants so that air and water cannot reach the waste.
parts.working: B1 covering/sealing waste; treating water with lime; collecting and treating drainage; constructed wetlands.

stem: In an illustrative example, a marble quarry in the Buner area removes 5,000 tonnes of rock in a month, of which 1,750 tonnes are sold as usable blocks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the rock removed that becomes usable blocks, and the mass of waste.
parts.working: B1 35%; B1 3,250 tonnes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which waste from marble quarries could be put to use. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Waste pieces can be crushed into chips and powder for terrazzo floors, tiles and wall coatings, creating extra income; marble powder can be used in making cement, lime, paint or animal feed, so less is dumped in rivers; small blocks can be cut into handicrafts and decorative items.
parts.working: 1 mark for each use + 1 for development. Uses: chips/terrazzo/tiles; powder for cement/lime/paint/fillers; handicrafts; road fill; reduces pollution of rivers and land.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why so much rock is wasted.
parts.answer: Blasting with explosives cracks the marble, so many pieces are too small or broken to be sold as blocks.
parts.working: 1 mark cause + 1 development: blasting; poor cutting tools; lack of wire saws; untrained workers.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is meant by subsidence?
parts.answer: The sinking of the ground surface.
parts.working: B1 sinking/collapse of the land surface.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why land above old underground mines may subside. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: When pillars or roof supports in the old workings weaken or collapse, the rock above falls into the empty spaces, so the ground surface sinks.
parts.working: 1 mark: empty spaces left by mining; 1 mark: roof/pillars collapse so overlying ground sinks.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two effects of subsidence on people living above old mine workings. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Cracks appear in walls and foundations, so houses may become unsafe and families must move; roads, pipes and canals are damaged, causing water leaks and expensive repairs; farmland becomes uneven and may flood.
parts.working: 1 mark for each effect + 1 for development. Effects: damage to buildings; damage to roads/pipes/canals; uneven/waterlogged land; loss of property value; danger of sudden collapse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)?
parts.answer: A study carried out before a project such as a mine is approved, to predict its effects on the environment and people and to suggest ways of reducing harm.
parts.working: 1 mark: study before project starts; 1 mark: predicts environmental/social effects and suggests mitigation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two things that an EIA for a new open-cast mine in a desert area should investigate. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: How much groundwater will be pumped out of the pit and whether this will dry up villagers' wells; how dust from blasting and lorries will affect people's health and crops; how many people and grazing lands will have to be moved and how they will be compensated; how the land will be restored afterwards.
parts.working: 1 mark for each item + 1 for development. Items: water use/groundwater; dust and air quality; noise; displacement of people/grazing; wildlife; waste disposal; land restoration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the recommendations of an EIA are not always followed.
parts.answer: Monitoring by government agencies is weak, so companies can ignore them.
