parts.working: B1 weak enforcement; cost to company; pressure to start quickly; corruption; lack of trained inspectors.

stem: In an illustrative example, pumps at an open-cast coal pit in Thar remove 2,500 m³ of groundwater per hour, 24 hours a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of water pumped out of the pit in one day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the pit must be pumped dry before and during mining. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The coal lies below layers of rock that hold groundwater, which flows into the pit, so it must be removed to keep the pit floor dry and the walls stable for machines to work.
parts.working: 1 mark: pit cuts into water-bearing layers (aquifers); 1 mark: flooding/unstable walls would stop machinery working.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two problems of disposing of this water in a desert area. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: The water is often salty, so if it is pumped into low-lying land it forms a reservoir that can flood grazing land and damage nearby villages' wells; if it soaks into the ground it can raise salinity of fresh groundwater; pumping lowers the water table so local wells dry up.
parts.working: 1 mark for each problem + 1 for development. Problems: saline water; flooding of land/villages; contamination of fresh groundwater; falling water table/wells drying; evaporation pond leaves salt crust; disputes with local people.

author: HomiLabs

stem:
Three coal deposits (illustrative figures):
Deposit P: seam 10 m thick under 120 m of overburden
Deposit Q: seam 6 m thick under 30 m of overburden
Deposit R: seam 2 m thick under 180 m of overburden

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the stripping ratio (thickness of overburden : thickness of coal) for each deposit, in the form n : 1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Open-cast mining is taken to be economic if the ratio is no more than 15 : 1. State which deposits should be mined open-cast.
parts.answer: P and Q.
parts.working: B1 P and Q.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why deposit R would have to be mined underground, and one problem this causes. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: To reach a 2 m seam open-cast, 90 m of rock would have to be moved for every metre of coal, so the cost would be far greater than the value of the coal; a shaft or drift is cheaper. However, underground mining is more dangerous because of gas, roof collapse and flooding, and less of the coal can be recovered because pillars must be left.
parts.working: 2 marks: reason (very high ratio → cost of removing overburden exceeds value; underground cheaper); 2 marks: problem developed (danger to miners/lower recovery/higher cost per tonne/ventilation needs).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two materials quarried from hills near Islamabad and Taxila.
parts.answer: Limestone; crushed stone (gravel) for construction.
parts.working: 1 mark each: limestone (for cement); crushed stone/gravel/bajri; sandstone; clay.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read the two views below.
View A: Quarrying in the hills near Islamabad should be banned completely.
View B: Quarrying in the hills near Islamabad should be allowed, but with strict controls.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: View A: the Margalla Hills are a national park; quarrying destroys forests, wildlife habitats and scenery, causes dust and noise for nearby housing, and the scars cannot easily be restored; stone can be brought from elsewhere. View B: the growing twin cities need limestone and crushed stone for cement and construction, and local quarries keep costs low and provide jobs; strict rules – limited zones outside the park, dust control, restoration and inspection – could reduce harm. Judgement, e.g. ban inside the national park, allow controlled quarrying outside it.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both sides/views, Pakistani examples and a clear, supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one side or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points only.

stem:
Coal mining in two provinces in one year (hypothetical figures):
Province X: 64 deaths, production 3.2 million tonnes
Province Y: 18 deaths, production 2.0 million tonnes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of deaths per million tonnes of coal produced in each province.
parts.answer: X: 64 ÷ 3.2 = 20; Y: 18 ÷ 2.0 = 9 deaths per million tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why comparing deaths per million tonnes is more useful than comparing the total number of deaths.
parts.answer: The provinces produce different amounts of coal, so a province with more mining would be expected to have more deaths; the rate shows how dangerous mining actually is for each tonne produced.
parts.working: 1 mark: different amounts produced/size of industry; 1 mark: rate allows fair comparison of safety.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why mining is more dangerous in Province X than in Province Y. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Mines in X may be small, privately run and use hand tools with little ventilation, so methane builds up and explosions occur; safety inspections may be rare in remote areas, so rules on gas testing and roof supports are not enforced; coal seams may be deeper and more gassy.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason + 1 for development. Reasons: small/old mines; poor ventilation/gas monitoring; weak inspection/enforcement; untrained workers; geology (deep, gassy seams, weak roofs); lack of rescue services.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, a coal mine employs 450 workers. A company plans to mechanise it so that only 120 workers would be needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of jobs that would be lost and the percentage of the workforce this represents. Give the percentage to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 'Using modern machinery would solve the main problems of mining in Pakistan.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: For: machines increase output per worker, reduce waste (e.g. wire saws instead of blasting in marble quarries), improve safety by reducing the number of people underground, and make deeper or lower-grade deposits profitable. Against: machinery is expensive and needs reliable power, skilled operators and spare parts; it does not solve problems of poor transport, lack of surveys, insecurity or weak enforcement of safety and environmental laws; it causes large job losses in poor mining areas, as the data show. Judgement on the extent.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both sides/views, Pakistani examples and a clear, supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one side or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points only.

author: HomiLabs

stem: In an illustrative example, 40 lorries each make one round trip a day between a mine and a railhead 180 km away (360 km in total). Each lorry uses 0.35 litres of diesel per km.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fuel used by the lorries each day and in a 300-day working year.
parts.working: B1 5,040 litres; B1 1,512,000 litres.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two environmental effects of carrying ore by road in this way. You should develop your answer.
parts.answer: Burning so much diesel releases carbon dioxide and smoke, adding to air pollution and climate change; heavy lorries throw up dust along unpaved roads, which settles on crops and harms people's lungs; the roads are damaged and accidents increase in villages along the route.
parts.working: 1 mark for each effect + 1 for development. Effects: CO₂/air pollution; dust; road damage; noise; accidents; spills of ore.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why a railway or conveyor belt might be a better choice.
parts.answer: It uses less energy per tonne carried, so it causes less pollution; it removes heavy lorries from village roads, making them safer.
parts.working: 1 mark each: less fuel/emissions per tonne; less dust; fewer accidents; lower running cost over time; reliable large capacity.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why gemstone mining in the high northern mountains takes place mainly in summer.
parts.answer: Heavy snow blocks the paths and covers the mine sites in winter; temperatures are far below freezing, making outdoor work impossible.
parts.working: 1 mark each: snow cover; extreme cold; roads/passes closed; danger of avalanches; miners have farm work in other seasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Read the two views below.
View A: Gemstone mining in northern Pakistan should be left to small local miners.
View B: Gemstone mining in northern Pakistan should be developed by large companies.
Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons to support your answer.
parts.answer: View A: local miners earn money in poor mountain valleys, keep control of their land and resources, and profits stay in the community. But they often use explosives and hand tools that damage the stones, work in unsafe conditions and sell rough stones cheaply to middlemen. View B: companies can invest in surveys, safer machinery and cutting and polishing, so gems fetch higher prices and exports rise; but they may take profits out of the area, employ few local people and damage the fragile mountain environment. Judgement, e.g. support local miners with training, cooperatives and cutting centres.
parts.working: Level 3 (5–6): developed points for both sides/views, Pakistani examples and a clear, supported judgement. Level 2 (3–4): developed point(s) for one side or simple points for both. Level 1 (1–2): simple points only.

subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Nehru Report of 1928.
parts.answer: Drawn up by a committee chaired by Motilal Nehru and approved at an all-parties meeting in 1928; it proposed dominion status for India; it recommended joint electorates; it rejected separate electorates and the one-third Muslim share of central seats that Jinnah had demanded; it gave no reserved Muslim seats in Punjab and Bengal.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: committee led by Motilal Nehru (1928); all-parties meeting approved it; dominion status; joint electorates; separate electorates rejected; one-third of central seats for Muslims not granted; no reserved seats for Muslims in Punjab or Bengal.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Muslim leaders objected to the Nehru Report of 1928.
parts.answer: (1) It rejected separate electorates, which Muslims had had since 1909 and which the Communal Award later confirmed, so Muslims would be outvoted in joint electorates. (2) It refused the one-third of seats at the centre that Muslims had asked for, so the minority would have little say at federal level.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained: separate electorates rejected (1) and the reason why it matters to a minority (1); no one-third central share (1) and its effect on Muslim influence (1). Any two developed reasons, up to 4.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the proposal made by Chaudhry Rahmat Ali in his pamphlet 'Now or Never' (1933).
parts.answer: He called for a separate federation of Muslim-majority states in the north-west of India, to be named Pakistan, covering Punjab, the North-West Frontier, Kashmir, Sindh and Baluchistan. The name was formed from the regions' names. The Muslim League leadership did not adopt the scheme, and Rahmat Ali was not a League leader.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: pamphlet of 1933 written by Rahmat Ali while he was a student in England; calls for a separate state in north-west India; named Pakistan; regions listed (Punjab, North-West Frontier, Kashmir, Sindh, Baluchistan); not accepted by the Muslim League leadership at the time.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Poona Pact of 1932.
parts.answer: An agreement between Gandhi and B. R. Ambedkar, signed in September 1932, which ended Gandhi's fast against the Communal Award. The depressed classes kept reserved seats, but these were filled in joint electorates instead of separate ones.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: signed 1932 by Gandhi and Ambedkar; ended Gandhi's fast; depressed classes kept reserved seats; seats in joint electorates instead of separate electorates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which the Poona Pact changed the Communal Award.
parts.answer: It replaced the separate electorates the Award gave to the depressed classes with reserved seats in joint electorates.
parts.working: 2 marks for a correct change, e.g. separate electorates for depressed classes replaced by reserved seats within a general electorate.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of years between the arrival of the Simon Commission in India (1928) and the royal assent to the Government of India Act (1935).
parts.answer: 7 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one reason why the Indian National Congress rejected the Government of India Act 1935.
parts.answer: Congress called the Act undemocratic: the franchise was narrow, the governors kept special powers to override elected ministers, and the federal part, which was meant to bring in the princely states, was not carried out.
parts.working: 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for development. Accept any valid reason: narrow franchise; reserve powers of governors; federal part not implemented; Congress wanted a constituent assembly and full self-government.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the Viceroy of India who was in office when the Simon Commission arrived in 1928.
parts.answer: Lord Irwin
parts.working: 1 mark: Lord Irwin (Viceroy 1926–1931).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the British Prime Minister in office when the First Round Table Conference met in London in 1930.
parts.answer: Ramsay MacDonald
parts.working: 1 mark: Ramsay MacDonald (Labour Prime Minister 1929–1931 in that period).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which the Government of India Act 1935 met the demands of Indian politicians and Muslim leaders made in the 1920s and early 1930s.
parts.answer: The Act met some demands: provinces gained autonomy under elected ministers, which gave Indians real experience of government; the wider franchise and the separation of Burma and Aden from India were steps forward; provincial councils were enlarged. It failed many demands: the Congress wanted full self-government and dominion status, but the central government stayed under British control; the governors kept special powers to override ministers; separate electorates were kept, which Congress opposed; the federal part was never brought into force. Overall the Act gave limited progress in the provinces, but it did not satisfy either Congress or the Muslim League's demands for a fair constitutional settlement.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): balanced judgement; both gains (provincial autonomy, enlarged franchise, separation of Burma and Aden) and failures (centre not responsible, governors' reserve powers, federation not implemented, Congress and League demands unmet); clear conclusion on extent. Level 2 (5–8): describes features with some judgement. Level 1 (1–4): description only, few relevant points.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Constitutional proposals and the Pakistan idea 1927–1935

parts.label: a
parts.text: An illustrative provincial assembly has 250 seats, of which 75 are reserved for Muslim members. (Illustrative figures.) Calculate the percentage of seats reserved for Muslims. Give your answer as a whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one way in which joint electorates with no reserved seats could reduce the political influence of a minority in an assembly.
parts.answer: Members of the majority community can win the general seats, so a minority's candidates may be defeated unless it has reserved seats; the minority's voters are a small share of each general constituency.
parts.working: 1 mark for the mechanism, 1 mark for a clear link to minority influence.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of years between the Lahore Resolution (1940) and the Indian Independence Act (1947).
parts.answer: 7 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the date on which Pakistan became an independent country.
parts.answer: 14 August 1947
parts.working: 1 mark: 14 August 1947 (India became independent on 15 August 1947).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Gandhi–Jinnah talks held in Bombay in September 1944.
parts.answer: The talks were based on the Rajagopalachari (Rajaji) formula. Gandhi offered that, after the war, the Muslim-majority districts would decide by plebiscite whether to separate, with a commission to settle the boundaries. Jinnah rejected the formula because it did not recognise Pakistan as a separate state or the Muslims' right to decide their own future. The talks broke down without agreement.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: held in Bombay in September 1944; based on the Rajaji formula; plebiscite of Muslim-majority districts after the war; Jinnah demanded recognition of a separate Pakistan state and the Muslims' right to self-determination; talks failed without agreement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Muslim League called Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946.
parts.answer: The Muslim League had withdrawn its acceptance of the Cabinet Mission Plan in July 1946, after disputes over the grouping of provinces and the Congress interpretation of the Plan. Jinnah called a day of 'direct action' to press the demand for Pakistan. The call led to serious communal violence in Calcutta.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: League rejected/withdrew from the Cabinet Mission Plan (July 1946) over grouping and Congress interpretation; League wanted to press its demand for Pakistan; Jinnah's call for direct action; result was communal riots in Calcutta and tension across India.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems caused by the Radcliffe Boundary Commission's award for the Punjab and Bengal.
parts.answer: The award was published after independence, on 17 August 1947, so many people had already begun to move. The boundary line passed through districts with mixed Muslim, Hindu and Sikh populations, which left communities on the wrong side and caused fear and mass migration. The Gurdaspur district, with a Muslim majority, went to India, which gave India a land route to Kashmir.
parts.working: 3 marks per problem, up to 6: award announced after independence (17 Aug 1947) and migration already underway; mixed populations on both sides causing fear and violence; uncertainty and rushed boundary drawing; Gurdaspur awarded to India, giving access to Kashmir.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the British mission of 1946 that proposed a three-tier structure for a united India.
parts.answer: Cabinet Mission
parts.working: 1 mark: the Cabinet Mission (1946).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one member of the Cabinet Mission.
parts.answer: Stafford Cripps (also accept Lord Pethick-Lawrence or A. V. Alexander)
parts.working: 1 mark for any one member: Stafford Cripps, Lord Pethick-Lawrence, A. V. Alexander.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of months between the announcement by the British Prime Minister Clement Attlee (February 1947) and the date by which Britain said it would transfer power (June 1948).
parts.answer: 16 months
parts.working: 1 mark for the year difference 1948 − 1947 = 1 year = 12 months; 1 mark for 12 + (6 − 2) = 16 months.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the Second World War affected Britain's willingness to grant India independence.
parts.answer: Britain was financially weakened by the war and could not afford to keep its empire at the same cost; Indian troops and resources had been used in the war, and Indian nationalists had grown stronger; the Atlantic Charter (1941) had promised self-government for peoples; the Labour government elected in 1945 was committed to independence.
parts.working: 2 marks for each explained point, up to 4: economic strain on Britain; the war effort raised Indian expectations; wartime Atlantic Charter principles; post-war Labour government's commitment to decolonisation.

stem: We have waited long enough for a homeland where our children may live by their own faith and laws. The promises made in 1946 have been broken, and we will not be dismissed with more words. (Extract written for this exercise.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two claims the speaker makes about the Muslim League's position.
parts.answer: The promises of 1946 were broken; Muslims need a homeland where they can live by their own faith and laws.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two claims: broken promises (1946); need for a homeland; right to live by Islamic faith and law; refusal to accept further delay or words.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this message was likely to appeal to Muslim voters in 1946–1947.
parts.answer: The League had won most Muslim seats in the 1945–46 elections, so its supporters saw it as the true voice of Muslims; the message promised a homeland, which answered fears of living under a Hindu-majority government; it used religion and identity, which was powerful in mass politics.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: League electoral success in 1945–46 gave authority; homeland promise answered fear of majority rule; religious identity; betrayal narrative linked to the Cabinet Mission.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which Jinnah's leadership was the main reason for the creation of Pakistan by 1947.
parts.answer: Jinnah was the central figure: he gave the Muslim League a clear goal in the Lahore Resolution (1940), built the party's organisation, used the 1945–46 elections to show Muslims supported Pakistan, and refused the offers that did not recognise a separate state. However, the creation of Pakistan also depended on other factors: the British decision to leave by 1947, the Congress refusal to accept a loose grouping of provinces, the League's strength in Punjab and Bengal and the failure of the Cabinet Mission and the wartime situation. Judgement: Jinnah was decisive in giving the demand unity and momentum, but it was the British decision and the collapse of the Cabinet Mission Plan that made partition possible.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): sustained judgement on Jinnah's role against British policy, Congress, wartime and communal factors; clear conclusion. Level 2 (5–8): one-sided or lacks balance. Level 1 (1–4): narrative only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the performance of the Muslim League in the 1945–1946 elections.
parts.answer: The League won the great majority of seats reserved for Muslims in the provincial assemblies, and all 30 Muslim seats in the central Legislative Assembly. The result was seen as proof that Muslims supported the demand for Pakistan.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: won most Muslim seats in provincial elections; won all 30 Muslim seats in the central assembly; treated as a mandate for Pakistan; Congress did not win Muslim seats in the same way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the terms of the Treaty of Sèvres (1920) for the Ottoman Empire.
parts.answer: The treaty took much of the Ottoman Empire's territory: the Arab provinces were placed under British and French control as mandates; parts of Anatolia were given to Greece; the Straits were placed under international control; the Ottoman Empire was reduced to a small Turkish state. The Turkish nationalists led by Mustafa Kemal rejected the treaty.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Arab lands placed under British/French mandates; Greek gains in Anatolia/Thrace; Straits internationalised; Ottoman territory reduced; Turkish nationalists rejected it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the Turkish leader who led the nationalist movement against the Treaty of Sèvres.
parts.answer: Mustafa Kemal (later known as Atatürk)
parts.working: 1 mark: Mustafa Kemal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of years between the Treaty of Sèvres (1920) and the abolition of the caliphate by the Turkish government (1924).
parts.answer: 4 years

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Chauri Chaura incident of February 1922 and explain its effect on the Non-Cooperation Movement.
parts.answer: In February 1922 a crowd in Chauri Chaura, in the United Provinces, set fire to a police station and killed the policemen inside. Gandhi was shocked by the violence and called off the Non-Cooperation Movement, which he believed had to stay peaceful. Many nationalists were disappointed because the movement had been gaining strength.
parts.working: Up to 5: crowd attacked and burned police station, police killed (1–2); Gandhi was shocked by violence (1); Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement (1); commitment to non-violence (1); disappointment among nationalists and Khilafat supporters (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of the Ali brothers, Muhammad Ali Jauhar and Shaukat Ali, in the Khilafat Movement.
parts.answer: They were leading Khilafat campaigners who organised protests and meetings across India; they linked the Khilafat cause with the Non-Cooperation Movement; Muhammad Ali Jauhar was a powerful journalist and speaker; both were arrested by the British for their speeches and campaigning.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: leaders of Khilafat campaign; organised meetings and protests; persuaded Congress to link Khilafat with non-cooperation; arrested for their speeches (or other valid role).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Hindu–Muslim unity was strong during the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movements.
parts.answer: Gandhi supported the Khilafat cause, which gave Muslims a reason to join the wider movement; both communities shared the goal of ending British rule; joint Hindu–Muslim meetings and the boycott of British goods united people across communities; Congress and the Khilafat Committee worked together.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason fully explained, up to 4: Gandhi's support for Khilafat; shared anti-colonial goal; joint meetings and co-operation; Congress and Khilafat leaders working together.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which the Non-Cooperation Movement achieved its aims by 1922.
parts.answer: The movement's aims were swaraj (self-government), the restoration of the Khilafat and the boycott of British institutions. It showed a huge capacity for mass action and brought Hindu and Muslim leaders together, and it made the British government more cautious. But the British did not grant swaraj, the Khilafat was not restored, and the movement was called off after Chauri Chaura. The Turkish abolition of the caliphate in 1924 showed the Khilafat aim could not succeed. Judgement: the movement achieved political awakening and unity, but not its formal aims.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): balanced judgement on aims (swaraj, Khilafat, boycott) with evidence for success (mass mobilisation, unity) and failure (no swaraj, movement ended early); clear conclusion. Level 2 (5–8): description with some judgement. Level 1 (1–4): description only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An illustrative district recorded 480 students enrolled in government schools in 1920 and 312 in 1921 (illustrative figures). Calculate the percentage fall in enrolment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why students leaving government schools was an important part of the Non-Cooperation Movement.
parts.answer: It was a direct way to show rejection of British institutions; it weakened the British education system; it encouraged nationalist national schools and colleges.
parts.working: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for development (e.g. rejection of British institutions and support for national education).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why the Khilafat Movement lost its importance by 1924.
parts.answer: The Turkish government abolished the caliphate in 1924, so the cause no longer existed; the Non-Cooperation Movement had been called off in 1922, and Hindu–Muslim unity had weakened after communal violence.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: caliphate abolished 1924; NCM called off 1922; Hindu–Muslim tension and communal violence (e.g. Moplah rising).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the effect of the Moplah rising of 1921 on Hindu–Muslim relations.
parts.answer: The rising in Malabar involved Muslim peasants who attacked landlords and Hindu communities, which caused many Hindus to be killed or forced to convert, and caused deep fear among Hindus; it damaged the trust that had been built during the Khilafat campaign; many Muslim leaders and Congress leaders found it hard to explain it, so Hindu–Muslim unity became harder to maintain.
parts.working: 2 marks each for any three developed effects, up to 6: violence against Hindus and forced conversions; loss of trust between communities; Congress and Khilafat leaders put on the defensive; growth of communal suspicion and later communal organisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the boycott of British goods and institutions during the Non-Cooperation Movement.
parts.answer: People refused to buy British cloth and used Indian khadi instead; students left government schools and colleges; lawyers gave up their practice in British courts; government titles and posts were given up; councils and elections were boycotted.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: boycott of foreign cloth and promotion of khadi; students leaving schools and colleges; lawyers leaving courts; giving up titles and jobs; boycott of elections/councils.

subtopic: Partition of Bengal and the Muslim League 1905–1906

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why Lord Curzon divided Bengal in 1905.
parts.answer: The province was too large for effective administration; the Bengali-speaking areas were scattered over several provinces so a new province could be made from them; the British wanted to weaken the strong Bengali nationalist movement by splitting Bengali politics;
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained, up to 4: size of Bengal too large to govern; administrative efficiency; reducing nationalist strength in Bengal; creating a Muslim-majority eastern province; Curzon's divide-and-rule approach.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Partition of Bengal and the Muslim League 1905–1906

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Swadeshi movement of 1905–1908.
parts.answer: A campaign that encouraged Indians to buy goods made in India and to boycott British goods, especially cloth; it promoted national education and Indian industry; it was closely linked to protest against the partition of Bengal; there were large public meetings and some clashes with authorities.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: boycott of British goods; promotion of Indian-made goods; national education; link to opposition to partition; public meetings, protests and clashes.

parts.answer: Assam

parts.label: b

parts.answer: Dacca (Dhaka)
parts.working: 1 mark: Dacca (Dhaka).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of years for which the Partition of Bengal (1905) lasted until it was reversed in 1911.
parts.answer: 6 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the year in which the partition was reversed and where the reversal was announced.
parts.answer: 1911, at the Delhi Durbar (announced by King George V)

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Partition of Bengal and the Muslim League 1905–1906

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why many Muslims in East Bengal welcomed the Partition of Bengal.
parts.answer: The new province had a Muslim majority, so Muslims would gain more political and administrative influence; new posts and jobs in the new administration were expected to go to Muslims; the partition was seen as protection from the dominance of the Hindu Bengali elite in Calcutta.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained, up to 4: Muslim majority gave political influence; more government jobs and posts; freedom from dominance of Hindu landowners and professionals in Calcutta.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Partition of Bengal and the Muslim League 1905–1906

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the reversal of the Partition in 1911 increased Muslim disappointment with British policy.
parts.answer: Muslims in East Bengal had gained a province with a Muslim majority and expected it to continue; the reversal removed that province and the Muslims felt the British had given way to Hindu nationalist pressure; this led some Muslim leaders to seek an organisation that could protect Muslim interests directly.
parts.working: 3 marks per way, up to 6: loss of the Muslim-majority province; perception that British gave way to Hindu nationalist pressure; reduced trust in British protection; support for a Muslim political organisation.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Partition of Bengal and the Muslim League 1905–1906

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the British reversed the partition of Bengal in 1911.
parts.answer: The partition had caused large protests, boycotts and violence, and the British wanted calm; the Bengali nationalists had united against the partition and the British wanted to end the crisis; the capital was to be moved to Delhi and a new arrangement made for Bihar and Orissa.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason fully explained, up to 4: widespread protest and violence; boycott and political unrest; need to restore order; wider reorganisation (capital moved to Delhi; Bihar and Orissa created).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Partition of Bengal and the Muslim League 1905–1906

parts.label: a
parts.text: An illustrative census shows 18.4 million Muslims and 12.6 million people of other religions in an area with a total population of 31 million. (Illustrative figures.) Calculate the percentage of Muslims in the area, correct to one decimal place.
parts.working: 1 mark for 18.4 ÷ 31 × 100 = 59.35…; 1 mark for 59.4% (one decimal place).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Partition of Bengal and the Muslim League 1905–1906

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that the partition of Bengal was the main cause of the founding of the All-India Muslim League in 1906.
parts.answer: The partition was an important trigger: it created a Muslim-majority province that Muslims wanted to protect, and the Simla Deputation of 1906 showed the need to lobby for Muslim interests. However, Muslim leaders had also been concerned about the future of their community and about Congress's growing influence since the 1880s; the League's founding also reflected the wish for a political organisation of Muslims with loyalty to the British government. Judgement: the partition gave the immediate reason, but the founding was the result of longer-term fears and the desire for a separate political voice.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): sustained judgement weighing partition against longer-term causes (Congress growth, Muslim concerns, Simla Deputation, loyalty to Britain); clear conclusion. Level 2 (5–8): describes causes with limited judgement. Level 1 (1–4): description only.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Partition of Bengal and the Muslim League 1905–1906

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of the Swadeshi movement on relations between Hindus and Muslims in Bengal.
parts.answer: The boycott of British goods was supported by many Hindu nationalists, but many Muslims in East Bengal supported the partition; this made the Swadeshi campaign look like a Hindu movement to many Muslims; tension and clashes occurred in some towns; Hindu–Muslim relations became more divided.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Swadeshi mainly led by Hindu nationalists; Muslims in the east supported partition; perception of a Hindu-led campaign; local clashes and increased communal tension.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two leaders who founded Home Rule Leagues in 1916.
parts.answer: Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant
parts.working: 1 mark each: Tilak; Annie Besant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one aim of the Home Rule Leagues.
parts.answer: To win self-government (home rule) for India within the British Empire.
parts.working: 1 mark: self-government / home rule for India, within the British Empire.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Rowlatt Act of 1919.
parts.answer: The Act allowed the government to imprison people without trial and to try political cases without a jury, for a period after the First World War.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: passed 1919 on the advice of the Rowlatt Committee; allowed detention without trial; political cases tried without juries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Indian leaders opposed the Rowlatt Act.
parts.answer: They saw it as an attack on basic freedoms, because people could be held without trial and political activity could be crushed; it was passed although Indians had supported Britain during the war and expected reforms; the Act provoked widespread protest and hartals.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: loss of civil liberties / detention without trial; betrayal of wartime expectations; widespread protest and hartals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of years between the Lucknow Pact (1916) and the Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms (1919).
parts.answer: 3 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the Viceroy of India when the Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms were introduced.
parts.answer: Lord Chelmsford
parts.working: 1 mark: Lord Chelmsford.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Disorders Inquiry Committee (Hunter Committee) was set up in 1919, and why Indians criticised its findings.
parts.answer: It was set up to investigate the disorders in the Punjab in 1919, including the events at Amritsar; it was a government body with British members. Indian leaders criticised its report of 1920 as too lenient: it did not condemn the Jallianwala Bagh firing strongly enough, and it was seen as a whitewash of the officers involved.
parts.working: Up to 5: set up to investigate Punjab disorders of 1919 (1); included the events at Amritsar (1); government committee with British members (1); report of 1920 criticised as too lenient (1); seen as whitewash of officers' conduct (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the Lucknow Pact of 1916 helped Hindu–Muslim co-operation.
parts.answer: The Congress and the Muslim League agreed a joint scheme of reforms for India, which showed they could work together; the Pact agreed to separate electorates for Muslims with reserved seats in provincial councils, which the Congress accepted as a compromise; it provided a common platform for the Home Rule campaign.
parts.working: 2 marks for each way explained, up to 4: joint Congress–League scheme; agreement on reserved Muslim seats and separate electorates as a compromise; common platform for demands for self-government.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which the reforms of 1909–1919 satisfied the political demands of Indians.
parts.answer: The Morley–Minto Reforms of 1909 gave Indians more seats in councils and created separate electorates, which pleased many Muslim leaders but angered Congress. The Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms of 1919 introduced dyarchy in the provinces, which gave elected Indians some control over education and health, and they were a step towards self-government. However, the central government remained under British control, the franchise was narrow, and the Rowlatt Act showed the government's readiness to restrict liberty. Many Indians, especially the Congress and the Home Rule leaders, wanted full self-government and felt the reforms were too limited. Judgement: the reforms gave some Indians experience of government but did not meet the main demand for self-government.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): balanced judgement on the 1909 and 1919 reforms, weighing partial gains (councils, dyarchy, separate electorates) against limits (central control, narrow franchise, Rowlatt Act); clear conclusion. Level 2 (5–8): description with some judgement. Level 1 (1–4): narrative only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the system of dyarchy introduced in the provinces by the Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms.
parts.answer: Dyarchy divided provincial government into 'reserved' subjects, which remained under the governor and his officials (such as finance, police and law and order), and 'transferred' subjects, such as education, health and local government, which were run by elected Indian ministers.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: divided government into two parts; reserved subjects under governor's control (e.g. law and order, finance); transferred subjects run by elected Indian ministers (e.g. education, health); limited Indian power in the provinces.

stem: The Rowlatt Bills would let the authorities hold a man for up to two years without trial. Our leaders have offered loyalty throughout the war, and this is our reward. (Extract written for this exercise.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two grievances expressed in the extract.
parts.answer: Detention without trial for up to two years; Indian loyalty during the war was not rewarded.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: detention without charge; two-year detention period; loyalty during the war not rewarded; betrayal of expectations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the views in this extract were typical of many Indian political leaders in 1919.
parts.answer: Indian leaders had expected political reform after supporting the war effort; the Rowlatt Bills seemed to show that the government intended to keep repressive powers; these feelings produced protests, hartals and the call for Satyagraha.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: war effort expected to bring reform; repressive powers seen as a betrayal; widespread political protest; support for passive resistance/satyagraha.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the Jallianwala Bagh massacre changed Indian attitudes to British rule.
parts.answer: Many Indians lost faith in the British government's sense of justice, and the massacre was seen as proof that British rule was based on force; it pushed many moderate leaders towards more radical nationalist action; the massacre encouraged national unity and the spread of non-cooperation.
parts.working: 2 marks for each way explained, up to 4: loss of trust in British justice; recognition of violent repression; shift from moderate to mass nationalism; support for non-cooperation and national unity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the Secretary of State for India and the Viceroy of India in office when the Morley–Minto Reforms of 1909 were introduced.
parts.answer: John Morley (Secretary of State) and Lord Minto (Viceroy)
parts.working: 1 mark each: John Morley; Lord Minto.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why many Muslim leaders feared majority rule after 1916.
parts.answer: Muslims were a minority in most of India, so elected majorities would be dominated by Hindus; they feared the loss of jobs, language and religious rights; the Hindu-led Congress's demand for a strong central government would reduce Muslim influence; separate electorates were seen as the only protection.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained, up to 4: minority status in most provinces; fear of loss of jobs, language and religious freedom; concern about a strong central government; need for separate electorates as protection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Pirpur Report of 1938.
parts.answer: The report was prepared by a Muslim League committee led by the Pir of Pirpur, and it accused Congress governments of 1937–1939 of discrimination against Muslims. It listed complaints about Muslim employment, education and the use of Hindu symbols in government institutions. It was used by the League to show that Muslims needed separate protection.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: prepared by a League committee; led by the Pir of Pirpur; criticised Congress rule for discrimination against Muslims; listed complaints (jobs, education, symbols); used to argue for separate protection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the Muslim League launched a 'mass contact' campaign after the 1937 elections.
parts.answer: The League had won fewer Muslim seats than it wanted and needed to build support among ordinary Muslims; the campaign aimed to show that the League, not Congress, represented Muslim interests; the League wanted to build an organisation in the provinces.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained, up to 4: poor results in some provinces; need for mass support among Muslims; to show League represented Muslim interests; building provincial organisation.

parts.answer: Sikander Hayat Khan; the Unionist Party
parts.working: 1 mark for Sikander Hayat Khan; 1 mark for the Unionist Party.

parts.answer: Any two of: Madras, Bombay, United Provinces, Bihar, Central Provinces, Orissa
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct provinces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why the Congress ministries resigned in 1939.
parts.answer: The Viceroy had declared India at war with Germany without consulting Indian leaders; Congress wanted a promise of independence in return for support in the war.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: Viceroy declared war without consultation; demand for independence after war; protest at lack of Indian voice; Congress withdrew from provincial governments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that the Congress ministries of 1937–1939 convinced many Muslims that separate electorates were essential for their protection.
parts.answer: Several Congress actions were seen by Muslims as discriminatory: the use of 'Bande Mataram' in schools, complaints about the treatment of Muslims in government jobs and the Pirpur Report's accusations gave the League evidence. Congress argued that its policies were for all Indians and not against Muslims, and some Muslim leaders in Punjab and Bengal still worked with non-League parties. Judgement: Congress rule played a major part in convincing many Muslims of the need for separate protection, although the League's campaign and the wider political situation were also important.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): sustained judgement weighing Congress actions (Bande Mataram, jobs, Pirpur evidence) and the League's campaign against Congress's view and non-League Muslim leaders; clear conclusion. Level 2 (5–8): one-sided or lacks balance. Level 1 (1–4): narrative only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Muslims objected to the singing of 'Bande Mataram' in government schools under Congress rule.
parts.answer: The song's lyrics praised a Hindu goddess and were seen as Hindu religious imagery; Muslims felt pressured to take part in Hindu worship, which conflicted with their faith; the League used this as evidence that Congress rule was against Muslims.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: lyrics seen as Hindu religious imagery; forced participation conflicted with Islamic belief; seen as Congress favouring Hindu culture; used by League as evidence of discrimination.
