parts.working: 2 marks for each advantage explained, up to 4: shared suppliers and lower costs; skilled labour pool; shared infrastructure; closeness to buyers and exporters; sharing ideas and technology.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two environmental problems caused by large-scale manufacturing in Karachi.
parts.answer: Factories release smoke and fumes that cause air pollution and respiratory illness for residents; untreated industrial effluent enters rivers and the sea, which harms fish and coastal water quality; industrial waste and solid waste add to land pollution and can block drains, which increases flooding risk.
parts.working: 3 marks per problem, up to 6: air pollution from smoke or fumes with a health effect; water pollution from untreated effluent; land or solid-waste pollution with a linked effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two advantages of large-scale production compared with small workshops.
parts.answer: Large factories can buy raw materials in bulk at lower prices; they can use machines and specialised labour to produce more goods at lower unit cost; they can sell to export markets and reach more customers; they can afford research and quality control.
parts.working: 2 marks for each advantage described, up to 4: bulk buying and lower costs; economies of scale and lower unit cost; access to larger or export markets; investment in research and quality control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An illustrative year shows that three steel plants produced 1,800 tonnes (Plant A), 2,700 tonnes (Plant B) and 1,500 tonnes (Plant C). (Illustrative figures.) Calculate the percentage of total output produced by Plant B.
parts.working: 1 mark for total output 6,000 tonnes; 1 mark for 2,700 ÷ 6,000 × 100 = 45.0%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Plant A increases its output by 15%, while the other plants stay the same. Calculate the new total output of the three plants in tonnes.
parts.answer: 6,270 tonnes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the province in which the Dhabeji Special Economic Zone is located.
parts.answer: Sindh
parts.working: 1 mark: Sindh.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the province in which the Rashakai Special Economic Zone is located.
parts.answer: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
parts.working: 1 mark: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two incentives that firms in export processing zones may receive.
parts.answer: Tax holidays or reduced taxes for a number of years; duty-free import of machinery and raw materials needed for export production; simplified customs procedures; facilities such as power, water and transport provided within the zone.
parts.working: 2 marks for each incentive described, up to 4: tax holidays or reduced taxes; duty-free imports of inputs; simplified customs; provided infrastructure (power, water, roads).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An illustrative export processing zone firm exports 40,000 units of a product at $12 each. (Illustrative figures.) Calculate the value of the exports in dollars.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The firm employs 800 workers. Calculate the value of exports per worker in dollars.
parts.answer: $600 per worker
parts.working: 1 mark for 480,000 ÷ 800 (or the equivalent); 1 mark for $600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which Special Economic Zones developed under CPEC will benefit poor people in rural areas of Pakistan.
parts.answer: SEZs can create jobs, bring investment in power and roads, and increase exports, which may raise incomes for local families and reduce migration to cities. However, many SEZ jobs require skills that local rural people may not have, and some land may be taken from farmers with low compensation. Benefits may go to large investors and urban workers, while rural poverty remains. Judgement: rural benefits depend on training, local hiring, fair land compensation and linkages with local suppliers; without these, the benefits are likely to be limited.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): sustained judgement weighing job and income gains against skills gaps, land issues and distribution of benefits, with conditions; clear conclusion. Level 2 (5–8): describes benefits and drawbacks with limited judgement. Level 1 (1–4): description only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why provincial governments set up industrial estates.
parts.answer: Estates provide ready-built plots with power, water and roads, so small firms do not need to build infrastructure themselves; they help to spread industry to different towns and reduce concentration in big cities; they make it easier for government to regulate and support small firms.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained, up to 4: ready infrastructure for small firms; spread of industry to towns; reduce pressure on large cities; easier support and regulation of small firms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'industrial estate'.
parts.answer: An area of land divided into plots for factories and workshops, with shared infrastructure such as roads, power and water supplied by a government or private agency.
parts.working: 1 mark for an area divided into plots for manufacturing; 1 mark for shared infrastructure provided.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A Special Economic Zone has three zones of 250 hectares each, and 60% of the land has been developed. Calculate the number of developed hectares.
parts.answer: 450 hectares
parts.working: 1 mark for total area 3 × 250 = 750 hectares; 1 mark for 750 × 0.6 = 450 hectares.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how tax holidays and good infrastructure can encourage foreign companies to invest in Pakistan's industrial zones.
parts.answer: Tax holidays lower the cost of setting up and running a business, so profits are higher for investors; good roads, ports and reliable power reduce transport and production costs and delays; the presence of incentives and facilities signals that the government is serious about investment, which reduces risk for foreign investors.
parts.working: 3 marks each for two developed explanations, up to 6: tax holidays lower costs and raise expected profit; infrastructure reduces costs and delays; both reduce risk and signal stable support for investors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages of export processing zones for the workers employed in them.
parts.answer: Wages may be low and working hours long, because firms compete to attract investment; workers may have limited trade union rights, so they cannot easily bargain for better conditions; jobs may be temporary, so workers have little security; the zones may provide poor health and safety protection.
parts.working: 2 marks for each disadvantage explained, up to 4: low wages and long hours; limited union rights; insecure or temporary jobs; poor health and safety.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two traditional handicrafts of Pakistan and the place for which each is well known.
parts.answer: Any two of: Multan blue pottery (Multan); Hala glazed pottery (Hala, Sindh); lacquerwork (Hala); Peshawari leather chappals (Peshawar)
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct craft; 1 mark for the correct place. Accept any two well-known correct pairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why cottage industries are labour-intensive.
parts.answer: They use simple hand tools rather than expensive machines, so labour makes up a large part of production; family members often work together in the home, which means many people are needed for each product; the work is detailed and skilled, so it cannot easily be done by machines.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained, up to 4: simple hand tools; low capital and reliance on labour; family or home-based production; detailed craft work needing people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A workshop makes 12 chairs each day, works 26 days in a month, and sells each chair for Rs 1,800. Calculate the monthly sales revenue of the workshop in rupees.
parts.working: 1 mark for 12 × 26 = 312 chairs; 1 mark for 312 × 1,800 = Rs 561,600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A women's cooperative of 18 members produces 540 embroidered shirts in one month. Calculate the average number of shirts produced by each member.
parts.answer: 30 shirts per member
parts.working: 1 mark for 540 ÷ 18; 1 mark for 30 shirts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which cottage industries can reduce rural poverty in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Cottage industries give rural families extra income without leaving home, which helps women in particular, and they use local materials and skills so money stays in the area. However, they usually earn low and irregular incomes, depend on middlemen who take most of the profit, and face competition from cheap machine-made goods. Without access to credit, markets and training, their effect on poverty is limited. Judgement: cottage industries can reduce poverty for some households, but reaching lasting improvement needs better markets, fair prices and finance.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): sustained judgement weighing income and social benefits against low incomes, middlemen, competition and lack of finance; clear conclusion. Level 2 (5–8): describes benefits and problems with limited judgement. Level 1 (1–4): description only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two problems that small-scale industries face when trying to obtain finance.
parts.answer: Banks often ask for property or collateral, which many small producers do not have; loans can be expensive or take a long time to arrange, and the paperwork is difficult for people without formal records.
parts.working: 2 marks for each problem described, up to 4: lack of collateral; high interest or cost of borrowing; slow and complicated loan process; lack of formal business records.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two sources of finance that small enterprises in Pakistan can use.
parts.answer: Any two of: microfinance banks; family savings; government loan schemes; loans from cooperatives or informal lenders
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct sources.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two effects of exporting handicrafts on the incomes of rural craft workers.
parts.answer: Export orders can raise the incomes of craft workers and create more regular work; export buyers may pay higher prices than local markets, which increases household income; but where middlemen take the profit, the gain may go to them rather than the producers.
parts.working: 2 marks for each effect explained, up to 4: higher prices and incomes; more regular orders; income for households and women; middlemen may keep much of the gain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two effects of competition from machine-made goods on handicraft workers.
parts.answer: Machine-made goods are cheaper and more uniform, so customers may buy them instead of handicrafts, which reduces demand and sales for craft workers; craft workers may be forced to lower their prices or leave the craft, which reduces household income and skills passed down the generations.
parts.working: 3 marks for each effect explained, up to 6: lower demand and sales (1) with reason (cheaper, uniform goods) (1) and effect on income or prices (1); workers leave the craft or cut prices (1) with consequence for skills or income (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which middlemen affect the incomes of craft workers.
parts.answer: Middlemen buy from producers at low prices and sell at higher prices, so much of the profit is kept by the middlemen; they may delay payment, which forces workers to borrow or sell early at a loss; they control access to markets, so workers have little choice of buyer.
parts.working: 2 marks for each way described, up to 4: low buying price and large margin; delayed payment; control of markets and limited bargaining power.

stem: A potter in Multan says: 'Clay used to cost a little, now the price has nearly doubled, and the middlemen pay us only when they have sold the pots. We cannot afford to buy the wood for the kiln, so we sell earlier at a loss.' (Extract written for this exercise.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two problems described in the extract.
parts.answer: Clay prices have nearly doubled; middlemen pay only after they sell and so delay payment; the potter cannot afford wood for the kiln.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: rise in clay prices; delayed payment by middlemen; cannot afford kiln fuel; forced to sell early at a loss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the middlemen's payment method can make the potter's situation worse.
parts.answer: Because payment is delayed, the potter has little cash to buy materials, so may have to sell pots early at a loss; the potter may then need to borrow money, which adds costs.
parts.working: 1 mark for delayed payment; 1 mark for the lack of cash to buy materials; 1 mark for the consequence (sale at a loss or borrowing).

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of employment in the informal sector.
parts.answer: Any two of: no written contract; no social security or pension; not registered with tax or labour authorities; work is often casual or irregular
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two features.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A formal sector worker is paid Rs 1,500 a day for 26 days in a month. Calculate the monthly pay in rupees.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An informal sector worker is paid Rs 1,000 a day for 22 days in a month. Calculate the difference between the two monthly pay amounts in rupees.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why many people in Pakistan work in the informal sector.
parts.answer: There are not enough formal jobs for the growing workforce, so people work in informal jobs to earn a living; many people lack qualifications or the documents needed for formal jobs; informal work can be done near home and at flexible hours, which suits women and those with family responsibilities.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained, up to 4: lack of formal jobs; low skills or lack of documents; flexibility and nearness to home; income needed when no other work is available.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that the informal sector helps economic development in Pakistan.
parts.answer: The informal sector provides large numbers of jobs and income to people who would otherwise be unemployed, and it supplies cheap goods and services to poorer households. It also gives entrepreneurs a start in business. However, informal workers pay little or no tax, so government revenue for schools, roads and health is reduced; they lack social security and training, which limits productivity and wages; and their businesses often cannot borrow or expand. Judgement: the informal sector supports livelihoods in the short term but holds back development unless workers and firms are brought into the formal economy.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): sustained judgement weighing employment and income benefits against tax loss, low productivity and limited growth; clear conclusion. Level 2 (5–8): describes benefits and drawbacks with limited judgement. Level 1 (1–4): description only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two problems that informal sector workers face.
parts.answer: They have no written contract, so employers can dismiss them without notice or compensation; they have no pension, sick pay or health insurance, so illness can leave a family without income; they are not protected by labour laws on minimum wage and working hours.
parts.working: 2 marks for each problem described, up to 4: no contract or job security; no pension, sick pay or insurance; not covered by labour laws; unsafe working conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two examples of informal sector work in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two of: street vending; rickshaw or motorbike taxi driving; home-based embroidery or stitching; daily-wage construction work; domestic work
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct examples.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A survey of 9,800 workers finds that 73% of them work in the informal sector. (Illustrative figures.) Calculate the number of workers in the informal sector.
parts.answer: 7,154 workers
parts.working: 1 mark for 9,800 × 0.73 = 7,154; 1 mark for the answer as a whole number of workers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the government could bring informal sector workers and firms into the formal sector.
parts.answer: Simple registration and tax systems for small businesses would bring them into the official economy while keeping costs low; social security and health schemes for informal workers, with contributions that are affordable, would give them protection; access to credit and training would help small firms grow and meet formal standards.
parts.working: 3 marks for each way explained, up to 6: simple registration or tax schemes (1) with benefit (1); social security or health scheme (1) with benefit (1); access to credit and training (1) with link to formalisation (1).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why informal sector workers have little protection under labour laws.
parts.answer: Labour laws usually apply only to workers in registered firms with written contracts, so informal workers are not covered; many informal workers do not know their rights or cannot afford legal action; enforcement by labour inspectors is weak in small and home-based workplaces.
parts.working: 2 marks for each point explained, up to 4: laws apply to registered firms and contracts; lack of awareness or cost of legal action; weak enforcement in small or home workplaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two groups of people who are most likely to work informally in rural Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two of: women doing home-based work; agricultural labourers; seasonal workers; small traders
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two groups.

stem: A woman who makes embroidered cloth at home says: 'I work from morning until night, but there is no contract, no leave and no pension. When the middleman is late with payment, I have nothing to feed my children.' (Extract written for this exercise.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two problems described in the extract.
parts.answer: No contract, no leave and no pension; payment is sometimes late.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: no contract; no leave or pension; late payment by the middleman.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the woman's situation is typical of many home-based workers in the informal sector.
parts.answer: Home-based workers are usually paid by middlemen rather than employers, so they have no legal right to fixed pay; they have no social security, so a delay in payment or illness causes hardship; their work is not recorded, so their situation is hidden from government.
parts.working: 1 mark for an informal pay link; 1 mark for the lack of social security; 1 mark for the work being unrecorded or middleman-based.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Eight home-based workers each earn Rs 450 a day for 20 days in a month. Calculate the total monthly earnings of the eight workers in rupees.
parts.working: 1 mark for 450 × 20 = 9,000 per worker; 1 mark for 9,000 × 8 = Rs 72,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a large informal sector can reduce government tax revenue.
parts.answer: Informal businesses and workers are not registered, so they do not pay income tax or sales tax, which reduces the money the government collects; with less revenue, the government has less money for schools, roads and health; the government may then raise taxes on the formal sector, which can discourage formal business.
parts.working: 2 marks for each point explained, up to 4: unregistered firms and workers do not pay tax; less revenue for public services; pressure to tax the formal sector more, which can discourage registration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'tariff' and give one example of a product that might face a tariff when imported.
parts.answer: A tax or duty charged on goods when they are imported (or exported); e.g. an import duty on foreign cars or electronic goods.
parts.working: 1 mark for a tax or duty on goods crossing a border; 1 mark for a correct example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how an import quota restricts trade.
parts.answer: A quota limits the quantity of a product that may be imported in a given period, so foreign suppliers cannot sell more than the allowed amount; this protects domestic producers from competition and can raise prices for buyers.
parts.working: 1 mark for a limit on the quantity; 1 mark for effect on foreign suppliers; 1 mark for protection of domestic producers or higher prices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A garment exporter's production cost for one batch is Rs 450 per item. The exporter adds a profit of 20% on cost. Calculate the profit per item in rupees.
parts.answer: Rs 90

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the selling price per item in rupees.
parts.answer: Rs 540

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which high transport costs make it harder for Pakistani exporters to sell abroad.
parts.answer: Higher transport costs raise the final price of exports, so Pakistani goods become less competitive against rival producers; delays in transport and at ports mean goods may arrive late, which can lose buyers or require expensive air freight; the extra cost reduces profit margins for exporters.
parts.working: 2 marks for each way explained, up to 4: higher final price and lower competitiveness; delays and late delivery; reduced profit margins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which the development of Gwadar port could increase Pakistan's trade.
parts.answer: Gwadar is a deep-sea port on the Arabian Sea, on the shipping routes to the Gulf and the Middle East, and it is part of the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor. It could shorten shipping routes for trade with the Middle East and Africa and give landlocked Central Asia a route to the sea, and it could bring investment in roads and industry. However, trade through Gwadar depends on good road and rail links, reliable power and water, and investment in the port's facilities; trade volumes also depend on Karachi's established role and on regional security. Judgement: Gwadar could raise trade substantially if the links and facilities are built and used, but its impact would be limited without better connections and stability.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): sustained judgement on Gwadar's advantages (location, CPEC, shorter routes) against infrastructure, security and competition from Karachi; clear conclusion. Level 2 (5–8): describes advantages and problems with limited judgement. Level 1 (1–4): description only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a free trade agreement.
parts.answer: An agreement between two or more countries to reduce or remove tariffs and other barriers on trade between them.
parts.working: 1 mark for an agreement between countries; 1 mark for reducing or removing tariffs and barriers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two effects of a fall in world demand for cotton textiles on Pakistan's economy.
parts.answer: Export earnings fall, which reduces foreign currency and makes it harder to pay for imports; textile mills reduce production or close, so workers lose jobs and farmers may find it harder to sell cotton, which reduces rural incomes.
parts.working: 2 marks for each effect explained, up to 4: fall in export earnings and foreign currency; job losses in mills; lower demand for cotton and lower farm incomes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between free trade and protectionism.
parts.answer: Free trade means goods can move between countries with few or no tariffs or quotas, so competition is open to all producers; protectionism uses tariffs, quotas or subsidies to protect domestic producers from foreign competition.
parts.working: 2 marks for a correct definition of free trade (open, few barriers); 2 marks for protectionism (tariffs, quotas or subsidies to protect domestic industry).

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a trade surplus.
parts.answer: The value of a country's exports is greater than the value of its imports over a period.
parts.working: 1 mark for exports greater than imports; 1 mark for a period of measurement (e.g. one year).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text: An illustrative table shows exports to the USA of US$2,400 million and imports from the USA of US$1,100 million in one year. (Illustrative figures.) Calculate the balance of trade with the USA in US$ million.
parts.answer: +1,300 (a surplus)
parts.working: 1 mark: 2,400 − 1,100 = 1,300 (positive, so a surplus).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether this is a surplus or a deficit.
parts.answer: Surplus
parts.working: 1 mark: exports exceed imports, so a surplus.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text: An illustrative year shows total exports of US$8,000 million, of which US$1,440 million went to China. (Illustrative figures.) Calculate the percentage of total exports that went to China, correct to one decimal place.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a country may have a trade surplus with one partner but a trade deficit with another.
parts.answer: The country may export high-value goods to one partner that buys them in large quantities, while buying from another partner products that are cheaper or essential, such as machinery or oil; the partners may have different levels of demand for each product, or different tariffs and trade agreements.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained, up to 4: different products traded with each partner; different demand or prices; trade agreements and tariffs that differ between partners; reliance on essential imports from one partner.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a persistent trade deficit could affect a country's exchange rate.
parts.answer: When imports are greater than exports, the country must sell its currency to buy foreign currency to pay for imports, which increases the supply of its currency; this tends to lower its value against other currencies, so the exchange rate depreciates; a weaker currency makes imports more expensive, which may increase inflation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six linked steps, up to 6: more domestic currency sold to buy foreign currency (1); supply of domestic currency rises (1); currency depreciates (1); imports become more expensive (1); inflation or pressure on the economy (1); clear link from the deficit to the exchange rate (1).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text: An illustrative year shows total exports of US$8,000 million and total imports of US$12,500 million. (Illustrative figures.) Calculate the total value of trade (exports plus imports) in US$ million.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the balance of trade and state whether it is a surplus or a deficit.
parts.answer: −4,500 (a deficit of US$4,500 million)
parts.working: 1 mark for 8,000 − 12,500 = −4,500; 1 mark for stating a deficit.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two neighbouring countries with which Pakistan trades across land borders.
parts.answer: Any two of: Afghanistan, China, Iran, India (via the Wagah border trade, where allowed)
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct neighbouring countries.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Trading partners and balance of trade

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which a persistent trade deficit is harmful to Pakistan's economy.
parts.answer: A trade deficit means the country must borrow or use foreign reserves to pay for imports, which can increase debt, reduce reserves and put pressure on the currency, and it may weaken the country's ability to pay for development. However, a deficit can also mean that the country is importing machinery, raw materials and energy that support growth, and it can be financed by remittances, foreign investment and loans that are used productively. Judgement: a deficit is harmful when it is financed by short-term borrowing and reflects weak exports, but it is less harmful when imports build productive capacity and exports are growing.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): sustained judgement weighing harm (debt, reserves, currency pressure) against benefits (productive imports, financing sources); clear conclusion linked to the type of imports and financing. Level 2 (5–8): one-sided or limited judgement. Level 1 (1–4): description only.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two of Pakistan's main imports other than petroleum products.
parts.answer: Any two of: machinery; edible oils; iron and steel; medicines; chemicals; tea; electrical goods
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct imports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan imports large quantities of edible oil.
parts.answer: Pakistan does not produce enough oilseeds such as rapeseed and sunflower to meet domestic demand, so it must import cooking oil and palm oil; the population is large and the demand for cooking oil is high; imported palm oil is often cheaper than locally produced oil.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained, up to 4: insufficient domestic oilseed production; large population and high demand; cost advantage of palm oil imports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why cotton yarn is an important export for Pakistan.
parts.answer: Pakistan grows cotton and has a large spinning industry, so yarn can be made from domestic raw materials and sold abroad; many countries that make garments buy yarn from Pakistan, which earns foreign currency and provides jobs in mills.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained, up to 4: domestic cotton supply and spinning industry; demand from garment makers abroad; foreign currency earnings and jobs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the difference between visible trade and invisible trade.
parts.answer: Visible trade is the trade in physical goods that can be seen and counted; invisible trade is the trade in services, such as banking, tourism, insurance and IT services.
parts.working: 1 mark for visible trade as physical goods; 1 mark for invisible trade as services.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An illustrative table gives exports (US$ million) for one year: textiles 16,000; rice 3,000; leather 1,200; sports goods 800; fish 500. (Illustrative figures.) Calculate the total value of these exports.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of these exports made up by textiles, correct to one decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which Pakistan should diversify its exports into IT and other services.
parts.answer: Services such as IT, freelancing and software exports bring in foreign currency, need less physical infrastructure than factories or ports, and can grow fast with skilled young people; they reduce dependence on textiles, which faces price competition. However, services need reliable internet, skills and good education, and many firms face problems with payment systems, internet speed and the lack of export-finance. Some services also depend on the same few markets. Judgement: diversification into services is important and can add to growth, but it cannot replace the goods trade in the short term and must be supported by skills and infrastructure.
parts.working: Level 3 (9–12): sustained judgement weighing gains (foreign currency, diversification, skills) against constraints (infrastructure, skills, market concentration, payment issues) with a clear conclusion. Level 2 (5–8): describes benefits and problems with limited judgement. Level 1 (1–4): description only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why mangoes and kinnow are exported to the Middle East and Europe.
parts.answer: Pakistan's mangoes and kinnow are well known for their taste and quality, so buyers in the Gulf and Europe want them; the Gulf is close, so fruit can reach the market quickly; there are large Pakistani communities abroad who create demand for these fruits.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained, up to 4: known quality and taste; short transport distance to the Gulf; demand from Pakistani communities or consumers in Europe; seasonal demand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two ports in Pakistan that handle international trade.
parts.answer: Any two of: Karachi Port, Port Qasim, Gwadar Port
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct ports.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two effects of importing machinery for the textile industry.
parts.answer: Imported machinery can improve the quality and speed of production, which helps exporters meet buyers' standards; it may lead to higher output and lower unit costs; but it can also add to the import bill and increase dependence on foreign suppliers.
parts.working: 2 marks for each effect described, up to 4: improved quality and productivity; lower unit cost or higher output; higher import bill; dependence on foreign suppliers and spare parts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Exports of fish fell from 3,200 tonnes in one year to 2,560 tonnes the next. (Illustrative figures.) Calculate the percentage fall in tonnes of fish exported.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why fish exports might fall in this way.
parts.answer: Overfishing or a ban on fishing in some seasons may reduce the catch; exports may be rejected if they do not meet quality or hygiene standards set by buyers; a fall in prices or demand from main buyers may reduce the quantities sold; bad weather or poor storage facilities may reduce the quantity that reaches the market.
parts.working: 2 marks for each reason explained, up to 4: reduced catch (overfishing or seasonal ban); failure to meet quality or hygiene standards; fall in demand or prices; weather or storage problems.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Sialkot is important for Pakistan's exports of sports goods.
parts.answer: Sialkot has a long tradition of making footballs and other sports goods, with skilled workers and small workshops that stitch and assemble products; the city has many exporters with contacts overseas, so it is a major centre for exporting sports goods to buyers in Europe and North America.
parts.working: 2 marks for each point explained, up to 4: skilled labour and traditional craft; many workshops and exporters; links to overseas buyers; significant export earnings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total value of these four exports (US$ million, illustrative figures): rice 1,100; cotton yarn 1,400; leather 650; mangoes 300.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the seasonal pattern of mango exports from Pakistan.
parts.answer: Mango exports are concentrated in the summer months, when the fruit is harvested; the exports are sent by air and by sea to the Gulf, Europe and other markets; exports are high for a few months and small or nil for the rest of the year; the season's quality and weather affect the size of the crop.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: exports concentrated in summer harvest; air and sea shipments; high peaks and low volumes for the rest of the year; weather and crop quality affect volumes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why rice exports from Pakistan depend on the water supply from the Indus river system.
parts.answer: Rice is a water-intensive crop grown in flooded fields, so it needs reliable irrigation; the Indus river system supplies much of the irrigation water in the rice-growing areas, so a shortage in the river flow can reduce the crop and the volume available for export; floods or drought can also damage the harvest.
parts.working: 2 marks for each point explained, up to 4: rice is water-intensive; Indus system supplies irrigation; reduced flows lower the crop and exports; floods or drought damage harvests.

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company
stem:
Timeline (well-established dates):
1757 Battle of Plassey
1764 Battle of Buxar
1765 Treaty of Allahabad
1849 Punjab annexed by the Company
1856 Awadh annexed by the Company

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the year in which the Company received the diwani (revenue rights) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
parts.answer: 1765 (Treaty of Allahabad)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of years between the Battle of Plassey and the annexation of the Punjab.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the Company's victory at Plassey was followed by the grant of the diwani in 1765.
parts.answer: Plassey put Bengal's army and government under Company control; Mir Jafar depended on the Company; the Company wanted secure revenue to pay for its army and trade; Shah Alam II had been beaten at Buxar (1764) and needed Company support, so he granted the diwani.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Company forces controlled Bengal after Plassey; Mir Jafar was installed and depended on the Company; the Company needed revenue to pay for armies and trade; Shah Alam II was defeated at Buxar (1764) and was weak; the grant gave the Company control of revenue without ruling directly.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of Robert Clive in the Company's rise in Bengal between 1756 and 1757.
parts.answer: Clive recaptured Calcutta from Siraj-ud-Daulah in early 1757, then defeated him at Plassey (June 1757) with a small force, and secured Mir Jafar's installation as Nawab.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Clive led Company forces; recaptured Calcutta (1757); victory at Plassey, June 1757, with a small army; Siraj-ud-Daulah defeated; Mir Jafar made Nawab; Clive later became Governor of Bengal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why most of the Company's army in India was made up of Indian soldiers (sepoys).
parts.answer: Sepoys were cheaper to pay than British soldiers; they knew the climate, languages and terrain; few British soldiers were available in India.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of the reasons given.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company
stem: Illustrative example (figures invented for this question): a zamindar collected Rs 96,000 a year in rent from his peasants and paid the Company a fixed revenue of Rs 60,000 a year under the Permanent Settlement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Permanent Settlement of Bengal (1793).
parts.answer: Introduced by Lord Cornwallis in 1793: zamindars became hereditary owners of their estates; they paid a fixed annual revenue to the Company; the amount did not change with the harvest; zamindars who failed to pay lost their estates.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: introduced by Cornwallis in 1793; zamindars made hereditary owners; revenue fixed permanently; revenue payable in good and bad harvests; estates lost for non-payment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the zamindar's profit as a percentage of the revenue he paid to the Company. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the Permanent Settlement was useful to the Company but harmful for many peasants.
parts.answer: The Company received a fixed, certain income and did not have to manage collection; peasants paid rents to zamindars, who could raise them and evict tenants, and peasants had no protection in poor harvests.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Company gained fixed and certain revenue; cheaper to administer; zamindars could raise rents; tenants could be evicted; peasants had no protection in bad years; many fell into debt and lost land.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company
stem: Source A (written for this question, summarising a policy of 1793): 'From 1793 the most senior posts in the Company's civil and judicial service were reserved for Europeans. Indians could hold only lower posts, and they were paid less for the same work.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: According to Source A, which group could hold the most senior posts in the Company's civil and judicial service?
parts.answer: Europeans (Englishmen)
parts.working: 1 mark: Europeans or Englishmen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Company wanted to keep Indians out of the most senior posts.
parts.answer: The British believed Indians were less trustworthy and capable of senior office; senior posts were kept for Britons to keep control of government in British hands; the Company feared that educated Indians would challenge its rule; it used senior posts and high pay to reward its own people.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: British racial and cultural prejudice; wish to keep control of government; fear of educated Indians challenging British rule; reserving posts and salaries for Britons (patronage).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company

parts.label: a
parts.text: 'Economic motives were more important than political ambition in the East India Company's expansion between 1757 and 1856.' How far do you agree? Give reasons for your answer.
parts.answer: A balanced judgement: economic motives (monopoly of trade, revenue from the diwani, profits from cotton, indigo and opium, the cost of wars and debts) against political and strategic motives (Subsidiary Alliance, Doctrine of Lapse, annexations to secure borders, rivalry with the French). Profit needed power; power protected profit.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–4): describes some economic and political motives. Level 2 (5–9): explains both with examples (diwani 1765; Subsidiary Alliance 1798; Doctrine of Lapse 1848–56; Sindh 1843 and Punjab 1849 for security) and reaches a partly supported view. Level 3 (10–14): clear, balanced judgement that links the two motives, with a supported conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: British expansion and the East India Company
stem: Annexations by the Company (dates well established): Sindh 1843; Punjab 1849; Awadh 1856. Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the grounds of misgovernment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the Governor-General who annexed Awadh in 1856.
parts.answer: Lord Dalhousie
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the annexation of Awadh (1856) differed from the Company's conquest of Bengal after Plassey as a method of expansion.
parts.answer: Bengal was won by battle and the Company then used a puppet Nawab; Awadh was taken without a battle, on the pretext of misgovernment, and its ruler was deposed and its administration taken over; the annexation depended on legal and political argument rather than war.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 5: Bengal taken by war at Plassey, Awadh by annexation without a major battle; misgovernment used as a pretext for Awadh; ruler (Nawab) deposed; Company took over revenue and courts; annexation of Awadh angered landlords (linked to 1857).

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and the Aligarh Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the book Sir Syed wrote about the historic buildings of Delhi and give the year it was first published.
parts.answer: Asar-us-Sanadid, 1847
parts.working: 1 mark: Asar-us-Sanadid. 1 mark: 1847.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the work of the Scientific Society founded by Sir Syed in 1864.
parts.answer: It translated important English scientific and historical books into Urdu so that Indians could read them; it spread modern knowledge among Muslims; it encouraged study of science and modern subjects.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: founded 1864; translated English books into Urdu; spread science and modern learning; encouraged Muslims to study modern subjects; aimed at Muslims who did not read English.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and the Aligarh Movement
stem: Illustrative figures (invented for this question): a college in the Aligarh tradition had 90 students in its first year and 360 students ten years later.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the number of students over the ten years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which the Aligarh college differed from traditional Muslim religious schools (madrasas) of the time.
parts.answer: The Aligarh college taught English and Western sciences and mathematics alongside Islamic studies; it had a modern curriculum with boarding and sports; it co-operated with the British government.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: taught English and Western subjects; modern curriculum; boarding and sport; sought co-operation with the British government; prepared students for government and professional careers.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and the Aligarh Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the town where the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College was founded and the year in which it was founded.
parts.answer: Aligarh; 1875
parts.working: 1 mark: Aligarh. 1 mark: 1875.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two aims Sir Syed hoped the college would achieve for Muslims.
parts.answer: To give Muslims a modern education in English and science; to prepare them for government service and public life; to improve the social and economic position of Muslims.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of the aims given.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and the Aligarh Movement
stem: After visiting England in 1869–70, Sir Syed started a journal in 1870.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two aims of the journal that Sir Syed started in 1870.
parts.answer: Any two of: to encourage social reform among Muslims; to promote modern education and scientific thinking; to criticise superstition and blind imitation (taqlid).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two aims.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Sir Syed believed a journal could help Muslim society.
parts.answer: A journal could spread modern ideas and encourage Muslims to adopt reform of manners and education; it could criticise outdated customs and superstition; it could reach readers beyond the college and explain Western ideas.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: spread modern ideas; encourage reform of social manners and customs; criticise superstition and blind imitation; reach a wide readership; explain Western learning to Muslims.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and the Aligarh Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Sir Syed encouraged Muslims to combine reason and science with their religious beliefs.
parts.answer: Sir Syed argued that Islam and reason were compatible; he encouraged a rational reading of the Quran; he believed the laws of nature were part of God's plan so science should be studied; Muslims had to learn science to progress; he opposed blind imitation of old scholars; this would help Muslims meet the challenge of Western knowledge.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 6: Islam and reason compatible; rational interpretation of scripture; study of nature and science is religious duty; progress requires modern learning; opposition to blind imitation (taqlid); meeting the challenge of Western knowledge.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and the Aligarh Movement
stem: Source A (written for this question): 'Let our young men learn the sciences and the languages of the rulers, but let them not forget their own faith and their own history. A nation that loses its learning falls behind; a nation that loses its faith loses itself.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: According to Source A, what two things should young Muslims not forget while they learn the sciences and languages of the rulers?
parts.answer: Their own faith and their own history.
parts.working: 1 mark each for the two things.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Sir Syed wanted Muslims to learn Western knowledge and also keep their own religion and history.
parts.answer: Western knowledge was needed for government jobs, the professions and economic success; religion and history gave Muslims identity and moral character; keeping their heritage stopped Muslims from losing identity; a balance would earn respect from the British and let Muslims take part in public life.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Western knowledge needed for jobs and progress; religion gives identity and moral discipline; heritage prevents loss of identity; balance earns respect and a place in public life; a nation without learning falls behind.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and the Aligarh Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: 'Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's loyalty to the British government was the most important feature of his political thought.' How far do you agree?
parts.answer: A judgement that weighs Sir Syed's loyalty to the British (after 1857, support for co-operation, advice against joining the Congress) against his educational, social and religious reforms (Aligarh college, Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq, Scientific Society) and his concern for Muslim identity.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–4): describes Sir Syed's loyalty and some reforms. Level 2 (5–9): explains loyalty and reforms with evidence and considers both sides. Level 3 (10–14): reaches a supported judgement, showing whether loyalty was the central principle or a means to the aim of Muslim progress.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and the Aligarh Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between the Aligarh approach to Muslim education and the approach of the Deoband seminary.
parts.answer: Aligarh taught English and Western sciences, while Deoband focused on traditional Islamic learning in Arabic and Urdu; Aligarh co-operated with the British government, while Deoband kept its distance from government.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the Aligarh and Deoband approaches each affected Muslims in India.
parts.answer: Aligarh produced English-educated Muslims for government service and the professions and helped shape Muslim political leadership; Deoband kept Islamic learning alive and built a network of madrasas, which preserved Muslim religious identity and independence.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 6: Aligarh produced English-educated graduates for government and professions; Aligarh supported loyalty and political voice; Deoband preserved Islamic learning and identity; Deoband built a network of madrasas; both shaped the debate on Muslim identity; differences between the two approaches divided Muslims.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
subtopic: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan and the Aligarh Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the claim that Sir Syed's reforms widened the gap between the Muslim and Hindu communities.
parts.answer: Arguments for: the Hindi–Urdu controversy and Sir Syed's opposition to the Congress made Muslims seem a separate political community, and Aligarh encouraged a distinct Muslim identity. Arguments against: his reforms aimed at Muslim progress, not hostility to Hindus, and the divide also had other causes, such as British policies of separate electorates and the rise of Hindu nationalism. Judgement: his work helped to shape Muslim separateness but was not the sole cause of communal division.
parts.working: 3 marks for evidence on both sides; 3 marks for a supported judgement that recognises other causes of communal division.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the town where Darul Uloom was founded and the year in which it was founded.
parts.answer: Deoband; 1866
parts.working: 1 mark: Deoband. 1 mark: 1866.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two aims of the Deoband movement.
parts.answer: To preserve traditional Islamic learning (Quran, hadith and fiqh) against Western influence; to train religious scholars; to keep Muslims faithful to Islamic practice and independent of government control.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two aims.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the founder of the Arya Samaj and the year in which it was founded.
parts.answer: Dayanand Saraswati; 1875
parts.working: 1 mark: Dayanand Saraswati. 1 mark: 1875.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one aim of the shuddhi movement of the Arya Samaj.
parts.answer: Purification: to reconvert Hindus who had converted to Islam or Christianity and bring them back into Hinduism.
parts.working: 1 mark for purification; 1 mark for reconversion of converts.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
stem: Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828. Dayanand Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of years between the founding of the Brahmo Samaj (1828) and the Arya Samaj (1875).
parts.answer: 47 years

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two aims of the Brahmo Samaj.
parts.answer: Belief in one God; rejection of idol worship and superstition; opposition to sati and child marriage; promotion of women's education.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two aims.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the aims of the Nadwat al-Ulama, founded in 1894.
parts.answer: To reconcile differences between Muslim sects; to combine religious education with modern subjects such as English and science; to unite Muslim scholars; to reform education without losing Islamic identity.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: founded 1894; reconcile sectarian differences; combine religious and modern education; unite scholars; reform of education while keeping Islamic identity.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Raja Ram Mohan Roy's campaign against sati.
parts.answer: He argued in writing that sati had no basis in true Hindu scripture; he campaigned publicly and petitioned the government; with the support of the British government under Lord William Bentinck, sati was banned in 1829.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: argued sati had no scriptural basis; wrote and published tracts; campaigned and petitioned; Bentinck's government banned sati in 1829.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the shuddhi campaigns of Hindu revivalists increased tension between Hindus and Muslims in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
parts.answer: Shuddhi campaigns aimed to win back converts and sometimes targeted Muslims and Christians; Muslims saw them as a threat to their community and a competition for converts; each side mobilised its own community; this increased suspicion and rivalry, and in some cities led to disputes and violence.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 6: campaigns targeted Muslims and Christians; seen as a threat by Muslims; competition for converts; Muslim organisations responded with their own missions; communal mobilisation; growing suspicion; disputes in cities; rivalry in politics and public life.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two reformers from religious or social revival movements of the nineteenth century, other than Sir Syed.
parts.answer: Any two of: Dayanand Saraswati; Raja Ram Mohan Roy; Syed Ahmad Barelvi; Muhammad Qasim Nanautvi.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two named reformers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many religious revival movements looked back to the 'pure' early age of their faith.
parts.answer: They believed the early age of their religion was purer and more correct; they blamed foreign rule and corruption for decline; a return to original teaching gave a basis for reform; it helped to resist Western influence and restore moral discipline.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: earlier age seen as purer; decline blamed on corruption and foreign rule; original teaching gave authority for reform; resistance to Western influence; restoration of faith and discipline.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: 'Religious revival movements did more to divide Indians than to unite them.' How far do you agree?
parts.answer: A balanced judgement: revival movements divided communities through competition for converts (shuddhi, tabligh), separate schools and organisations, and communal politics; but they also united people in shared moral reform (sati ban, opposition to some customs, shared concern about British influence). Conclusion should weigh the evidence.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–4): describes some revival movements. Level 2 (5–9): explains divisive and unifying effects with examples. Level 3 (10–14): clear, balanced judgement reaching a supported conclusion.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the success of religious revival movements in changing the everyday behaviour of ordinary Muslims and Hindus.
parts.answer: Evidence of success: spread of schools, changes in customs such as the banning of sati, growth of religious institutions. Limits: influence was mostly among educated urban elites; rural practice changed slowly; the movements divided communities; judgement.
parts.working: 3 marks for evidence of success; 3 marks for limits and a supported judgement.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
stem: Illustrative figures (invented for this question): an Islamic madrasa had 240 students in 1866 and 960 students in 1900.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the number of students was in 1900 than in 1866.
parts.answer: 4 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the average increase in students per year between 1866 and 1900. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: 21.2 students per year

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the number of students in religious schools might have grown in this period.
parts.answer: Religious schools grew in response to demand for religious identity after the decline of Muslim rule; new institutions such as Deoband gave training to scholars; communities wanted their children to learn their faith in a changing political situation.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: demand for religious identity after loss of political power; new institutions founded; community demand for Islamic education; reformers encouraged enrolment.

parts.answer: Lord Canning (Charles Canning)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.answer: 1858; the British Crown (the government in London), which ruled through a Viceroy
parts.working: 1 mark: 1858. 1 mark: British Crown / government in London, through a Viceroy.

parts.answer: 5 years

author: HomiLabs

parts.text: Describe the rumour about the cartridges for the new Enfield rifles.
parts.answer: Sepoys were told the cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat; to load the rifle they had to bite the paper cartridge; this offended both Hindu and Muslim soldiers; the rumour spread quickly through the army.

parts.answer: Any two of: sepoys (Indian soldiers); landlords (taluqdars); peasants; some Indian rulers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two groups.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement

parts.text: Name two cities other than Delhi where fighting took place in 1857.
parts.answer: Any two of: Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, Meerut.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two cities.

parts.text: State one reason why Lucknow was an important place for the rebels.
parts.answer: Lucknow was the capital of Awadh; Awadh had been annexed in 1856, and its nobles and people were angry.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
stem: Source A (written for this question): 'After Awadh was annexed in 1856, the taluqdars, the landowners who had collected revenue and kept armed followers, lost their estates to new British officials. Many of their tenants lost their old protection as well.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: According to Source A, what happened to the taluqdars after the annexation of Awadh?
parts.answer: They lost their estates to new British officials.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the annexation of Awadh angered people and helped to spark the rebellion of 1857.
parts.answer: The taluqdars lost power, income and their armed followers; tenants and peasants lost the protection of their landlords and faced new demands; the Nawab was removed and his court lost prestige; the annexation was seen as unjust.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: taluqdars lost power and armed followers; tenants lost protection; the Nawab was removed; the annexation was seen as unjust; soldiers from Awadh had families who suffered.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the part played by Tantia Tope in the rebellion of 1857.
parts.answer: He led rebel forces in central India and fought alongside the Rani of Jhansi and Nana Sahib; after the main defeats he carried on a guerrilla campaign; he was captured and executed in 1859.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: led rebel forces in central India; joined with Nana Sahib and the Rani of Jhansi; carried on a guerrilla war; captured and hanged in 1859.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement

parts.text: Explain why many landlords and peasants in northern India supported the rebellion of 1857.
parts.answer: Many landlords had lost land and power through annexation and new revenue systems; peasants faced high taxes and debts; many feared the loss of traditional protection and religious practices; rulers such as the Rani of Jhansi and Nawab of Awadh had lost their states; the revolt offered a chance to restore old rights.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 6: land and power lost through annexation; high revenue demands and debt; loss of traditional rights; rulers dispossessed; fear of religious and social change; hope of restoring old order.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement
stem: Illustrative figures (invented for this question): a town had 1,200 Indian soldiers and 150 British soldiers. In May 1857, 900 of the Indian soldiers mutinied.

parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the Indian soldiers who mutinied.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement

parts.text: Name two leaders of the rebellion of 1857.
parts.answer: Any two of: Bahadur Shah Zafar; Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi; Nana Sahib; Tantia Tope; Kunwar Singh; Begum Hazrat Mahal.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two named leaders.

parts.text: Explain why the British were able to recapture Delhi in September 1857.

author: HomiLabs

topic: Cultural and historical background to the Pakistan Movement

parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: lower incomes and fewer appliances; rural areas without grid; less industrialisation; load-shedding limits use; climate-related use differs.

author: HomiLabs

stem: On one day, a grid's peak demand was 20,000 MW and its average demand over the day was 14,000 MW (illustrative figures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the load factor as a percentage. Load factor = average demand ÷ peak demand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a utility wants a high load factor.
parts.answer: A high load factor means the plant runs more steadily, so less capacity is idle while still costing money; the cost per unit is lower; less capacity has to be built just for short peaks; fuel and staff are used more efficiently.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: steady running and less idle capacity; lower cost per unit; less need to build for short peaks; efficient use of fuel and staff.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three measures that the government or utilities can use to reduce electricity demand.
parts.answer: Any three of: promoting energy-efficient bulbs and appliances; time-of-use tariffs that make peak electricity dearer; public awareness campaigns; building codes that require insulation and efficient design; reducing waste in transmission.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three described measures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why reducing demand at peak times can be more useful than reducing total annual demand.
parts.answer: Peak demand sets how much generating capacity must be built and kept; cutting the peak avoids load-shedding in the evening; it avoids running expensive peaking plants; it helps keep the grid stable.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: peak sets capacity needed; avoids evening load-shedding; avoids expensive peaking plants; helps grid stability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that reducing energy demand is more effective than building new power stations in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Arguments for demand reduction: it is cheaper and quicker, cuts waste and losses, and can ease shortages at peak times. Arguments against: demand is growing with population and industry, households and businesses need reliable supply, and demand reduction is hard to achieve in full. Judgement: both are needed, but the balance depends on local conditions.
parts.working: 3 marks for arguments on demand reduction and for new capacity; 3 marks for a supported judgement.

stem: An industrial unit has a constant load of 500 kW. It runs for 16 hours a day for 25 days in a month. The tariff is Rs 45 per kWh (illustrative figures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy used in the month, in kWh.
parts.working: 1 mark: 500 kW × 16 h = 8,000 kWh per day. 1 mark: 8,000 × 25 = 200,000 kWh.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the monthly electricity bill, in rupees.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways the factory could reduce its bill.
parts.answer: Any two of: install energy-efficient motors; shift heavy machinery to off-peak hours; improve power factor; install solar panels; maintain equipment to cut waste.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid suggestions.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two fuels that thermal power stations in Pakistan burn.
parts.answer: Any two of: natural gas; furnace oil or diesel; coal (local or imported); LNG.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid fuels.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the sequence of energy conversions in a thermal power station, from fuel to electricity.
parts.answer: Chemical energy in the fuel is released as heat; the heat boils water to steam; the steam turns a turbine (kinetic energy); the turbine turns a generator that produces electrical energy.
parts.working: 1 mark for chemical to heat to steam; 1 mark for turbine and generator producing electrical energy.

stem: A thermal power station receives 900 MW of thermal energy from its fuel and produces 360 MW of electrical power (illustrative figures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the efficiency of the station as a percentage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two places where most of the energy is lost in such a station.
parts.answer: Any two of: hot flue gases up the chimney; heat in the cooling water; friction and other mechanical losses; heat escaping from the boiler.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid losses.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two gases released by burning fossil fuels in thermal stations that contribute to (i) climate change and (ii) acid rain.
parts.answer: (i) carbon dioxide (CO₂); (ii) sulphur dioxide (SO₂) or nitrogen oxides (NOₓ).
parts.working: 1 mark each part.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one method used to reduce sulphur dioxide emissions from a coal-fired station.
parts.answer: Flue gas desulphurisation (scrubbers) or switching to low-sulphur fuel.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of thermal power over hydel power for a country such as Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any two of: thermal stations can be built close to demand, such as cities; output does not depend on river flow or rainfall; output can be controlled; they can be built more quickly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid advantages.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why thermal power stations in Pakistan often depend on imported fuel.
parts.answer: Domestic gas and oil production has fallen short of demand, so plants burn imported LNG to make up the gap; some plants also use imported coal.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 2: domestic gas and oil production below demand; imported LNG (and imported coal for some plants) fills the gap.

stem: A 300 MW thermal station runs at 80% of its capacity for 24 hours (illustrative figures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy generated by the station in one day, in MWh.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a thermal station is not kept running at 100% of its capacity all the time.
parts.answer: Plant needs maintenance and shutdowns; demand varies through the day and year; fuel supply may be limited; breakdowns force the station to stop or reduce output.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 2: maintenance; varying demand; fuel supply limits; breakdowns.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Source A (written for this question): 'The power station draws large volumes of river water for cooling. The warm water returned to the river is several degrees hotter than the water taken in. Fish and other river life near the outlet have been reported to decline, and the chimney releases sulphur dioxide that falls as acid rain on nearby farmland.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: According to Source A, identify two environmental effects of the station.
parts.answer: Any two of: the warm water returned to the river harms fish and river life; sulphur dioxide from the chimney falls as acid rain on nearby farmland.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two effects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why hotter water returned to a river can harm fish and other river life.
parts.answer: Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, and fish need oxygen to breathe; warmer water increases the fish's oxygen demand; a sudden rise in temperature causes thermal shock; species that cannot tolerate heat die.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: less dissolved oxygen in warm water; fish need oxygen; higher metabolic rate; thermal shock; heat-intolerant species die.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT) station works.
parts.answer: A gas turbine burns gas and spins a generator; its hot exhaust passes through a heat-recovery boiler that makes steam; the steam drives a second turbine and generator. Using waste heat gives a higher overall efficiency.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: gas turbine burns gas and generates electricity; hot exhaust passes through a heat-recovery boiler; steam drives a second turbine; the waste heat is reused, giving higher efficiency.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of a CCGT station over a conventional gas-fired station.
parts.answer: Higher efficiency; less fuel and less CO₂ per unit of electricity.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why thermal power stations are less suitable than hydel stations for meeting sudden rises in demand over a few minutes.
parts.answer: Steam plant takes hours to heat its boilers and reach full output; it cannot be started or stopped quickly; hydel gates can be opened within minutes, so hydel is used to meet short peaks and to control frequency; thermal plant is best used for steady base load.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: steam plant needs hours to start; cannot be started or stopped quickly; hydel responds in minutes; hydel used for peaks and frequency; thermal used for base load.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one type of thermal station that can start faster than a steam plant.
parts.answer: An open-cycle gas turbine station.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effects of smoke and fly ash from a coal-fired station on people living nearby.
parts.answer: Breathing problems and asthma increase; fine particles enter the lungs and cause illness; fly ash and dust settle on crops and houses; smog and reduced visibility affect daily life; ash waste pollutes land and water.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: respiratory illness and asthma; fine particles harm health; dust and ash on crops and homes; smog; ash waste pollution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: 'Pakistan should stop building new thermal power stations.' Evaluate this view.
parts.answer: A balanced judgement: thermal stations provide reliable base-load power and are quicker to build than large dams, and the country still needs new capacity to meet growing demand; but they depend on imported fuel, add greenhouse gases and air pollution, and their costs rise with fuel prices. The conclusion should weigh renewables, hydro and gas efficiency against reliability.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–4): describes thermal power and its strengths or weaknesses. Level 2 (5–9): evaluates the view with evidence (fuel imports, pollution, reliability, renewables). Level 3 (10–14): supported judgement that weighs reliability, cost and environment.

stem: A thermal station generates 2 TWh of electricity in a year. Its fuel cost is Rs 12 per kWh generated (illustrative figures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total fuel cost in rupees, in billions.
parts.answer: Rs 24 billion
parts.working: 1 mark: 2 TWh = 2 × 10⁹ kWh. 1 mark: 2 × 10⁹ × Rs 12 = Rs 24 billion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why fuel costs can change sharply from year to year for a country that burns imported fuel.
parts.answer: Exchange-rate changes make imports dearer or cheaper in rupees; world oil and LNG prices are volatile; the country has little control over supply; shortages or delayed shipments force the use of dearer fuel; subsidies or tariffs change with the budget.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: exchange-rate changes; volatile world fuel prices; limited control over supply; shortages and shipping delays; subsidies and budget pressure.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the choice of fuel (coal, oil or gas) affects the carbon dioxide emitted per unit of electricity and the cost of generation.
parts.answer: Coal releases the most CO₂ per unit of energy; natural gas releases the least of the fossil fuels; oil lies between them; the cheapest fuel depends on local prices and supply; gas plants are cheaper and faster to build, while coal needs high capital and fuel-handling costs; fuel price swings affect the cost of each option.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 6: coal highest CO₂ per unit; gas lowest of fossil fuels; oil in between; cost depends on local price and supply; capital cost and build time differ; coal needs fuel handling; price volatility.

stem: Illustrative figures for two new 500 MW stations (invented for this question): a coal station emits 0.9 kg of CO₂ per kWh; a gas station emits 0.4 kg of CO₂ per kWh. Both run at 80% load for a full year of 8,760 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the annual electricity generated by one station, in GWh.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many tonnes less CO₂ the gas station emits per year than the coal station.
parts.answer: 1,752,000 tonnes (about 1.75 million tonnes)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why a gas-fired station might not always be the best choice for Pakistan.
parts.answer: Gas supply is limited and partly imported as LNG, so prices and availability can change; gas shortages can force the station to stop.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid reason; 1 mark for the link to supply or price.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a hydroelectric power station produces electricity from falling water.
parts.answer: Water stored behind the dam at height has potential energy; it flows down a pipe (penstock) and turns the turbine; the turbine turns a generator that produces electricity.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: stored water has potential energy; flows through penstock to turbine; turbine turns generator producing electricity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the energy transformation that takes place in the turbine.
parts.answer: Kinetic energy of moving water to kinetic energy of the rotating turbine (then electrical energy in the generator).
parts.working: 1 mark for kinetic energy of water to kinetic energy of turbine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the river on which Warsak Dam is built and the province where it is located.
parts.answer: Kabul River; Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
parts.working: 1 mark: Kabul River. 1 mark: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the river on which Ghazi Barotha Dam is built.
parts.answer: Indus River
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: A dam holds water that falls through a height of 100 m. The water flows through the turbines at 50 m³ per second. The overall efficiency is 90%. Take g = 9.81 m/s² and the density of water as 1,000 kg/m³ (illustrative figures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the power output, in MW, using P = ρ × g × Q × h × efficiency. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which the power output could be increased.
parts.answer: Any two of: increase the height of the water (head); increase the flow rate through the turbines; improve the turbine or generator efficiency.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid ways.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'run-of-river' hydel scheme.
parts.answer: A scheme that uses the natural flow of a river with little or no large storage, so its output varies with river flow.
parts.working: 1 mark for natural flow of river; 1 mark for little or no storage and varying output.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage of a run-of-river scheme.
parts.answer: Low environmental impact because no large reservoir is needed; cheaper to build.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one disadvantage of a run-of-river scheme.
parts.answer: Output varies with seasonal river flow; little storage for dry periods.
parts.working: 1 mark.
