stem: Illustrative figures (invented for this question): a reservoir had a storage capacity of 9,000 million m³ when it was built. After 40 years of silt deposits its capacity was 7,650 million m³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the capacity lost to silt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects of silt build-up on a hydel dam.
parts.answer: Less water is stored, so less power is available in dry periods; silt can damage turbines and intakes; the reservoir has less room to store flood water; the life of the dam is shortened.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: less water stored and less power; damage to turbines and intakes; less flood-control space; shorter life of dam.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Source A (written for this question): 'Under the Indus Waters Treaty of 1960, which was negotiated with the help of the World Bank, Pakistan was allocated the three western rivers of the Indus system, while India was allocated the three eastern rivers. Water from the western rivers is essential to Pakistan's irrigation and to its hydel power.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two of the three western rivers that Pakistan was allocated under the Indus Waters Treaty.
parts.answer: Any two of: Indus; Jhelum; Chenab.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important for Pakistan's hydel power that the western rivers flow reliably.
parts.answer: Dams such as Tarbela and Mangla depend on steady river flows; snow and glacier melt gives summer water that fills the reservoirs; reliable flow supports power generation through the year; uncertain flows make planning difficult; disputes could affect the flow.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: dams depend on river flow; snow and glacier melt fills reservoirs; reliable supply for year-round power; planning difficulty if flows are uncertain; disputes could affect flow.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how water stored in a dam is used for both irrigation and electricity in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Water released from the reservoir passes through turbines to generate power, then flows into canals for irrigation; releases are planned so that power and irrigation both get water; storage helps supply water in the dry season.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: water passes through turbines before canals; releases generate power; canals carry water to fields; storage supplies water in the dry season; Tarbela and Mangla used this way.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one conflict that can arise between power generation and irrigation.
parts.answer: Releases timed for peak electricity demand may not match when farmers need water; the two uses may compete for the same stored water.
parts.working: 1 mark for the conflict; 1 mark for a valid explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan has a large potential for hydel power.
parts.answer: Steep rivers fall from the mountains, giving large height differences; rivers are fed by snow and glacier melt and by summer monsoon flows; narrow gorges provide good dam sites; electricity demand is high.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: steep rivers with large fall; snow and glacier-fed flows; monsoon summer flows; suitable narrow gorges for dams; high demand for electricity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two environmental impacts of large dams.
parts.answer: Any two of: flooding of land and displacement of people; changes to river ecology and fish migration; trapping of sediment downstream; water loss through evaporation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid impacts.

stem: A 1,000 MW hydel station operates for 3,000 hours in a year (illustrative figures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy generated, in TWh.
parts.answer: 3 TWh

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a hydel station may generate less than this figure in practice.
parts.answer: Low river flows in drought reduce water in the reservoir; maintenance outages take turbines offline; silt can damage turbines; floods may force the gates to close; the head of water may be lower than design.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: low river flows and reservoir levels; maintenance outages; silt damage; gates closed in floods; lower head than design.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: 'Large dams are essential to Pakistan's development.' How far do you agree?
parts.answer: A balanced judgement: large dams such as Tarbela and Mangla provide storage for irrigation, flood control and large amounts of cheap power; but they cause displacement, sedimentation, environmental change and cost overruns, and small schemes or other renewables may serve some areas better. The conclusion should weigh the evidence.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–4): describes the benefits and costs of dams. Level 2 (5–9): explains both sides with examples. Level 3 (10–14): supported judgement on how far large dams are essential.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the risks that earthquakes and floods pose to hydel dams in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Risks: earthquakes can crack dam walls and damage gates; floods may overtop spillways and erode foundations; silt and landslides into the reservoir reduce capacity and can cause waves; a dam failure would threaten people downstream. Ways to manage risk: design to seismic standards, spillway capacity, monitoring and early warning.
parts.working: 3 marks for risks with explanation; 3 marks for management and a supported judgement.

stem: Illustrative figures (invented for this question): a set of small hydel schemes would give 200 MW at a total cost of Rs 60 billion. A large dam would give 4,500 MW at a total cost of Rs 900 billion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost per MW for the small schemes, in Rs billion per MW.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost per MW for the large dam, in Rs billion per MW.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the large dam may still be preferred despite its size.
parts.answer: It provides storage for dry periods, irrigation and flood control; its total energy output is much larger; it may have a lower running cost per unit over its life; fewer sites are needed to connect to the grid.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: storage for irrigation and floods; much larger total output; lower running cost over life; fewer sites needed; grid integration.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a large dam's storage can help a country cope with both floods and droughts.
parts.answer: The reservoir stores floodwater in the monsoon and releases it gradually, reducing peak flows downstream; the stored water supplies irrigation and power in dry seasons; it maintains river flow for power when inflows fall; but the reservoir needs spare capacity to take flood water.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 6: stores flood water; gradual release reduces downstream peaks; stores water for dry season; supplies irrigation in drought; maintains flow and power output; needs spare capacity for floods.

stem: Illustrative figures (invented for this question): a forest covers 80,000 hectares. Each year 2,400 hectares are cleared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the forest cleared each year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many years it would take to clear half of the forest at this rate. Give your answer to one decimal place.
parts.answer: 16.7 years
parts.working: 1 mark: half the forest = 40,000 ha; 40,000 ÷ 2,400 = 16.7 years.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way to reduce the rate of forest clearance.
parts.answer: Any valid method, e.g. enforcing a ban on illegal clearance; providing alternative fuel; replanting cleared land.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of tree roots in preventing soil erosion.
parts.answer: Roots bind soil particles together and hold the soil on slopes; roots slow surface runoff so that topsoil is not washed away.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two accurate points (binding soil; holding soil on slopes; slowing runoff).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two effects of deforestation on the local climate or water supply.
parts.answer: Any two of: less moisture and lower rainfall; higher temperatures at ground level; faster run-off and floods; drying of springs and streams.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid effects.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three non-timber products that forests provide to people in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any three of: fodder for animals; wild fruit; honey; medicinal plants; resin; grass for thatch.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three valid products.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by 'sustainable yield' in forestry.
parts.answer: The amount of timber or other products that can be harvested without reducing the forest's ability to regenerate.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 2: harvest amount; does not reduce regeneration or future yield.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a sustainable yield is hard to keep when local people depend on the forest for fuelwood and fodder.
parts.answer: Local people cut fuelwood and graze animals every year, so trees are removed faster than they regrow; the forest cannot keep giving the same yield without limits on cutting and grazing.
parts.working: 1 mark: demand for fuelwood and fodder is greater than the forest can regrow. 1 mark: unlimited cutting and grazing reduce regrowth and future yield.

stem: Source A (written for this question): 'Every winter the village cuts fuelwood from the hillside, and goats graze the young shoots before they can grow. Since the road was built, trucks have also taken timber out at night. The hillside now has fewer trees each year than it had ten years ago.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: According to Source A, identify two causes of the loss of trees on the hillside.
parts.answer: Any two of: cutting of fuelwood; goats grazing the young shoots; night-time logging of timber by trucks.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two causes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how each of these causes stops new trees from growing up.
parts.answer: Fuelwood cutting removes mature trees and the seed sources; goats eat the young shoots before they can grow; trucks take timber from the hillside, leaving fewer trees to regenerate; the cumulative loss means fewer trees each year.
parts.working: 2 marks for a valid explanation of the first cause (mechanism and consequence); 2 marks for the second and third causes together.

author: HomiLabs

stem: A district planned to plant 150,000 saplings. In year 1, 60,000 were planted; in year 2, 45,000 were planted (illustrative figures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the planting target achieved after two years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why tree-planting targets are often not met in practice.
parts.answer: Many saplings die because of drought, grazing and poor after-care; funding and staff are short; land ownership disputes prevent planting; animals and fire damage young trees; sites are poorly chosen.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: saplings die without care; lack of funding and staff; land disputes; animals and fire; poor site choice.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why women and children often spend long hours collecting firewood in rural Pakistan.
parts.answer: Many rural homes have no gas or electricity connection, so wood is the only fuel for cooking and heating; household incomes are too low to buy gas or other fuels; firewood is free to collect; the work often falls to women and children while men work away.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: no gas or electricity connection; low incomes; firewood is free; men work away and women and children collect; cooking needs are high.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways to reduce the amount of firewood collected.
parts.answer: Any two of: improved cookstoves; solar cookers; LPG or biogas schemes; planting nurseries or woodlots near villages.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid suggestions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a forest cover percentage is calculated.
parts.answer: Forest area divided by total land area, multiplied by 100.
parts.working: 1 mark for division by total land area; 1 mark for multiplying by 100.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why official forest figures may be inaccurate.
parts.answer: Any two of: different definitions of 'forest' (plantations may be counted); figures based on old surveys; illegal clearance is not recorded; satellite and ground survey results differ.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A district of 5,000 km² has 375 km² of forest. Calculate its forest cover percentage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that community-managed forests are more effective than government forest reserves in stopping deforestation.
parts.answer: For community management: local people have a stake in the forest, know local needs, and can guard it against theft and fire. Against: communities may lack funds, authority or rights, and fuelwood collection may still continue; government reserves can enforce rules and cover large areas. Judgement: success depends on rights, support and enforcement.
parts.working: 3 marks for evidence on both sides; 3 marks for a supported judgement.

stem: Illustrative figures (invented for this question): a mangrove restoration project covers 2,500 hectares. Each hectare of healthy mangrove stores about 6 tonnes of CO₂ a year. An average car emits about 4 tonnes of CO₂ a year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many tonnes of CO₂ the project stores each year, and how many cars' yearly emissions this equals.
parts.answer: 15,000 tonnes of CO₂ per year, equal to the yearly emissions of 3,750 cars

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why mangrove restoration needs a supply of fresh water (river flow) and suitable tidal mud.
parts.answer: Mangrove seedlings need fresh water to lower salinity so they can survive; river sediment builds the mud flats where roots can grow; river flow maintains the balance of tidal flooding; without fresh water the land becomes too salty for mangroves.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: fresh water lowers salinity for seedlings; sediment builds mud flats; river flow keeps tidal balance; without fresh water the soil is too salty.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which a logging ban can reduce deforestation in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Benefits: stops commercial logging, protects remaining forest and allows regeneration. Limits: illegal logging continues without enforcement; fuelwood collection and grazing are often not covered; poor households lose income; enforcement is costly. Judgement: a ban helps only if it is combined with alternatives and enforcement.
parts.working: 3 marks for benefits and limits with explanation; 3 marks for a supported judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two trees found in the moist temperate forests of Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan.
parts.answer: Any two of: walnut (Juglans regia); wild cherry; oak (Quercus incana); maple.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why these forests receive more rainfall than the forests of the southern plains.
parts.answer: They lie at high altitude and face moist winds, so the air is forced up and cools and produces rain.
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: A plantation of Shisham (sheesham) trees covers 500 hectares. There are 200 trees per hectare (illustrative figures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of Shisham trees in the plantation.
parts.answer: 100,000 trees
parts.working: 1 mark: 500 ha × 200 trees per ha = 100,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one use of the timber from Shisham trees.
parts.answer: Furniture, doors or cart wheels (any valid use).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one ecological benefit of planting Shisham trees in a plantation.
parts.answer: Shade; windbreak; soil protection; habitat for birds.
parts.working: 1 mark.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two reasons why mangrove trees need regular tidal flooding.
parts.answer: Any two of: tidal water flushes out salt that would build up around roots; tides bring in nutrients and sediment; tides carry seedlings or aid their dispersal; the roots need oxygen when the tide falls.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the roots of mangroves help the forest to grow on muddy coasts.
parts.answer: The roots spread widely and trap mud and sediment; they bind the soil, so the forest is stable against waves and tides.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two accurate points (trapping sediment; binding soil; stabilising the coast).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the location of chir pine forests in Pakistan.
parts.answer: On the lower and middle slopes of the Himalayas and Hindu Kush in northern Pakistan, typically at about 900 to 1,800 metres.
parts.working: 1 mark for mountain slopes in northern Pakistan; 1 mark for altitude about 900–1,800 m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two uses of chir pine wood or resin.
parts.answer: Any two of: resin for turpentine and rosin; timber for construction and boxes; fuel.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid uses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'xerophyte'.
parts.answer: A plant adapted to survive in very dry conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which desert plants reduce water loss.
parts.answer: Any two of: small or waxy leaves; spines instead of leaves; water-storing stems; deep roots; leaves shed in dry periods.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid ways.

stem: Illustrative average annual rainfall at three places (invented for this question): Place X in the northern hills 1,800 mm; Place Y in central Punjab 500 mm; Place Z in the Cholistan desert 150 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in rainfall between Place X and Place Z.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using the rainfall data, name the most likely vegetation type at Place Z and give one reason.
parts.answer: Desert or xerophytic scrub; rainfall of 150 mm is too little to support forest.
parts.working: 1 mark for the vegetation type; 1 mark for the reason linked to low rainfall.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the natural vegetation of the Punjab plains has been largely replaced by crops.
parts.answer: The alluvial soils are very fertile; canal irrigation makes farming possible; the flat land was cleared for farming; population growth and demand for food expanded cultivation; trees were cut for timber and fuel.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: fertile alluvial soils; canal irrigation; land cleared for farming; population and food demand; trees cut for timber and fuel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one place in the plains where natural forest still survives.
parts.answer: Riverine (bela) forests along the Indus.
parts.working: 1 mark.

stem: Illustrative figures (invented for this question): a country has 2.5 million hectares of natural forest and 0.5 million hectares of planted forest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total forest that is planted.
parts.working: 1 mark: total forest = 2.5 + 0.5 = 3.0 million ha. 1 mark: 0.5 ÷ 3.0 × 100 = 16.7%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of planted forests compared with natural forests.
parts.answer: Advantage: planted forests grow fast and can be managed for timber supply. Disadvantage: they usually contain fewer species, provide less habitat, and regenerate less naturally.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid advantage; 1 mark for a valid disadvantage; 1 mark for a clear comparison with natural forest.

author: HomiLabs

stem: Source A (written for this question): 'In the thorn forest the acacia trees are small and scattered. Their leaves are tiny and many shrubs have spines instead of leaves. Some trees send roots deep down to reach water that lies far beneath the dry surface.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: According to Source A, identify two adaptations of thorn-forest plants.
parts.answer: Any two of: small leaves; spines; deep roots.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how each of these adaptations helps the plants survive dry conditions.
parts.answer: Small leaves and spines reduce the area through which water is lost by transpiration; deep roots reach water far below the dry surface.
parts.working: 2 marks for a correct explanation of the first adaptation; 2 marks for a correct explanation of the second.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how natural vegetation changes with altitude in the mountains of northern Pakistan.
parts.answer: Subtropical broadleaved forests grow on the lower slopes; coniferous forests cover the middle slopes; alpine meadows grow above the tree line; bare rock and scrub are found at the highest levels; temperature falls with altitude.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: subtropical broadleaved forest at lower altitudes; coniferous forest on middle slopes; alpine meadows above the tree line; bare rock and scrub at the highest levels; falling temperature with height.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two factors other than altitude that affect natural vegetation.
parts.answer: Any two of: rainfall; soil type; slope and aspect; human activity such as grazing and cutting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid factors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two animals that live in mangrove forests.
parts.answer: Any two of: crabs; mudskippers; prawns; fish; wading birds.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which mangrove forests benefit coastal communities.
parts.answer: Mangroves act as a nursery for fish and prawns, supporting fisheries; they protect the coast from storm surges and erosion; they provide firewood and fodder; they trap sediment and keep the coast stable.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: fish and prawn nursery; coastal protection from storms; firewood and fodder; sediment trapping and stability.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the moist temperate forests of the northern mountains with the tropical thorn forests of the south, using (i) annual rainfall and (ii) one named tree from each type.
parts.answer: (i) the northern moist temperate forests have much higher rainfall than the southern thorn forests, which receive very little; (ii) walnut or oak in the north; kikar (Acacia nilotica) or jand (Prosopis cineraria) in the thorn forest.
parts.working: 1 mark for higher rainfall in the north; 1 mark for lower rainfall in the thorn forest; 1 mark for a named northern tree; 1 mark for a named thorn-forest tree.

stem: A 50 m by 80 m plot of thorn forest contains 36 trees (illustrative figures). 1 hectare = 10,000 m².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of trees per hectare.
parts.answer: 90 trees per hectare
parts.working: 1 mark: plot area = 50 × 80 = 4,000 m² = 0.4 ha. 1 mark: 36 ÷ 0.4 = 90 trees per hectare.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why thorn forests have fewer trees per hectare than moist forests.
parts.answer: Low rainfall limits tree growth; trees are spaced apart to reduce competition for scarce water; poor soils support fewer plants; grazing and cutting remove young trees.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: low rainfall limits growth; spacing to reduce competition for water; poor soils; grazing and cutting.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain how forest and vegetation types change from the northern mountains to the southern coast of Pakistan.
parts.answer: A complete account: moist temperate and coniferous forests in the north with altitude and high rainfall; subtropical broadleaved forests on the Pothwar and Margalla hills; irrigated plantations and riverine forests on the plains; tropical thorn forests in drier central and southern areas; desert scrub in Cholistan and Thar; mangroves on the Indus delta coast; explanation through rainfall, temperature, altitude and soils.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–4): lists some forest types and locations. Level 2 (5–9): describes the sequence of types and gives some explanation. Level 3 (10–14): describes the sequence in detail and explains it clearly with rainfall, temperature, altitude and soils.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that irrigated plantations can replace the ecological value of natural forests.
parts.answer: Plantations give timber, shade, windbreaks and jobs; but they have fewer species, less habitat, poorer soil protection and little natural regeneration, so they cannot fully replace natural forests. Judgement: they add value but are not a full replacement.
parts.working: 3 marks for benefits and limits with explanation; 3 marks for a supported judgement.

stem: A forest reserve covers 20 km². Coniferous forest covers 10 km², riverine forest covers 4 km² and mangrove covers 6 km² (illustrative figures).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the reserve covered by each forest type.
parts.answer: Coniferous 50%; riverine 20%; mangrove 30%
parts.working: 1 mark: coniferous 10 ÷ 20 = 50%. 1 mark: riverine 20% and mangrove 30%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the angle for coniferous forest on a pie chart.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this reserve would be unlikely to contain all three forest types in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Coniferous forest grows at high altitude in the mountains; mangroves grow on the tidal coast; riverine forest grows on the floodplains of the rivers, so the three types are too far apart to occur in one reserve.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 3: coniferous forest at altitude; mangroves on the coast; riverine forest on floodplains; the three habitats are far apart.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why mangrove forests in the Indus delta are threatened when river flow falls.
parts.answer: Less freshwater raises salinity, which kills seedlings and stresses mature trees; less sediment is deposited, so the mud flats are eroded; reduced flow lowers nutrient supply; fish nurseries decline and so do the communities that depend on them; dams and barrages reduce the flow reaching the delta.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 6: rising salinity; less sediment and erosion of mud flats; less nutrient supply; loss of fish nurseries; loss of livelihoods; dams and barrages reduce flow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a warming climate may change the distribution of coniferous forests in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Warmer temperatures push tree species to higher altitudes, so the coniferous zone may move upward and shrink; less snow and more drought stress young trees; fire and pest outbreaks may increase; alpine meadows may move upward; forests may not be able to migrate quickly enough.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 6: species move to higher altitude; zone shrinks; less snow and drought stress; fire and pest risk; alpine meadows move upward; slow migration of forests.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how overgrazing of alpine pastures can damage the sub-alpine forest zone below, and suggest one sustainable management measure.
parts.answer: Overgrazing reduces ground cover, so soil is exposed to erosion and landslides; trampling compacts the soil; animals move down into the forest and eat seedlings; a sustainable measure is rotational grazing or limits on the number of animals (community grazing rules).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four explanation points (ground cover loss; erosion and landslides; trampling; animals move down into forest; seedlings eaten), and 2 marks for a valid management measure with explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Balochistan crisis of 1973–1977.
parts.answer: In February 1973 Bhutto dismissed the elected NAP–JUI provincial government in Balochistan and imposed governor's rule. Baloch nationalists took up armed resistance in the mountains, and the army ran a major military operation until 1977. Thousands died on both sides.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: NAP–JUI provincial government dismissed (Feb 1973); governor's rule imposed; armed Baloch nationalist resistance; large army operation (1973–77); heavy casualties or civilian suffering; foreign support for the rebels/government named correctly (optional).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many Baloch leaders rejected the policies of the central government between 1972 and 1977.
parts.answer: The dismissal of an elected provincial government convinced many Baloch leaders that the centre would not respect provincial autonomy. They had demanded control of Balochistan's natural resources and a fair share of revenue, but the centre resisted. Arrests of nationalist leaders and the use of the army made many Baloch feel their culture and politics were being suppressed, so armed resistance seemed the only option to them.
parts.working: Level marking. L1 (1–2): general statements such as "they wanted independence". L2 (3–4): reasons named, not explained. L3 (5–7): one reason explained in depth for 5, two or more explained for 7. Reasons: dismissal of the NAP–JUI government and autonomy; control of resources and revenue; arrests of leaders and military repression; cultural/linguistic identity; the army's presence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways in which the 1972 nationalisation of private schools and colleges changed education in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Private educational institutions were taken over by the state. Management passed from private owners to government control. Teachers and staff became government employees.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three: private schools and colleges taken over by government; management moved from private owners to the state; teachers became government employees/salaries and conditions set by the state; admission and fee policies changed; schools brought under state curriculum control.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why some parents and private owners were unhappy with this change.
parts.answer: Parents who had chosen private schools for better standards lost that choice, and owners lost their property and income. Some feared that standards would fall once government took over.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reason, 1 for development: loss of choice/private schools seen as better; owners lost property and income; fear that quality would fall under government management; loss of control over curriculum or fees.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Second Amendment to the Constitution passed in 1974 concerning the Ahmadiyya community.
parts.answer: In September 1974 the National Assembly passed the Second Amendment, which declared persons of the Ahmadiyya community non-Muslims for the purposes of the law. It was passed after street protests and demands from religious parties.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: passed by the National Assembly in 1974 (Second Amendment); Ahmadis declared non-Muslim for legal purposes; passed after protests/agitation by religious groups; the decision was a constitutional change, not a religious ruling.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Bhutto's government agreed to the Second Amendment in 1974.
parts.answer: Bhutto needed the support of religious parties after the 1973 constitution was passed, and the agitation in 1974 threatened law and order. Bhutto also wanted to strengthen his own Islamic credentials, particularly after the 1974 Islamic Summit in Lahore. By passing the amendment within parliament, he hoped to end the public disorder and reduce pressure from the religious right.
parts.working: Level marking. L1: general answer. L2: reasons named. L3 (5–7): at least two reasons explained, e.g. pressure from religious parties and street protests; wish for Islamic legitimacy and political support; desire to restore law and order; use of parliament to settle a controversy. Accept any well-explained reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the nuclear programme that Bhutto started in 1972.
parts.answer: In January 1972 Bhutto called a meeting in Multan of scientists and officials that launched a nuclear programme. An Atomic Energy Commission was used to co-ordinate work, and an agreement with France in 1976 was made for a reprocessing plant.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: meeting at Multan (January 1972) launching the programme; work co-ordinated through the Atomic Energy Commission; attempts to acquire nuclear technology from abroad; agreement with France (1976) for reprocessing; secret pursuit of enrichment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Bhutto believed Pakistan needed nuclear capability.
parts.answer: Pakistan had lost East Pakistan in 1971 and needed to deter a larger Indian army. India's nuclear test in May 1974 confirmed the threat for Pakistan. Bhutto also argued that nuclear capability would bring prestige and help Pakistan keep its independence in foreign affairs. Many Pakistanis supported the programme on security grounds.
parts.working: Level marking. L1–2: general statements. L3 (5–7): explains at least two reasons: deterrence of a stronger India after 1971; India's nuclear test (1974) as a threat; national security and prestige; independence in foreign policy; public support for security.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the results of the general election of March 1977 and the reaction of the opposition.
parts.answer: The Pakistan People's Party won a large majority of seats in the National Assembly. The opposition alliance, the Pakistan National Alliance (PNA), a group of nine parties, rejected the results and claimed the election had been rigged. The PNA led protests and strikes across the country.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: PPP won a large majority in March 1977; nine-party Pakistan National Alliance (PNA) formed to oppose it; PNA rejected the results and alleged rigging; mass protests, strikes and demonstrations followed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Pakistan National Alliance (PNA) refused to accept the 1977 results.
parts.answer: The PNA believed that officials had rigged the vote in favour of the PPP, and there were reports of unopposed candidates and of violence at polling stations. It also blamed Bhutto's policies, such as high prices and the repression of opponents, for losing public trust. The PNA demanded fresh elections and a new government, and it used street protests to press these demands.
parts.working: Level marking. L1–2: general. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained, e.g. belief in rigging supported by unopposed seats and violence at polls; loss of trust over the economy and repression; political strategy of street agitation; demand for fresh elections. Accept reasoned alternatives.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two causes of the oil price rises that affected Pakistan's economy in 1973–1974.
parts.answer: The Arab–Israeli war of 1973 led oil-producing countries to cut supply and raise prices. The world oil price rose sharply in 1973–1974.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any two: oil-exporting countries (OPEC) cut production/embargo after the 1973 Arab–Israeli war; OPEC raised prices sharply; increased demand for oil from industrialised countries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two effects of the higher oil prices on Pakistan's economy.
parts.answer: Pakistan imported most of its oil, so the bill for imports rose sharply, which increased the balance of payments deficit. Higher fuel and transport costs also pushed up prices, so inflation rose and many people struggled to afford basic goods.
parts.working: 2 marks per effect (1 for the effect, 1 for development), up to 6: higher import bill / balance of payments deficit; inflation and higher transport costs; pressure on foreign reserves; rising cost of living for the poor; higher costs for industry and agriculture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main aims of the Pakistan People's Party's manifesto of 1970, including the slogan "Roti, Kapra aur Makan".
parts.answer: The PPP promised food, clothing and housing for ordinary people, shown in the slogan "Roti, Kapra aur Makan". It also promised socialist-style policies, land reform and the redistribution of wealth, and presented itself as the party of the poor and the workers.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: food (roti), clothing (kapra), housing (makan) for the common people; land reform and redistribution; socialist-style economic policy; promise to help workers and peasants; a strong anti-feudal message.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the PPP's message appealed to many voters in the 1970 election.
parts.answer: Many ordinary people, especially in Punjab and Sindh, were poor and had little land. The PPP promised to end feudal domination and improve their lives, which offered them hope of change. The slogan was simple and easy to remember, and Bhutto's charisma and his attacks on the old landlords made the party popular.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained, e.g. poverty and hope of land reform; anti-feudal message; simple slogan and clear promises; Bhutto's personal appeal and campaign; support from workers and peasants in Punjab and Sindh.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main features of the Balochistan and North-West Frontier policies of Bhutto's government between 1972 and 1977.
parts.answer: In both provinces Bhutto moved against opposition governments of the NAP and JUI. In Balochistan the government was dismissed and military force used; in the NWFP the provincial government was dismissed in 1975. Opposition leaders were arrested and charged with treason.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: dismissal of NAP–JUI government in Balochistan (1973); military operation in Balochistan; dismissal of NWFP government (1975); arrests and charges of treason against opposition leaders; ban or pressure on opposition parties.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "Bhutto's government did more to weaken national unity than to strengthen it between 1972 and 1977." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Candidates may agree or disagree but must support a judgement. Points that weaken unity: dismissal of provincial governments; military operation in Balochistan; arrests and repression; ban on NAP. Points that strengthen unity: 1973 Constitution agreed by all parties, the federal system, the 1972 Land Reforms, and national consensus over the Simla Agreement and Bangladesh recognition. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, and a clear judgement on which side outweighs the other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways in which Bhutto changed the role of the army in politics after 1971.
parts.answer: Bhutto removed some senior officers after 1971 and reduced the army's control of politics. He also brought the army under civilian control, but later appointed General Zia-ul-Haq as Chief of Army Staff over more senior officers.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three: senior officers removed or retired after 1971; army placed under civilian/government control in theory; creation of a new army chief appointment process; appointment of Zia over seven more senior generals (1976); use of the army in Balochistan and against opponents.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Bhutto's decision to appoint Zia-ul-Haq as Chief of Army Staff in 1976 was later seen as a serious mistake.
parts.answer: Zia was chosen over seven more senior generals, which was expected to keep him loyal. Instead, Zia later overthrew Bhutto in July 1977 and took over the government. The choice showed that Bhutto had given a military officer the power to remove him.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): explains at least one link: Zia superseded seven senior generals so his promotion was seen as an insult to others; the army's chain of command gave Zia control of the coup; Bhutto had given him the power to remove him. Accept reasonable hindsight explanations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main steps in the removal of Bhutto's government in July 1977.
parts.answer: After protests and talks with the PNA, General Zia-ul-Haq took power in a coup on 5 July 1977, declared martial law and detained Bhutto. Bhutto was later tried and hanged in April 1979.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: PNA protests and talks with the government; army coup on 5 July 1977 led by Zia; martial law declared; Bhutto detained; Bhutto later tried and executed (1979).

parts.label: b
parts.text: "The 1977 general election was the main reason for Bhutto's downfall." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: the PNA alleged rigging and mass protests followed, giving the army an excuse; the election dispute led to martial law. Points that disagree: Bhutto's authoritarian style, economic difficulties, loss of support from the army and the judiciary, and the Balochistan operation had weakened him long before 1977; the election was a trigger, not the cause. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main features of the Labour Policy of 1972.
parts.answer: The Labour Policy of 1972 gave workers the right to take part in the management of industrial units through representation on management committees. It also strengthened the rights of trade unions and protected workers against unfair dismissal.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: workers' representation in the management of industrial units; strengthened trade union rights; protection against arbitrary dismissal; improvements in workers' welfare/pay for industrial workers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Bhutto's labour reforms did not satisfy all industrial workers by 1977.
parts.answer: Workers wanted higher wages and more job security, but inflation after 1973 reduced the value of wages. Some employers and managers resisted the reforms and found ways around them. Strikes and disputes continued, and workers felt that the reforms were applied unevenly.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: inflation and falling real wages; resistance from employers and managers; uneven application of the reforms; continued strikes; limited coverage for rural and informal workers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main points of Jinnah's speech to the Constituent Assembly on 11 August 1947.
parts.answer: Jinnah told the Constituent Assembly that the state would not concern itself with the religion of citizens. He said that all citizens were equal, whatever their religion, caste or creed, and that they should work together for the good of Pakistan.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: citizens free to practise any religion; religion not the business of the state; all citizens equal regardless of religion, caste or creed; minorities to be treated fairly; state to be governed by law and co-operation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Jinnah's speech of 11 August 1947 was important for the new state.
parts.answer: The speech was a reassurance to the non-Muslim minorities who feared discrimination after Partition. It showed the new state would be a democratic country based on law rather than a religious state. Some Muslim religious leaders disagreed with the message, so the speech also raised questions about the nature of Pakistan that would be debated for decades.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: reassurance to minorities after Partition; the vision of a secular/civil state of equal citizens; the speech was the founding statement of the nation; it created debate over the state's religious identity. Accept any reasoned interpretation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of the civil service (bureaucracy) in Pakistan in the years 1947–1951.
parts.answer: The civil service was the most experienced part of the new government, because many senior officials were trained under British rule. Civil servants ran the districts, managed supplies of refugees and provided the administrative machinery for the government of the country.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: senior civil servants ran most of the government; experience from British India; district administration and law and order; managing refugee relief and resettlement; administration of the new capital and ministries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the civil service grew more powerful in Pakistan in the 1950s.
parts.answer: Politicians were weak and divided, and the Muslim League had few trained organisers outside the Punjab and Sindh. Civil servants such as Ghulam Mohammad used their expertise and their control of the administration to dominate policy. As governments changed often, the bureaucracy provided continuity and gained influence over the political leaders.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: weakness and division of politicians; expertise and administrative control; frequent changes of government gave bureaucrats continuity; the role of Ghulam Mohammad as Governor-General and minister; links with the army.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Nehru–Liaquat Pact of April 1950.
parts.answer: The Nehru–Liaquat Pact was an agreement between Pakistan and India, signed in April 1950, to protect the rights of minorities in both countries. Both governments agreed to guarantee the safety and equal rights of minorities, and to allow the return of migrants who wished to return.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: signed by Liaquat Ali Khan and Nehru (April 1950); guarantee of minority rights in both countries; equal treatment of minorities; permitting migrants to return to their homes; protection of property and security for minorities.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Nehru–Liaquat Pact did not put an end to communal tension between India and Pakistan.
parts.answer: Communal violence continued in parts of India and East Pakistan, and both sides blamed each other for attacks. Many refugees had already lost their property and could not return. The agreement depended on governments enforcing it, which they often did not. The dispute over Kashmir kept relations poor, so the Pact could not calm suspicions.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained, e.g. continued violence and mutual blame; property lost by migrants and difficulty of return; weak enforcement by the two governments; the Kashmir dispute kept suspicion high; competing nationalist politics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Punjab disturbances of 1953.
parts.answer: In 1953 religious parties, including the Majlis-e-Ahrar, organised agitation in Lahore and other Punjab cities demanding that the Ahmadis be declared non-Muslims. Violence broke out, martial law was imposed in Lahore in March 1953, and the central government dismissed the provincial government of Khawaja Nazimuddin in April 1953.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: anti-Ahmadi agitation by religious parties; violence in Lahore and the Punjab; martial law in Lahore (March 1953); Khawaja Nazimuddin dismissed as prime minister by Governor-General Ghulam Mohammad in April 1953; commission of inquiry (Munir Commission) appointed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Munir Report of 1954 was important for Pakistan.
parts.answer: The Munir Report examined the causes of the disturbances and concluded that the ulama could not agree on a definition of a Muslim. This showed that religious leaders were divided and the state could not settle the question by religious authority alone. The report also revealed how religious agitation could threaten public order and the government.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: the report exposed the disagreement among the ulama over who is a Muslim; it showed that religious agitation could threaten public order; it raised questions about the role of religion in the state; it set a precedent for official inquiries into political disorder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three prime ministers of Pakistan who held office between 1951 and 1958.
parts.answer: Khawaja Nazimuddin (1951–1953), Mohammad Ali Bogra (1953–1955), Chaudhry Muhammad Ali (1955–1956), H. S. Suhrawardy (1956–1957), I. I. Chundrigar (1957) and Feroz Khan Noon (1957–1958). Any three of these names.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three correct names: Khawaja Nazimuddin; Mohammad Ali Bogra; Chaudhry Muhammad Ali; H. S. Suhrawardy; I. I. Chundrigar; Feroz Khan Noon. Deduct for dates or names not in the list.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why governments changed so often in Pakistan between 1951 and 1958.
parts.answer: The Muslim League had weak organisation and was divided between factions. Parties depended on alliances in the Assembly that often broke down. Governors-General and the bureaucracy dismissed governments when they lost favour, and the lack of a constitution made it hard to settle the balance of power between the centre and the provinces.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: weak and divided political parties; unstable coalitions in the Assembly; use of the Governor-General's powers to dismiss ministers; no constitution until 1956; rivalry between East and West Pakistan and between provinces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events in Pakistan of October 1958.
parts.answer: On 7 October 1958 President Iskander Mirza abrogated the 1956 Constitution, dissolved the central and provincial assemblies and declared martial law. He appointed General Ayub Khan as Chief Martial Law Administrator. Within weeks Ayub Khan removed Mirza and took over as president.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: abrogation of the 1956 Constitution (7 Oct 1958); assemblies dissolved and martial law declared; General Ayub Khan appointed Chief Martial Law Administrator; Mirza removed and exiled by Ayub (late October 1958).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why the army was able to take control of the government in 1958.
parts.answer: The army was the most organised institution, and the political parties were divided and weak. Politicians had failed to make the system work, so many people accepted military rule. Any two of these.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any two: army the most organised and cohesive institution; political parties weak and divided; repeated government instability; Mirza's alliance with the army; public tolerance of military rule after the failure of politicians.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's membership of SEATO and the Baghdad Pact (later CENTO).
parts.answer: Pakistan joined the South-East Asia Treaty Organisation (SEATO) in 1954, a defence alliance led by the USA. In 1955 it also joined the Baghdad Pact with Turkey, Iran, Iraq and Britain, which was later renamed the Central Treaty Organisation (CENTO).
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: SEATO membership (1954); US-led defence alliance; Baghdad Pact (1955) with Turkey, Iran, Iraq and Britain; renamed CENTO; Pakistan a member of both pacts/alliances.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan joined these US-backed alliances in the 1950s.
parts.answer: Pakistan feared a threat from India, especially over Kashmir, and wanted military support against India. The alliances promised arms and economic aid from the USA, which Pakistan needed to build its army and economy. Pakistan also wanted to show its commitment to the West in the Cold War,.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: fear of India and need for security (Kashmir); US military and economic aid; Cold War alignment with the West; a bid for status and a wider role in world politics; concern about Soviet influence in the region (Baghdad Pact membership was backed by the USA but the USA was not a member).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of Muhammad Ali Jinnah as Governor-General of Pakistan from August 1947 to September 1948.
parts.answer: Jinnah was head of state and presided over the Constituent Assembly. He dealt with the refugee crisis, pressed for a settlement in Kashmir, and advised the government on the founding of the state's institutions. He also set out the principles of the new state in public statements.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: head of state and president of the Constituent Assembly; involvement in refugee relief; Kashmir policy and the 1947–48 war; setting out principles of the state; advising on administrative and constitutional matters.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "Jinnah's leadership was the main reason Pakistan survived its first year as an independent state." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: Jinnah's authority held the new government together; his public statements reassured minorities and refugees; his leadership held the army and the civil service together. Points that disagree: the survival depended on the army, the civil service, refugee relief from ordinary people, the Muslim League organisation and foreign relations; Jinnah was ill and was not able to deal with everything personally. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the economic problems faced by Pakistan in 1947–1948.
parts.answer: Pakistan had very few factories, banks and skilled managers, because most industry and finance had been in India. India delayed paying Pakistan its agreed share of the cash balances. There was a shortage of goods, administrators and money, and the arrival of refugees put pressure on food and housing.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: most industry and finance remained in India; shortage of skilled personnel; India withheld/delayed Pakistan's share of cash balances; shortage of goods and money; refugees putting pressure on food, housing and jobs; a weak tax base.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three measures that the new government took to deal with these problems.
parts.answer: The government set up relief and refugee resettlement, took over evacuee property and began to build the administration and banking system. Any three of these would earn the marks.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three: refugee relief camps and resettlement; allocation of evacuee property; setting up the State Bank of Pakistan (1948); new administration and ministries; appeals for foreign aid and trade agreements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events that followed the death of Muhammad Ali Jinnah on 11 September 1948.
parts.answer: Jinnah died in Karachi on 11 September 1948. Khawaja Nazimuddin became Governor-General, and Liaquat Ali Khan remained prime minister. The government had to continue without its founder, and Liaquat's leadership was tested by refugee problems and disputes with India.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Jinnah died 11 September 1948 in Karachi; Khawaja Nazimuddin became Governor-General; Liaquat Ali Khan remained prime minister; the new leadership faced disputes over Kashmir and refugees; loss of the founder's authority.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the death of Jinnah made it harder for Pakistan to build stable government.
parts.answer: Jinnah had been the one leader trusted by all Muslim League factions, and his authority held them together. After his death the party split into rival groups, and there was no leader with the same prestige. Politicians fought for power, while the civil service and army grew stronger, and no constitution was agreed until 1956.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: loss of a unifying figure for the Muslim League; rival factions and struggle for power; growing influence of the civil service and army; delay in agreeing a constitution; lack of a strong party organisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the assassination of Liaquat Ali Khan in October 1951.
parts.answer: Liaquat Ali Khan, the prime minister, was shot dead at a public meeting in Rawalpindi on 16 October 1951. The assassin was killed at the scene, and the killing left the country without its most experienced political leader. Khawaja Nazimuddin then became prime minister.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: shot dead at a public meeting in Rawalpindi on 16 October 1951; assassin killed at the scene; loss of the most experienced leader; Khawaja Nazimuddin became prime minister afterwards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "The assassination of Liaquat Ali Khan was the main cause of political instability in Pakistan during the 1950s." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: no leader of his stature followed; Nazimuddin lost control; the Governor-General began dismissing governments; rival factions multiplied. Points that disagree: the causes were structural: no constitution until 1956, the weakness of the Muslim League, provincial and East–West rivalry, the rise of the bureaucracy and army. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Thirteenth Amendment of 1997.
parts.answer: The Thirteenth Amendment removed the President's power under Article 58(2)(b) to dismiss the National Assembly and the government. It was passed under Nawaz Sharif's government in 1997, so the power to dismiss elected governments rested with the Prime Minister and Parliament.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: removed the President's power to dismiss the National Assembly (Article 58(2)(b)); passed in 1997 under Nawaz Sharif; power of dismissal moved away from the President; reduced the risk of governments being dismissed by the President.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the removal of the President's power to dismiss governments was welcomed by many politicians in 1997.
parts.answer: Since 1988 several elected governments had been dismissed by Presidents using the 58(2)(b) power, including Benazir Bhutto's twice and Nawaz Sharif's in 1993. Politicians wanted to end this cycle, so they welcomed a measure that made governments more secure. It also strengthened parliament and the principle that elected representatives, not the President, should decide who governs.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: repeated dismissals of elected governments (1990, 1993, 1996); desire for stability and a fixed term; the principle that parliament should rule rather than the President; reduced presidential interference and the role of the military in politics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the general election of November 1988 and the formation of Benazir Bhutto's first government.
parts.answer: The Pakistan People's Party won the largest number of seats in the National Assembly in November 1988 elections held after Zia-ul-Haq's death. Benazir Bhutto became Prime Minister, leading a coalition government.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: elections held in November 1988 after Zia's death; PPP won the largest number of seats; Benazir Bhutto became Prime Minister; she formed a coalition government with other parties.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Benazir Bhutto's election as Prime Minister in 1988 was historically significant.
parts.answer: She became the first woman to head the government of a Muslim-majority country. Her election showed that women could lead political parties and the state in Pakistan, after years of military rule and an Islamisation programme that had limited women's public role. It also showed the return of civilian rule after eleven years under Zia.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: first woman to lead a government of a Muslim-majority country; end of Zia's military rule and return of civilian politics; sign of women in public leadership after the Zia era; the PPP's popularity and the Bhutto legacy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the privatisation policy introduced in Pakistan in the early 1990s.
parts.answer: The government sold state-owned enterprises and banks to private investors in order to reduce the losses of the public sector. A Privatisation Commission was set up in 1991 to manage the sales, and the policy formed part of the economic reforms that were recommended by international lenders.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: sale of state-owned enterprises or banks to private owners; Privatisation Commission set up (1991); reduce losses and debt of the public sector; part of wider economic liberalisation/reform policy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three arguments that were used to support the privatisation drive of the 1990s.
parts.answer: Privatisation would make companies more efficient, raise money for the government, and attract foreign investment. Any three of these.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three: greater efficiency of privatised firms; reduced losses and the burden on the budget; raised revenue from sales; attracted foreign and private investment; reduced the government's role in business.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Accountability (Ehtesab) campaign launched by Nawaz Sharif's second government in 1997–1999.
parts.answer: The government set up an Ehtesab (accountability) Bureau in 1997 to investigate corruption by politicians and officials. Its chairman investigated many leading opposition politicians, including Benazir Bhutto and her husband, and cases were brought against them for alleged corruption.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Ehtesab Bureau set up in 1997; campaign against corruption by politicians and officials; cases against leading opposition figures including Benazir Bhutto; investigations often seen as politically motivated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many people believed the Ehtesab campaign was politically motivated.
parts.answer: The bureau targeted opposition leaders far more than members of the ruling party, which suggested that it was being used against rivals. Its chairman was seen as close to the Prime Minister, and critics said the cases were brought selectively against opposition figures. Critics also said the campaign weakened the courts and the rule of law.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: targeting of opposition leaders more than ruling party members; close links between the bureau's chairman and the Prime Minister; selective cases against opposition figures; the bureau bypassed normal courts and the rule of law.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events that led to the dismissal of Nawaz Sharif's government in April 1993.
parts.answer: In April 1993 President Ghulam Ishaq Khan used Article 58(2)(b) to dismiss the National Assembly and the government of Nawaz Sharif, accusing him of corruption and mismanagement. Nawaz challenged the decision in the Supreme Court, which restored him in May 1993.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: President Ghulam Ishaq Khan dismissed the government in April 1993 under Article 58(2)(b); charges of corruption and mismanagement; Nawaz challenged it in the Supreme Court; Supreme Court restored the government in May 1993.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Nawaz Sharif and Ghulam Ishaq Khan both resigned in July 1993.
parts.answer: The army chief was seen as mediating between the two leaders, and pressure built to end the crisis. Both men agreed to step down, which allowed a caretaker government to hold elections. The resignations were a compromise that avoided further damage to the state and showed that neither could rule effectively after the dispute.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: a deadlock between the President and the Prime Minister; pressure and mediation by the army; a compromise to hold fresh elections under a caretaker government; loss of public trust and political stability; neither leader could govern effectively.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the outcome of the general election of February 1997.
parts.answer: The Pakistan Muslim League (N), led by Nawaz Sharif, won a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly. The Pakistan People's Party lost heavily, and Nawaz Sharif became Prime Minister for a second time.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: PML(N) won a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly; Nawaz Sharif became Prime Minister again; PPP suffered heavy defeat; the election was held in February 1997.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Pakistan Muslim League (N) won so decisively in 1997.
parts.answer: Many voters were dissatisfied with the corruption charges against Benazir Bhutto's government and the economic problems of the 1990s. The PML(N) presented itself as a party of stability and development, and it benefited from its strong organisation in the Punjab, which had the largest number of seats. Its campaign on economic growth and national pride also appealed to many voters.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: voter dissatisfaction with corruption charges against the PPP government; the PML(N)'s message of stability and development; strong organisation and support in the Punjab; effective campaign; the weakness of the opposition after the 1996 dismissal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events that led to the dismissal of Benazir Bhutto's second government in November 1996.
parts.answer: On 5 November 1996 President Farooq Leghari dismissed Benazir Bhutto's government under Article 58(2)(b), accusing it of corruption, mismanagement and the murder of her brother Murtaza Bhutto. A caretaker government was formed and elections were held in February 1997.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: dismissal on 5 November 1996 by President Farooq Leghari under Article 58(2)(b); charges of corruption and mismanagement; murder of Murtaza Bhutto in 1996 cited in the case against the government; caretaker government and elections in February 1997.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many people believed the dismissal of 1996 was not based only on the government's failings.
parts.answer: The timing of the dismissal suited the rival PML(N), which was expected to gain most from a new election, and many people saw the corruption charges as political rather than a fair judgement on the government. The dismissal also showed that the President, not the voters, could decide who governs.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: the timing suited the rival PML(N), which won the February 1997 election; the charges were seen as politically motivated; dismissal by the President rather than parliament or voters; a pattern of dismissals showing that the system was controlled by the presidency.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events of 12 October 1999 that led to General Musharraf taking control of the government.
parts.answer: Nawaz Sharif tried to dismiss General Musharraf as Chief of Army Staff while he was abroad. Musharraf's plane was refused landing rights, and the army took control of Karachi airport. The army then removed the government, arrested Nawaz Sharif and declared a state of emergency.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Nawaz tried to replace Musharraf as army chief while he was abroad; Musharraf's return flight was refused landing rights; army took control of Karachi airport and the government; Nawaz Sharif arrested and emergency declared.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the army acted against the government in October 1999.
parts.answer: Musharraf and senior officers believed that the decision to remove him was an attack on the army and its reputation. The army was angry at the Kargil withdrawal, which had been agreed without its support, and it feared that its position would be weakened. Many generals also believed that the civilian government had become corrupt and unable to govern.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: the attempt to remove the army chief threatened the army's status; anger at the Kargil withdrawal; belief that the civilian government was corrupt and ineffective; the army's institutional interests; public tolerance of military rule after 1999.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the 1992 military operation against the Muhajir Qaumi Movement (MQM) in Karachi.
parts.answer: In June 1992 the army and police began an operation in Karachi against the MQM, which the government said was involved in violence and crime. Thousands of MQM activists were arrested, and many people alleged that killings and torture took place. The MQM later split into factions.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: operation launched in June 1992 under Nawaz Sharif's government; aim to stop violence and crime linked to the MQM; mass arrests of activists; allegations of extrajudicial killings and torture; the MQM split into factions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "The Karachi operation of 1992 solved the problem of violence in the city." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: the operation reduced some of the armed violence and the power of armed groups in the short term. Points that disagree: the operation was accompanied by allegations of human rights abuses, the MQM remained a major political force, and violence returned in later years; underlying grievances about political representation and urban services were not addressed. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the 15th Amendment proposed by Nawaz Sharif in 1998.
parts.answer: The 15th Amendment was a proposal to make Shariah the supreme law of Pakistan. It was passed by the National Assembly but was defeated in the Senate in October 1998, where the government lacked a two-thirds majority.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: proposal to make Shariah the supreme law of Pakistan; proposal to strengthen the Prime Minister and the government; passed by the National Assembly; defeated in the Senate (October 1998) for lack of two-thirds majority.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "Nawaz Sharif's attempts to strengthen his personal power were the main reason for his removal in October 1999." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: the 15th Amendment, the attack on the Supreme Court and the army chief, and the Ehtesab campaign showed a drive for personal power that alarmed the army and the judiciary. Points that disagree: the Kargil crisis, economic problems, the nuclear tests and the trust deficit with the army were important; the military's own interests and the Kargil withdrawal played a direct role. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main steps taken by General Musharraf between October and December 1999 after he took power.
parts.answer: Musharraf suspended the constitution and declared a state of emergency. He took the title of Chief Executive and set up a National Accountability Bureau (NAB) in 1999 to investigate corruption. He also promised to hold elections after a period of reform.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: suspension of the constitution and emergency declared; took the title of Chief Executive; National Accountability Bureau set up (1999); promise of elections and reform after a delay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many civilian politicians supported the new regime in its first months.
parts.answer: Many politicians were discredited by corruption charges and political rivalry, so they hoped that the new government would clean up politics. The public also welcomed the removal of an unpopular government. Some politicians hoped to gain influence by co-operating with the new regime.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: public and political disgust with corruption; discredit of the former government and its rivals; hope for accountability and a clean-up of politics; the chance to gain influence with the new regime.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the economic problems faced by Pakistan's civilian governments between 1988 and 1999.
parts.answer: Governments borrowed heavily from abroad and their budget deficits were large. Debt repayments took a big share of revenue, inflation rose and foreign exchange reserves fell. Growth was slow, and the economy could not create enough jobs for a growing population.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: large budget deficits and heavy foreign borrowing; debt repayments taking a large share of revenue; inflation and falling reserves; slow growth and not enough jobs; dependence on IMF or other loans.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "Economic problems were the main cause of the failure of civilian governments between 1988 and 1999." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: the debt crisis and inflation weakened governments and made them unpopular; governments were dismissed partly because of economic failure; economic reforms were politically costly. Points that disagree: the failures were also caused by corruption charges, presidential dismissals, rivalry between the PPP and PML(N), the Eighth Amendment and the weakness of institutions. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

subtopic: Yahya Khan and the separation of East Pakistan 1969–1971

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the talks between Yahya Khan, Mujibur Rahman and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto in Dhaka in early 1971.
parts.answer: Yahya Khan met Mujibur Rahman in Dhaka in February and March 1971 to discuss a new constitution. Bhutto also took part. The talks failed because they could not agree on the transfer of power and the Six Points, and Yahya postponed the National Assembly on 1 March 1971.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: talks in Dhaka in February–March 1971 involving Yahya, Mujib and Bhutto; disagreement over the Six Points and the transfer of power; Yahya postponed the National Assembly session on 1 March 1971; talks collapsed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the talks of early 1971 failed to produce an agreement.
parts.answer: Mujib insisted that the Awami League's majority gave it the right to frame the constitution, based on the Six Points. Bhutto feared that his party would be excluded from power, and he refused to accept the Awami League's majority as final. Yahya was unwilling to give up central control, and the army refused to accept such a shift of power.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Mujib's insistence on the Six Points and on the Awami League's majority; Bhutto's demand for a share of power and refusal to accept the majority; Yahya and the army's reluctance to give up central control; mistrust between the parties.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Yahya Khan and the separation of East Pakistan 1969–1971

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps taken by Yahya Khan after he became President in March 1969.
parts.answer: Yahya Khan declared martial law and promised free elections on the basis of adult franchise. He dissolved the One Unit scheme, which restored the old provinces of West Pakistan, and announced a Legal Framework for a new constitution.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: martial law declared; promise of elections on adult franchise; One Unit dissolved (1970); announcement of a legal framework for a constitution; release of political prisoners or changes in administration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why Yahya Khan agreed to hold direct elections in 1970.
parts.answer: Mass protests in 1968–69 had made it impossible to keep military rule for long, and Yahya wanted to restore legitimacy. The army also wanted to show that the regime was moving towards civilian rule. Any two.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any two: pressure from mass protests of 1968–69; need for legitimacy for the regime; promise to return to civilian rule; belief that elections would produce a stable government; the army's wish to show it was not permanent.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Yahya Khan and the separation of East Pakistan 1969–1971

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the refugee crisis that developed in East Pakistan and India in 1971.
parts.answer: Military action in East Pakistan from March 1971 caused millions of people to flee across the border into India. The refugees lived in camps in West Bengal and other Indian states, and India faced a huge burden of relief costs. The crisis drew international attention to the conflict.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: millions fled from East Pakistan into India from March 1971; refugees lived in camps in India; a huge cost of relief for India; international attention and concern for the refugees; pressure on India to intervene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three ways in which India responded to the refugee crisis.
parts.answer: India set up refugee camps, gave support to the Mukti Bahini, and began a diplomatic campaign to draw attention to the crisis. Any three of these.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three: setting up and funding refugee camps; support and training for the Mukti Bahini; diplomatic campaign to win international support; pressure on the international community; preparations for military intervention.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Yahya Khan and the separation of East Pakistan 1969–1971

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Bhola cyclone that struck East Pakistan in November 1970.
parts.answer: The cyclone struck the coast of East Pakistan on 12 November 1970 with very high winds and a storm surge. Hundreds of thousands of people were killed, and the central government was criticised for a slow and inadequate response to the disaster.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: struck East Pakistan on 12 November 1970; storm surge and high winds; very high loss of life (hundreds of thousands); slow and inadequate government relief; criticism of the central government.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the government's response to the cyclone increased tension between East and West Pakistan.
parts.answer: East Pakistan felt that the central government had neglected it, because relief was slow and the government seemed unconcerned about the suffering. The cyclone came just before the 1970 election, and many Bengalis blamed the government's failures for the disaster. The response confirmed the existing belief that the West was controlling the country and ignoring East Pakistan.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: slow and inadequate relief reinforced a sense of neglect; timing before the 1970 election increased anger; the belief that the West ignored East Pakistan; the cyclone strengthened support for the Awami League's Six Points demand for autonomy.

author: HomiLabs
