subtopic: Yahya Khan and the separation of East Pakistan 1969–1971

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the arrest of Mujibur Rahman in March 1971.
parts.answer: Mujibur Rahman was arrested in Dhaka on 25 March 1971, during the night of military action. He was taken to West Pakistan and put on trial for treason. He was not released until January 1972, after the separation of East Pakistan.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: arrested on 25 March 1971 in Dhaka; taken to West Pakistan; charged with treason; released in January 1972 after the creation of Bangladesh.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the arrest of Mujib made the crisis more serious.
parts.answer: Mujib was the leader of the Awami League and the most popular figure in East Pakistan, so his arrest removed the main negotiator and seemed to close off a political settlement. It led to open armed resistance, and many Bengali leaders and soldiers joined the Mukti Bahini. The arrest also convinced many Bengalis that the West Pakistan government would not accept their demands.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: removal of the main negotiator and most popular leader; closure of political options; spread of armed resistance and the Mukti Bahini; belief that West Pakistan would never accept Bengali demands; the army's brutal response.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Yahya Khan and the separation of East Pakistan 1969–1971

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how power passed from Yahya Khan to Zulfikar Ali Bhutto in December 1971.
parts.answer: Yahya resigned as President on 20 December 1971 after the defeat of the Pakistani army in East Pakistan. Bhutto, leader of the PPP, took over as President and Chief Martial Law Administrator, and he later became Prime Minister in 1973.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Yahya resigned on 20 December 1971 after the defeat; Bhutto took over as President; Bhutto became Chief Martial Law Administrator; Bhutto later became Prime Minister (1973).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Bhutto was able to take power in December 1971.
parts.answer: The army was discredited by the defeat in East Pakistan and the surrender, so it could not keep Yahya in power. Bhutto's PPP had the largest number of seats in West Pakistan, and his party had a strong base in Punjab and Sindh. The other West Pakistani leaders accepted his leadership because there was no other credible alternative.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: discrediting of the army after the defeat; PPP's majority in West Pakistan and its popular base in Punjab and Sindh; lack of an alternative leader acceptable to the army and other parties; Bhutto's skill in negotiating with the army and rival politicians.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Yahya Khan and the separation of East Pakistan 1969–1971

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the surrender of Pakistani forces in Dhaka on 16 December 1971.
parts.answer: Pakistan's eastern command, led by Lieutenant-General A. A. K. Niazi, surrendered to the joint Indian and Bengali forces in Dhaka on 16 December 1971. Pakistani soldiers became prisoners of war in India, and the surrender marked the creation of Bangladesh.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: surrender on 16 December 1971 in Dhaka; signed by Lieutenant-General A. A. K. Niazi; joint Indian and Bengali forces accepted the surrender; Pakistani soldiers taken as prisoners of war; creation of Bangladesh.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Pakistani army in East Pakistan surrendered so quickly once the Indian army entered the war.
parts.answer: The Pakistani forces were far from their bases and had been scattered by the Mukti Bahini guerrilla campaign. They were outnumbered and short of supplies, and they had no air cover or naval support after the Indian navy and air force took control. The loss of Dhaka's defences made the position hopeless, so further resistance would have caused heavy losses for little purpose.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: isolated forces with no reinforcement or supply; air and naval superiority of India; outnumbered by the joint forces; the Mukti Bahini had weakened them; the surrender of Dhaka made resistance pointless.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Yahya Khan and the separation of East Pakistan 1969–1971

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Indo–Soviet Treaty of Friendship signed in August 1971.
parts.answer: India and the Soviet Union signed a treaty of friendship in August 1971. Each side agreed to consult the other on security matters and to refrain from helping an enemy of the other. The treaty gave India diplomatic backing from the Soviet Union during the crisis in East Pakistan.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: treaty signed in August 1971 by India and the USSR; commitment to consult on security; commitment not to support an enemy of the other; diplomatic support for India during the East Pakistan crisis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "Foreign powers had more influence than Pakistan's internal problems on the separation of East Pakistan in 1971." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: India gave military and diplomatic support to the Mukti Bahini and then intervened; the Indo-Soviet treaty and US/China positions shaped the outcome; the war was decided by India's army. Points that disagree: the separation was caused by internal failures, such as the 1970 election dispute, the army's repression, the economic disparities and the failure to share power. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Yahya Khan and the separation of East Pakistan 1969–1971

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the failure of the National Assembly session planned for March 1971.
parts.answer: The National Assembly session was due to open on 3 March 1971, but Yahya postponed it indefinitely on 1 March. The decision caused protests and strikes in East Pakistan, and Mujib called for civil disobedience and non-co-operation with the West Pakistani government.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: session due on 3 March 1971; postponed indefinitely on 1 March by Yahya; protests and strikes in East Pakistan; Mujib called for non-co-operation or civil disobedience.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "The postponement of the National Assembly in March 1971 was the main reason why Pakistan broke up." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: the postponement destroyed trust, led to mass protests and made a political settlement impossible; it triggered the military crackdown. Points that disagree: the causes went back to the 1970 election dispute, the failure of the Legal Framework, economic disparities, the Six Points and the army's role; the postponement was the trigger, not the root cause. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Yahya Khan and the separation of East Pakistan 1969–1971

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the purpose and findings of the Hamoodur Rahman Commission.
parts.answer: The Hamoodur Rahman Commission was set up in December 1971 to examine the causes of the defeat in East Pakistan and the surrender. Its report, completed in 1974, identified failures of the military and political leaders, but the government did not make it public for many years.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: set up in December 1971; to inquire into the causes of the military defeat and the separation; report completed in 1974; identified failures of military and political leaders; not made public for many years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the government did not publish the report for a long time.
parts.answer: Its findings may have embarrassed the army and political leaders, and the government wanted to protect the reputation of the armed forces. Any reasoned answer.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reason and 1 for development: embarrassing findings about the army or political leaders; wish to protect the reputation of the armed forces; fear of public anger or national division.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Yahya Khan and the separation of East Pakistan 1969–1971

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the mass movement of 1968–1969 that forced Ayub Khan out of office.
parts.answer: Students, workers and political parties organised mass protests in 1968–1969 against Ayub Khan's rule. The protests spread across both wings of the country, and Ayub resigned in March 1969. Yahya Khan, the army commander, then took power and declared martial law.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: mass protests by students, workers and parties (1968–69); protests in East and West Pakistan; Ayub Khan resigned (March 1969); Yahya took over and declared martial law.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the mass movement of 1968–1969 succeeded in forcing Ayub Khan from power.
parts.answer: The movement drew in students, workers and political parties across both wings at once, so no single government could contain it. Ayub had lost legitimacy after years of economic grievance, the concentration of wealth and the restriction of opposition, and his own army commanders were unwilling to order repeated repression. Ayub had no broad base left, so he resigned rather than face a wider crisis.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: broad coalition of students, workers and parties across both wings; loss of Ayub's legitimacy from economic grievance and restriction of opposition; reluctance of the army to use mass repression; Ayub had no remaining base of support.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Yahya Khan and the separation of East Pakistan 1969–1971

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Mukti Bahini, the armed resistance force that fought in East Pakistan in 1971.
parts.answer: The Mukti Bahini was a Bengali guerrilla force formed in 1971 from East Pakistani soldiers, police, students and volunteers who opposed the army. It was trained and supplied from bases in India and carried out attacks on roads, bridges and army posts.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Bengali guerrilla force formed in 1971; members from soldiers, police, students and volunteers; trained and supplied from India; attacks on communications, bridges and army posts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Mukti Bahini was able to carry on its resistance against the Pakistani army.
parts.answer: The army was spread thinly across a large region with rivers, and it could not guard every road and bridge. The Mukti Bahini knew the local terrain and had popular support, so it could hide and get information. Indian training and weapons gave it the means to keep fighting, and the army's brutal tactics drove more young men into its ranks.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: knowledge of the terrain and rivers; local popular support and information; training and weapons from India; the army spread too thin to guard all targets; repression drove recruitment.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the decision by Liaquat Ali Khan to accept an invitation from the United States in 1950.
parts.answer: In 1950 Liaquat Ali Khan accepted an invitation to visit the United States, and he made the visit in May 1950, instead of accepting an invitation to Moscow. The visit began closer ties with the USA, and it was followed by a request for American economic aid.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Liaquat accepted a US invitation (visit May 1950); declined an invitation from the Soviet Union; start of closer ties with the USA; US economic aid was discussed or followed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Liaquat Ali Khan preferred closer links with the USA rather than with the Soviet Union.
parts.answer: Pakistan needed economic aid and technical help to develop, and the USA was the richest country with a strong economy to offer that help. Pakistan also feared India and the Soviet support for India, so it wanted a powerful ally. The Soviet Union was seen as a communist power, and most of Pakistan's establishment was anti-communist.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: need for economic aid and technology; wish for a strong ally against India; anti-communist outlook of Pakistan's establishment; the Soviet Union seen as a rival of the West; the Kashmir dispute and fear of Soviet support for India.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's role in the improvement of US–China relations in 1971.
parts.answer: Pakistan acted as a channel of communication between the USA and China. In July 1971 Henry Kissinger made a secret visit to China from Pakistan, which prepared for President Nixon's visit to China in February 1972.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Pakistan served as a secret channel between USA and China; Kissinger's secret visit to China via Pakistan (July 1971); preparation for Nixon's visit (February 1972); Pakistan's good relations with both powers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the USA did not use its influence to stop the military action in East Pakistan in 1971.
parts.answer: The USA was focused on its relations with China and the Soviet Union, and it saw Pakistan as a valuable partner in opening relations with China. The US government was also reluctant to criticise an ally in public. It sent some diplomatic protests but did not take strong action, which made critics argue that the USA ignored the humanitarian crisis.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: priority given to the opening to China and Cold War strategy; Pakistan as a valuable partner and channel; reluctance to criticise an ally; limited diplomatic pressure; concerns about the Soviet Union and the Cold War balance.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of the US decision in September 1965 to stop military supplies to Pakistan and India.
parts.answer: In September 1965 the USA suspended military supplies to both India and Pakistan during the war. Pakistan, which depended on American weapons, had to look for arms elsewhere, and it turned to China and to other suppliers.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: US suspended military supplies to both countries (September 1965); Pakistan depended on US weapons and spare parts; Pakistan had to turn to other sources (China and others); a sense of betrayal and reduced trust in the USA.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three consequences of the US embargo for Pakistan's relations with other countries.
parts.answer: Pakistan moved closer to China, which supplied arms and political support. Pakistan also began to question its reliance on the USA and sought a more independent foreign policy. Any three.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three: closer ties with China; search for arms from other suppliers (e.g. the Soviet Union, France or Britain); reduced trust in the USA; a more independent foreign policy; diversification of diplomatic relations.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Pressler Amendment and its effect on Pakistan's relations with the USA.
parts.answer: The Pressler Amendment was a US law of 1985 that required the President to certify each year that Pakistan did not possess a nuclear explosive device before aid could be given. In October 1990 the US suspended most military and economic aid, which damaged the relationship.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: US law (Pressler Amendment) of 1985; annual certification that Pakistan did not have a nuclear device; US suspension of aid in October 1990; damage to Pakistan's military and economic relations with the USA.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan felt badly treated when US aid was suspended in 1990.
parts.answer: Pakistan had supported the USA in the war against Soviet forces in Afghanistan, and it had provided bases and support to the mujahideen. Many Pakistanis believed that the USA had used them and then abandoned them after the Soviet withdrawal. The aid cut also hurt the armed forces and the economy at a time of difficulty.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Pakistan's role in the Afghan war and the sacrifice it made; sense of being used and then abandoned; damage to the armed forces and the economy; anger at the nuclear condition as unfair. Accept the view that Pakistan's own nuclear programme was a cause.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the withdrawal of Soviet forces from Afghanistan and its effect on Pakistan.
parts.answer: The Soviet army completed its withdrawal from Afghanistan in February 1989. Pakistan had supported the mujahideen during the war, and the end of the occupation allowed many Afghan refugees to think of returning, but the fighting between Afghan factions continued and refugees stayed in Pakistan.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Soviet army completed withdrawal in February 1989; Pakistan had supported the mujahideen; some Afghan refugees hoped to return; continued fighting between Afghan groups; refugees remained in Pakistan.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Soviet withdrawal did not bring stability to Pakistan.
parts.answer: The Soviet army left, but the Afghan government survived for three more years and the mujahideen factions fought one another. This left Afghanistan without a settlement, so Afghan refugees stayed in Pakistan and the arms and drug trade continued. Pakistan also had to deal with the rise of militant groups that had grown during the war.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: no political settlement in Afghanistan; factional fighting among the mujahideen; refugees remained in Pakistan; arms and drugs trade continued; militant groups formed during the war stayed active.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Pakistani community in Britain and the origins of its growth from the 1950s.
parts.answer: Pakistani migrants began to settle in Britain in the 1950s, many from rural Punjab and Mirpur in Azad Kashmir. The construction of the Mangla Dam in the 1960s displaced many people from Mirpur, and many of them later migrated to Britain. These communities sent remittances to Pakistan.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: settlement from the 1950s; migrants from Punjab and Mirpur (Azad Kashmir); displacement by the Mangla Dam led many to migrate; families and communities formed in Britain; remittances sent to Pakistan.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the Pakistani community in Britain strengthened links between Pakistan and the UK.
parts.answer: Remittances from Britain supported families and the economy in Pakistan, and Pakistani migrants kept close ties with their home villages. Pakistani-British groups took an interest in politics on both sides, and they helped to build cultural and business links. Their presence also meant that British and Pakistani governments had to consider the needs of the community.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: remittances and economic links; family and cultural ties; political interest and lobbying on Kashmir and Pakistani affairs; business and trade links; the need for both governments to consider the community.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the suspension of Pakistan from the Commonwealth after October 1999.
parts.answer: After General Musharraf took power in October 1999, the Commonwealth suspended Pakistan from its councils because the military regime had overthrown an elected government. Pakistan was readmitted in 2004 after the government had promised a return to civilian rule and elections.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: suspended after the October 1999 military takeover; reason: overthrow of an elected government; suspension was from Commonwealth councils and decisions; Pakistan readmitted in 2004.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Commonwealth took a firm line on Pakistan's military government in 1999.
parts.answer: The Commonwealth has a commitment to democracy and the rule of law, and it applies these standards to its members. Its members had suspended other countries after military coups. Pakistan's suspension showed that the Commonwealth would not accept a coup against an elected government, even from a member with strong links to Britain.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Commonwealth commitment to democracy and the rule of law; precedent of suspending members after coups; a clear message against military takeovers; pressure to restore elections and civilian rule.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's withdrawal from the Commonwealth in January 1972.
parts.answer: In January 1972 Pakistan announced its withdrawal from the Commonwealth. The decision was a protest against the recognition of Bangladesh by other Commonwealth members, which Pakistan regarded as unacceptable while the separation was still disputed. Pakistan rejoined the Commonwealth in October 1989.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: announced withdrawal in January 1972; protest against recognition of Bangladesh by other members; Pakistan regarded this as unacceptable; Pakistan rejoined in October 1989.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan's government wished to rejoin the Commonwealth in 1989.
parts.answer: Membership gave Pakistan access to trade links, aid and diplomatic support from other member countries. It also reflected the return of civilian government under Benazir Bhutto, who wanted better relations with the West. Pakistan had lost influence after leaving, and it wanted a voice in Commonwealth councils again.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: access to trade, aid and diplomatic networks; the return of civilian rule and a wish for better Western ties; loss of influence after 1972; the value of Commonwealth membership in international affairs.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the US and Pakistani response to the shooting down of an American U-2 spy plane over the Soviet Union in May 1960.
parts.answer: In May 1960 a US U-2 spy plane was shot down over the Soviet Union. The plane had taken off from Badaber, a US base near Peshawar in Pakistan. The incident caused a major crisis in US–Soviet relations and drew Pakistan into the controversy.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: U-2 spy plane shot down over the USSR in May 1960; the plane had flown from Badaber near Peshawar in Pakistan; major crisis in US–Soviet relations; Pakistan was drawn into the controversy and embarrassed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the U-2 incident damaged Pakistan's relations with the Soviet Union.
parts.answer: The Soviet Union was angered that Pakistan had allowed a US base to be used for spy flights against it. Pakistan had been seen as an ally of the USA in the Cold War, and the incident confirmed Soviet fears of Pakistan as an American base. Soviet leaders became more hostile, and this made co-operation with Pakistan harder in the years that followed.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Pakistan allowed a US base used for spy flights against the USSR; confirmation of Soviet suspicions of Pakistan as a US ally; more hostile Soviet attitudes; reduced prospects of co-operation; Pakistan's US alignment made relations harder.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the US economic sanctions imposed on Pakistan after its nuclear tests in May 1998.
parts.answer: After Pakistan carried out nuclear tests in May 1998, the USA imposed sanctions. These included the suspension of most economic aid, restrictions on loans from some US institutions and bans on some military sales. The sanctions affected Pakistan's economy at a time of financial weakness.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: sanctions imposed after the May 1998 tests; suspension of most economic aid; restrictions on loans or credit from US-backed bodies; bans on some military sales; damage to a weak economy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the sanctions of 1998 hurt the Pakistani economy at a time when it was already weak.
parts.answer: Pakistan had large foreign debts and limited foreign exchange reserves, so the loss of aid and loans made it harder to pay for imports and debt repayments. Investors became cautious, and the rupee came under pressure. The sanctions also cost jobs and made it harder to raise money abroad.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: large foreign debt and low reserves; loss of aid and loans made it harder to pay for imports and debts; investors became cautious; pressure on the rupee; loss of jobs and reduced growth.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's military alliance and aid relationship with the USA during the Cold War.
parts.answer: Pakistan joined US-led defence pacts in the 1950s and received US military and economic aid. The relationship was close in the 1950s and 1980s, but it was strained when the USA cut aid or imposed conditions on Pakistan's nuclear programme.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: membership of US-led pacts (SEATO, CENTO) in the 1950s; US military and economic aid; close relations in the 1950s and in the 1980s; strained relations when aid was cut or nuclear conditions imposed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "Pakistan's relations with the USA were based mainly on shared interests rather than on shared values between 1947 and 1999." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: alliances were based on Cold War strategy (SEATO, CENTO, Afghan war); aid was given for strategic reasons; the USA cut aid when its interests changed (1965, 1990, 1998). Points that disagree: some shared values existed, such as opposition to communism and common interest in democracy, and the relationship was not only strategic; the Pakistani public and the military had different views of the USA. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with the USA, USSR/Russia and UK

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways in which Pakistan's alliance with the USA affected its relations with India.
parts.answer: It made India suspicious that Pakistan would be supported by the USA in disputes, which increased mistrust. It also led India to move closer to the Soviet Union. It encouraged an arms race and higher military spending in the region. Any three of these.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three: Indian suspicion of Pakistan as a US ally; India moved closer to the Soviet Union; increased arms race and military spending; Indian fears of encirclement; alliances gave Pakistan military support but made India less willing to compromise on Kashmir.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the USA supported Pakistan's military alliances despite India's objections.
parts.answer: The USA wanted to contain Soviet influence in South Asia and the Middle East, so it valued Pakistan as a partner. Any reasoned answer.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reason and 1 for development: containment of Soviet influence in South Asia; Pakistan's strategic location near Afghanistan, Iran and the Gulf; desire for allies in the Cold War; US view of India as neutral and independent.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Sino–Pakistan Boundary Agreement of 1963.
parts.answer: In 1963 Pakistan and China signed an agreement fixing the boundary between Pakistani-controlled Kashmir and the Chinese region of Xinjiang. The agreement settled a disputed border area and removed a source of possible conflict between the two countries.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: signed in 1963 between Pakistan and China; fixed the boundary between Pakistani-controlled Kashmir and Xinjiang; settled a disputed area; removed a potential source of conflict between the two countries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan was willing to sign this agreement with China in 1963.
parts.answer: Pakistan had poor relations with India and wanted to avoid a second front on its northern border. It also wanted to strengthen its links with China, which supported its position on Kashmir. The agreement helped Pakistan improve its relations with an important regional power.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: avoid a second front on the northern border; desire for China as a friend against India; support of China on Kashmir; wish to improve relations with an important power; settling a dispute that could cause conflict.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the building of the Karakoram Highway between Pakistan and China.
parts.answer: The Karakoram Highway links Pakistan's northern areas with China. It was agreed in 1966 and built with Chinese help over more than a decade, and it was opened in the late 1970s. The highway linked Gilgit and Hunza to Xinjiang through the mountains.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: link between Pakistan and China through the mountains; agreed in 1966; built with Chinese help; completed/opened in the late 1970s; connecting Gilgit and Hunza with Xinjiang.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three benefits that the Karakoram Highway brought to the northern areas of Pakistan.
parts.answer: It provided a trade route with China, improved transport for local people and made it easier for the government to provide services. Any three.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three: trade route with China; improved transport and access to markets; easier movement of people and services; tourism and economic opportunities; a strategic link for the government.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Indus Waters Treaty signed by Pakistan and India in 1960.
parts.answer: The Indus Waters Treaty was signed in Karachi in September 1960 by Ayub Khan and Nehru, with the World Bank helping to bring about the agreement. The treaty divided the rivers of the Indus system, giving the eastern rivers to India and the western rivers mainly to Pakistan.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: signed in Karachi in September 1960; by Ayub Khan and Nehru; World Bank helped to reach the agreement; eastern rivers allocated to India and western rivers mainly to Pakistan.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Indus Waters Treaty was important for Pakistan's agriculture.
parts.answer: Pakistan's farming depended on irrigation from the Indus river system, and the treaty secured water supplies from the western rivers for canals in Punjab and Sindh. It allowed Pakistan to build large canal systems and dams, and it gave security to farmers and food production.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: farming depended on Indus irrigation; the treaty secured water from the western rivers for canals; allowed dams and link canals to be built (e.g. Mangla, Tarbela, with the help of the treaty framework); food production and farmers' security.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Kargil conflict of May to July 1999.
parts.answer: In May 1999 Pakistani troops and armed militants occupied positions on the Indian side of the Line of Control in the Kargil area. India launched military operations to recapture the positions, and after heavy fighting Pakistan agreed to withdraw in July 1999 following US pressure.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: May–July 1999; Pakistani troops and militants occupied positions on the Indian side of the Line of Control; India launched military operations to recapture them; withdrawal agreed in July 1999 after US pressure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Pakistani government withdrew from Kargil in July 1999.
parts.answer: The operation had failed to achieve its aims and had cost many lives. India had made clear that it would not accept the occupation. The USA put strong pressure on Pakistan to withdraw, because it feared a wider war between two nuclear-armed states. The government also feared economic sanctions and diplomatic isolation.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: the operation had failed and was costly; Indian military response and refusal to accept the occupation; US pressure to avoid a nuclear war; fear of sanctions and isolation; the Prime Minister's wish to negotiate.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Lahore Declaration signed by the Prime Ministers of Pakistan and India in February 1999.
parts.answer: In February 1999 Nawaz Sharif and Atal Bihari Vajpayee met in Lahore and signed a declaration committing both countries to resolving disputes peacefully, including Kashmir, and to measures to reduce the risk of nuclear war. The visit by bus from Delhi was seen as a sign of goodwill.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: signed in Lahore in February 1999 by Nawaz Sharif and Vajpayee; commitment to peaceful settlement of disputes including Kashmir; measures to reduce the risk of nuclear conflict; a goodwill visit to Lahore by bus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Lahore Declaration failed to prevent conflict in Kargil a few months later.
parts.answer: The declaration did not settle the Kashmir dispute, and each side had different views on how to resolve it. Military leaders in Pakistan were not fully committed to the peace process and planned the Kargil operation without consulting the government. The agreement had no means of enforcement, so it depended on goodwill that was soon lost.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: the declaration did not solve Kashmir; the army planned Kargil without the government fully involved; no enforcement mechanism; the peace process depended on goodwill; mutual suspicion and different strategies.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Pashtunistan issue between Pakistan and Afghanistan from 1947 to 1979.
parts.answer: Afghanistan questioned the Durand Line, the border between Pakistan and Afghanistan, and it supported the demand for an independent Pashtun state called Pashtunistan. Afghanistan voted against Pakistan's admission to the United Nations in 1947, and relations were often hostile, with border closures and diplomatic rows.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Afghanistan questioned the Durand Line; support for a Pashtun state or Pashtunistan; Afghanistan voted against Pakistan's UN membership in 1947; border closures and diplomatic rows in the 1950s and 1960s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan was concerned about Afghanistan's support for Pashtunistan.
parts.answer: The demand for Pashtunistan threatened Pakistan's territorial unity, especially in the NWFP and Balochistan. Pakistan feared that Afghanistan would encourage Pashtun nationalism inside Pakistan. Afghan support for Pashtun groups also led Pakistan to support rival Afghan politicians, which increased tension.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: threat to Pakistan's territory and unity, especially the NWFP and Balochistan; fear of Pashtun nationalism inside Pakistan; Afghan links with Pashtun politicians; rivalry led Pakistan to back rival Afghan groups; the Durand Line dispute remained unresolved.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the problem of the stranded Biharis in Bangladesh after 1971.
parts.answer: Many Urdu-speaking Biharis who had supported Pakistan in 1971 lived in camps in Bangladesh and were not accepted as citizens there. Pakistan agreed to repatriate some of them, but the process was slow and many remained in the camps for decades.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Urdu-speaking Biharis who supported Pakistan in 1971; living in camps in Bangladesh; not accepted as Bangladeshi citizens; Pakistan agreed to repatriate some, but progress was slow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the question of the Biharis made relations between Pakistan and Bangladesh difficult.
parts.answer: Bangladesh did not want to grant citizenship to people who had supported the Pakistani army, so the issue was politically sensitive. Pakistan felt responsibility for people who had supported it, and it wanted them repatriated. Both governments had domestic pressure on the issue, so progress was slow and the camps remained a sore point.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Bangladesh's reluctance to grant citizenship to those who supported the army; Pakistan's sense of responsibility; domestic political sensitivity in both countries; slow repatriation; living conditions in the camps as an ongoing grievance.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the cricket diplomacy between Pakistan and India in 1987.
parts.answer: In February 1987 President Zia-ul-Haq attended a cricket match in Jaipur during a visit to India. The visit was part of a cricket diplomacy that eased tension, after a period of serious military alarm between the two countries in 1986–1987.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: President Zia-ul-Haq attended a cricket match in Jaipur (February 1987); the visit was described as cricket diplomacy; it followed a period of military tension; it eased relations between the two countries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cricket diplomacy had only a limited effect on relations between Pakistan and India.
parts.answer: The visit improved the atmosphere and led to talks, but the basic disputes, especially Kashmir, were not settled. Both governments were suspicious of each other's military plans, and the arms race continued. Domestic pressure in each country also made it hard for leaders to make concessions.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: the basic disputes over Kashmir were not settled; mutual suspicion over military plans and the arms race continued; domestic pressure limited concessions; the improvement in atmosphere was temporary; other crises followed.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the water disputes between Pakistan and India after 1960.
parts.answer: After the Indus Waters Treaty, disputes continued over how India used its share of the eastern rivers, and over projects on the Chenab and Jhelum. Pakistan complained that some Indian projects broke the spirit of the treaty, and the two countries used the Permanent Indus Commission to discuss disagreements.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: disputes over India's use of the eastern rivers; complaints about Indian projects on the Chenab and Jhelum; Pakistan's complaints under the treaty; use of the Permanent Indus Commission to discuss problems.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "Water disputes have been the main source of conflict between India and Pakistan since 1947." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: water sharing was a central issue in 1947–48 (the canal dispute) and the treaty was needed to settle it; water projects remain a source of tension. Points that disagree: Kashmir, the wars of 1947–48, 1965 and 1971, nuclear rivalry and the Kargil conflict were more central; water was a serious but secondary cause. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Pakistani Chinese relations during the 1971 crisis.
parts.answer: China supported Pakistan diplomatically during the 1971 crisis and condemned Indian action in East Pakistan. It did not send troops, but it gave political backing and warned India about the risks of an attack on Pakistan.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: China gave diplomatic support to Pakistan; condemned Indian action; no Chinese troops sent; political backing; warnings to India.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why China gave Pakistan only limited support in the 1971 war.
parts.answer: China was seeking better relations with the USA and did not wish to be drawn into a war with India, which was also a power on its border. Its support was mainly diplomatic, because it wanted to avoid a direct confrontation. Also, China did not want to be seen as encouraging the break-up of a state, which might influence its own minorities.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: China pursuing détente with the USA and avoiding conflict; not wishing to fight a war with India; mostly diplomatic support as a limit; concerns about breakaway movements within China; China's own priorities and interests.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the visit of President Zia-ul-Haq to India and its place in Pakistan's relations with India in the 1980s.
parts.answer: The visit of 1987 was one of several steps to improve relations in the late 1980s. Relations had been tense because of military alarm and the Siachen dispute, and leaders on both sides used sports and talks to ease the situation.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Zia's visit in 1987 as one of several steps; relations tense due to military alarm; the Siachen dispute; use of sport and talks to ease relations; part of efforts to improve relations in the late 1980s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the nuclear programme of Pakistan and India made their relations more dangerous from the 1980s onwards.
parts.answer: Both countries built the capacity for nuclear weapons, and each feared the other's intentions, so a military crisis could quickly escalate. Nuclear weapons also raised the stakes of the Kashmir dispute. Their competition led to an arms race and to suspicion that each side would move first in a crisis.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: both countries developed nuclear capacity; mutual fear and suspicion; a crisis could escalate quickly; raised the stakes of Kashmir and other disputes; an arms race and pre-emption fears.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Relations with India, China, Afghanistan and Bangladesh

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Siachen glacier dispute between Pakistan and India.
parts.answer: Siachen is a glacier in the Karakoram mountains in the disputed Kashmir region. India occupied the glacier in 1984, and Pakistan contested the claim, so both sides have kept troops there at very high altitude. It is often called the world's highest battlefield, and talks to end the dispute have not produced a settlement.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: glacier in the Karakoram in disputed Kashmir; India occupied it in 1984; Pakistan contested the claim; troops kept at very high altitude; talks have not settled the dispute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three reasons why the Siachen dispute has been difficult to settle.
parts.answer: Both sides regard the glacier as strategically important, and neither trusts the other to withdraw. The boundary beyond the glacier was never agreed, and the dispute is linked to the wider Kashmir issue. Any three of these.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three: strategic importance and fear of losing ground; boundary beyond NJ9842 never agreed/delimited; mutual mistrust; linked to the wider Kashmir dispute; extreme conditions make withdrawal and verification difficult.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the presidential election of January 1965.
parts.answer: In January 1965 Ayub Khan stood for president against Fatima Jinnah, the sister of the Quaid-e-Azam, who was supported by a coalition of opposition parties. The election was held through the Basic Democrats, the electoral college created by the 1962 system, and Ayub won.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: held in January 1965; Ayub Khan against Fatima Jinnah; opposition coalition supported Fatima Jinnah; elected by the Basic Democrats (the electoral college); Ayub won.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Ayub Khan won the 1965 presidential election.
parts.answer: The Basic Democrats were chosen under government control and many were grateful to Ayub's government for development projects. The opposition was divided and had limited access to the media, while the government had the resources of the state. The Decade of Development had also given many people a sense of progress, and Ayub portrayed himself as a leader who had brought stability.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: the electoral college was controlled by government and grateful to it; opposition divided and restricted; government resources and media; Decade of Development gave a sense of progress; Ayub's image of stability and strong leadership.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Decade of Development that Ayub Khan's government celebrated in 1968.
parts.answer: The government celebrated the Decade of Development, from 1958 to 1968, which showed rapid economic growth in industry and agriculture. Large projects such as dams and industrial estates were highlighted, and the government presented the decade as a success of its planning.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: period 1958–1968; rapid economic growth in industry and agriculture; large projects such as dams and industrial estates; government planning presented as a success.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the benefits of the Decade of Development were unevenly shared.
parts.answer: Industrial growth was concentrated in a small number of large business families, which controlled most industry. East Pakistan received less development spending, so many Bengalis felt they gained little. Farmers with large holdings benefited from the Green Revolution, while small farmers and labourers often gained less.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: industry concentrated in a few families; regional imbalance and less spending in East Pakistan; benefits of the Green Revolution went mainly to large landowners; small farmers and workers gained less; the urban poor did not share growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the press restrictions introduced by Ayub Khan's government in 1963.
parts.answer: In 1963 the government issued the Press and Publications Ordinance, which gave the state powers to control newspapers and the press. Newspapers could be warned, fined or closed, and journalists faced restrictions on what they could publish about government policy and the regime.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Press and Publications Ordinance (1963); state powers to control newspapers; power to warn, fine or close newspapers; restrictions on criticism of government policy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three ways in which Ayub Khan's government limited political opposition during his rule.
parts.answer: The government banned or restricted political parties, arrested opposition leaders, and used the press laws and the Basic Democrats to control public debate. Any three.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three: restrictions on political parties and their activities; arrests and detention of opposition leaders; press laws and censorship; control of elections through the Basic Democrats; use of state security agencies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance of 1961.
parts.answer: The Muslim Family Laws Ordinance of 1961 reformed some aspects of family law. It required a man who wished to take a second wife to obtain permission from an arbitration council, and it set out procedures for divorce and the registration of marriages.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: introduced in 1961; a man needed permission from an arbitration council to take a second wife; procedures for divorce; registration of marriages; reforms to protect women within marriage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Family Laws Ordinance of 1961 was opposed by many religious leaders.
parts.answer: Religious leaders argued that the ordinance changed rules that they believed came directly from Shariah, so they saw it as an attack on religion. The limits on polygamy and divorce were resented by some men, and the government seemed to be acting against the wishes of religious scholars. The opposition was also a way for religious parties to challenge Ayub's government.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: belief that the reforms changed Shariah rules; restrictions on polygamy and divorce; a way for religious parties to challenge the government; the government was seen to override religious scholars; public and religious anger at reforms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the concentration of industry under Ayub Khan that was criticised as the "twenty-two families" problem.
parts.answer: Under Ayub's policies, a small number of business families came to control a large share of Pakistan's industry, banking and insurance. Critics referred to these as the "twenty-two families", who were seen as having gained most from government loans, licences and protection.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: a small number of families controlled a large share of industry, banking and insurance; government licences, loans and protection given to them; the phrase "twenty-two families" used by critics; the concentration of wealth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the concentration of wealth became a political issue by 1968.
parts.answer: The gap between the rich and the poor widened, and this created resentment among workers and small traders. The concentration of wealth was seen as proof that the government favoured its friends. This resentment was used by opposition parties, including the PPP, in their campaigns against Ayub's government.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: a widening gap between rich and poor; resentment among workers and traders; belief that licences and loans favoured friends of the regime; opposition parties such as the PPP used the issue; the protests of 1968–69 reflected the grievance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the formation of the Pakistan People's Party in November 1967.
parts.answer: Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who had left Ayub's cabinet, helped to found the Pakistan People's Party at a convention in Lahore in November 1967. The party criticised Ayub's rule, the concentration of wealth and the lack of democracy, and it promised socialist reforms.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: founded in November 1967 in Lahore; Bhutto, who had left Ayub's cabinet, was a founder; criticism of Ayub's rule and the concentration of wealth; promise of socialist reforms and democracy.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Bhutto chose to found a party opposed to Ayub Khan in 1967.
parts.answer: Bhutto had lost his position in government after disagreements with Ayub, and he wanted a political base of his own. He saw public anger about the economy and the lack of democracy as an opportunity. He also believed that a party based on social justice could appeal to the poor and to students, and so could win power in a future election.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: loss of his government position and wish for a political base; public anger about the economy and democracy; a socialist message to attract the poor and students; the opportunity to win future elections; personal ambition and rivalry with Ayub.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the recommendations of the National Commission on Education of 1959.
parts.answer: The National Commission on Education, chaired by Syed Sharif, was set up in 1959. It recommended a larger expansion of schools and colleges, more attention to science and technical training, and the spread of education to rural areas.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: commission set up in 1959 under Syed Sharif; expansion of schools and colleges; emphasis on science and technical education; attention to education in rural areas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the education commission's recommendations were only partly carried out under Ayub Khan.
parts.answer: Government spending on education was limited, because much of the budget went to defence and the development of industry. Many recommendations needed new teachers and buildings, which took time to provide. Local and provincial authorities did not always have the means or the commitment to put them into practice.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: limited government spending, with defence and industry given priority; the cost and time to build schools and train teachers; weak administrative capacity in provinces; regional differences in response.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Agartala Conspiracy Case brought against Mujibur Rahman in 1968.
parts.answer: In 1968 the government charged Mujibur Rahman and other Bengali leaders with conspiring with India to separate East Pakistan, in what became known as the Agartala Conspiracy Case. The charges were withdrawn in February 1969 after protests and a mass movement in East Pakistan.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: charges brought in 1968 against Mujib and others; alleged conspiracy with India to separate East Pakistan (Agartala case); charges withdrawn in February 1969; protests and mass movement forced the withdrawal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Agartala case increased support for Mujibur Rahman in East Pakistan.
parts.answer: Many Bengalis believed the charges were false and were designed to discredit the Awami League. Mujib was seen as a victim of a government that refused to listen to Bengali demands for autonomy. The case united students and the public behind him, and it made his Six Points more popular.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: belief that the charges were false and politically motivated; Mujib seen as a victim of the government; united students and public behind him; boosted popularity of the Six Points; increased Bengali nationalism.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of the army in Ayub Khan's government between 1958 and 1969.
parts.answer: Ayub Khan was a military officer who relied on the army for support. Senior officers were given posts in government and in state corporations, and the army was the main source of security for the regime. Ayub's military background shaped his style of government.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Ayub was a serving officer who relied on the army; senior officers appointed to government and state corporations; the army provided security for the regime; military style of government and decision-making.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the army's role in government made it harder for democratic politics to develop under Ayub Khan.
parts.answer: Politicians were kept out of key decisions, and the army and the bureaucracy controlled policy. Opposition parties were restricted, so there were few chances to build a democratic tradition. The army also had an interest in preserving its own privileges, which made it reluctant to accept civilian control.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: politicians excluded from key decisions; army and bureaucracy dominated policy; restrictions on parties prevented a democratic tradition; the army's own interests and privileges; a model of military rule that others later copied.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the 1960 election of Ayub Khan as President by the Basic Democrats.
parts.answer: In 1960 the Basic Democrats, who had been elected under the 1959 system, voted to make Ayub Khan president. The vote confirmed his position after he had taken power in 1958, and it was presented as a democratic endorsement of his rule.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Basic Democrats voted in 1960 to elect Ayub as president; they had been elected under the 1959 system; the vote confirmed his position after 1958; presented as democratic endorsement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "Ayub Khan's system of government was more democratic than critics have suggested." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: the system included elections, a Basic Democrats electoral college, a national assembly and a constitution; development and some economic gains were made. Points that disagree: 80,000 Basic Democrats were elected under government control, opposition parties were restricted, the press was controlled, and the army's role gave Ayub the final say. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the economic disparity between East and West Pakistan under Ayub Khan.
parts.answer: Most of the industrial investment and government spending was directed to West Pakistan, although East Pakistan earned much of the foreign exchange from jute exports. The Bengali population was larger, but its share of development spending and government jobs was lower.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: most industrial investment and spending in West Pakistan; East Pakistan earned large foreign exchange from jute; East Pakistan's share of development spending was lower; Bengalis had a smaller share of government jobs; the Bengali population was larger.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the economic disparity between the two wings became a political issue during Ayub's rule.
parts.answer: East Pakistan's people felt that the wealth they produced was used to benefit the West, which fuelled Bengali nationalism. The disparity was used by Mujib in his Six Points, which demanded control over the revenue and foreign exchange of East Pakistan. Protests against Ayub's government in the late 1960s also included demands for regional justice.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: the sense that East Pakistan's export earnings benefited the West; the Six Points demanded control of revenue and foreign exchange; regional injustice in jobs and spending; the protests of 1968–69 included demands for autonomy; growth of Bengali nationalism.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Hudood Ordinances introduced in 1979.
parts.answer: The Hudood Ordinances set out punishments under Shariah for offences such as theft, adultery, fornication and the consumption of alcohol. They included hadd punishments, such as flogging and amputation, and changed the way rape and adultery cases were dealt with in the courts.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: introduced in 1979; punishments under Shariah for theft, adultery, fornication and alcohol; hadd punishments such as flogging and amputation; changed the handling of rape and adultery cases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the Hudood Ordinances caused concern among women's groups.
parts.answer: Women who reported rape could be charged with adultery if they could not prove it, which made victims afraid to come forward. Any reasoned answer.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reason and 1 for development: women who reported rape risked being charged with adultery if they could not prove the crime; victims feared to report; the evidence rules were seen as unfair to women; women's rights groups campaigned against the laws.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Federal Shariat Court set up in 1980.
parts.answer: The Federal Shariat Court was set up in 1980 to examine whether laws were in line with Islamic injunctions. It could strike down laws that it found to be un-Islamic, and it had power to review existing laws and advise on changes.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: set up in 1980; examines whether laws conform to Islamic injunctions; power to declare laws un-Islamic; review of existing laws; advice on changes to legislation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which the Federal Shariat Court changed the legal system.
parts.answer: It gave religious scholars a formal role in reviewing legislation, and it increased the importance of Islamic law in courts. Any two of these.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any two: gave religious judges a formal role in reviewing laws; increased the role of Islamic law in the courts; power to strike down laws as un-Islamic; a new court with appeals to the Supreme Court.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Movement for the Restoration of Democracy (MRD) formed in 1981.
parts.answer: The MRD was an alliance of opposition parties formed in February 1981 to demand the restoration of democracy and free elections. It organised protests and strikes, the largest of which was in Sindh in 1983, when there was violence and many deaths.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: alliance of opposition parties formed in 1981; demand for restoration of democracy and free elections; protests and strikes; major protests in Sindh in 1983 with violence and deaths.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the MRD failed to force Zia-ul-Haq out of power.
parts.answer: The alliance included parties with different aims, which made it hard to agree on a strategy. The government used repression and arrests to suppress protests, and many people did not join because they feared violence. Zia also kept support among the army and some business and religious groups, so the MRD could not split the regime.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: divided parties with different aims; repression, arrests and fear of violence; Zia kept support among the army, business and religious groups; the protests were largely confined to Sindh; the government avoided a national crisis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the referendum held in December 1984 in Pakistan.
parts.answer: In December 1984 Zia-ul-Haq held a referendum asking voters whether they supported the Islamic system that he had introduced. The government announced that a large majority had voted yes, and Zia used the result to extend his presidency for five years.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: referendum held in December 1984; question on support for the Islamic system; government announced a large majority in favour; result used to extend Zia's presidency for five years.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Zia-ul-Haq held the referendum in 1984.
parts.answer: Zia needed a democratic basis for his rule, and a referendum seemed to give legitimacy to his position. He wanted to show that Islamisation had popular support and to counter his critics. The referendum also allowed him to extend his term without an election, which strengthened his control.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: need for legitimacy without an election; to show popular support for Islamisation; to counter critics and opponents; to extend his presidency and control; use of a plebiscite to avoid a contested election.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the national and provincial elections held in February 1985 on a non-party basis.
parts.answer: The National Assembly elections of February 1985 were held without political parties taking part as organised groups. Candidates stood as individuals, and afterwards a new Prime Minister, Mohammad Khan Junejo, was chosen by the Assembly in March 1985.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: National Assembly elections in February 1985; candidates stood as individuals without party labels; parties barred from taking part as organised groups; Junejo chosen as Prime Minister in March 1985.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Zia-ul-Haq wanted elections without political parties in 1985.
parts.answer: Zia distrusted political parties, which had opposed his rule, and he wanted a parliament that would support his policies. Non-party elections were expected to produce members who depended on local influence rather than party discipline. This gave Zia more control over the assembly and let him present the system as a return to democracy.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: distrust of parties that had opposed Zia; expectation of a more compliant assembly; local and personal candidates rather than party discipline; control over the assembly and the government; a claim to democratic credentials.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's role in the Afghan war from 1979 to 1988.
parts.answer: Pakistan became the main base for the Afghan mujahideen after the Soviet invasion of December 1979. It gave shelter to millions of Afghan refugees, trained and armed resistance groups with US and Saudi support, and played a central part in the negotiations that led to the Geneva Accords of 1988.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: base for the mujahideen after the Soviet invasion of December 1979; shelter for millions of Afghan refugees; training and arming resistance groups with foreign support; central part in the Geneva Accords (1988).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Zia-ul-Haq supported the Afghan mujahideen.
parts.answer: The Soviet occupation of Afghanistan threatened Pakistan's security, and a pro-Soviet government on its border was seen as dangerous. Supporting the mujahideen also brought Pakistan substantial US and Saudi aid, which strengthened the army. Zia saw the struggle as a religious duty and a way to win support from Muslim countries.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: security threat from a pro-Soviet Afghan government and Soviet troops; substantial US and Saudi aid; strengthening the army; Islamic and ideological motives, such as the wish to support fellow Muslims; a way to gain prestige in the Muslim world.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the death of General Zia-ul-Haq in August 1988.
parts.answer: On 17 August 1988 President Zia-ul-Haq died when the aircraft carrying him crashed near Bahawalpur. Several senior military officers and the US ambassador were also on board. Zia's death ended the military regime and led to the return of elected government.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: died on 17 August 1988 in a plane crash near Bahawalpur; senior military officers on board; US ambassador also killed; end of military rule and return to elections.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many people believed that the crash that killed Zia-ul-Haq was not an accident.
parts.answer: Many people suspected sabotage, because Zia had made enemies among political and military groups. The investigation did not produce a clear and widely accepted conclusion, which encouraged rumours. The political changes that followed the crash were seen as favourable to some groups, which made suspicion stronger.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: enemies among political and military groups; the inquiry did not give a conclusive public answer; rumours and suspicion of sabotage; political benefits to some groups after his death; the scale of the loss of senior officers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Ordinance XX of 1984 concerning the Ahmadiyya community.
parts.answer: In 1984 Zia issued Ordinance XX, which made it an offence for Ahmadis to call themselves Muslims, to use Islamic terms or to preach their faith in public. Ahmadis were restricted in their religious practices, and the ordinance was criticised by human rights groups.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Ordinance XX (1984); offence for Ahmadis to call themselves Muslims; restrictions on use of Islamic terms and preaching in public; restriction of religious practices; criticism by human rights groups.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Zia's government introduced Ordinance XX in 1984.
parts.answer: The government wanted to build public support for its Islamisation programme and to satisfy religious groups that had campaigned against the Ahmadis since the 1950s. The ordinance was also an attempt to define Islam in law, which the regime saw as part of its political legitimacy. Anti-Ahmadi groups pressed for stronger measures.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: to satisfy religious groups and build support for Islamisation; long-standing religious campaigns against the Ahmadis; an attempt to define Islam in law and legitimise the regime; pressure from anti-Ahmadi groups; the government's wish to show it was enforcing Shariah.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order of 1984 and its effect on the evidence of women in court.
parts.answer: The Qanun-e-Shahadat Order of 1984 changed the law of evidence. In certain cases the testimony of two women was treated as equal to that of one man, so that women's evidence was given less weight in some cases.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order (1984); changes to the law of evidence; in some cases the evidence of two women equalled one man; women's evidence given less weight in some cases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "Zia-ul-Haq's Islamisation policies were more successful in theory than in practice." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: many policies, such as zakat and the Federal Shariat Court, were introduced in law but applied unevenly; the Hudood laws caused injustice and the state failed to implement a full Islamic system; the system became a tool of political control. Points that disagree: the policies changed the legal and educational system in lasting ways, and the Islamisation process did change public life, religious institutions and the role of the ulama. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the reaction in Pakistan to the Tashkent Declaration of January 1966.
parts.answer: The Tashkent Declaration, signed by Ayub Khan and Indian Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri, ended the 1965 war without a settlement of Kashmir. Many Pakistanis felt that the terms gave away the gains of the war, and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who had been foreign minister, attacked the agreement publicly and later resigned from the cabinet in June 1966.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: signed by Ayub Khan and Shastri (January 1966); no settlement of Kashmir; criticism that the terms gave away gains from the war; Bhutto resigned as foreign minister and publicly attacked the declaration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Tashkent Declaration damaged Ayub Khan's reputation.
parts.answer: Ayub had claimed that the war was a victory, and the agreement seemed to undo that claim. The lack of any progress on Kashmir disappointed people who had hoped that the war would settle the dispute in Pakistan's favour. The opposition used the declaration to attack Ayub as weak, and the criticism spread among students and in the army.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: contradicted Ayub's claim of victory in 1965; no progress on Kashmir disappointed public hopes; opposition and Bhutto used it to attack Ayub; loss of prestige among students and some army officers; it weakened his legitimacy in the later 1960s.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Afghan refugees who came to Pakistan during Zia-ul-Haq's rule.
parts.answer: After the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979, millions of Afghans fled to Pakistan, where they lived in camps in the NWFP and Balochistan and in cities. The number of refugees was estimated at around three million at the height of the crisis, and the Pakistani government and UN agencies provided relief.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: refugees fled after the Soviet invasion (1979); estimated about three million; camps in NWFP and Balochistan and cities; relief provided by Pakistan and UN agencies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Zia-ul-Haq's government accepted the Afghan refugees.
parts.answer: Zia saw the Afghans as fellow Muslims who were fighting a Soviet-backed regime, and it was seen as a religious and moral duty to help. Pakistan also received large amounts of foreign aid for the refugees, which helped the economy. Accepting the refugees was part of the strategy of supporting the mujahideen, which was supported by the USA and Saudi Arabia.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Islamic brotherhood and moral duty; foreign aid for the refugees; part of the strategy to support the mujahideen with US and Saudi backing; security concerns about a Soviet-backed regime next door; humanitarian response and pressure from the international community.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Zakat and Ushr Ordinance of 1980.
parts.answer: The Zakat and Ushr Ordinance of 1980 made zakat a state-collected tax on Muslims with certain savings. Zakat was deducted from bank accounts each year, and ushr was a tax on the produce of agricultural land. The funds were collected and distributed through government arrangements.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: introduced in 1980; zakat collected by the state; deducted from bank accounts each year; ushr collected on agricultural produce; funds distributed through government arrangements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Zakat ordinance caused controversy among some Muslim groups.
parts.answer: Shia groups objected because their jurisprudence did not accept the same rules for zakat, and they argued that the state should not impose a Sunni interpretation. Many people also disliked the compulsory deduction from bank accounts, which they saw as an interference with personal choice. Protests in 1980 by Shia groups in several cities showed how divided opinion was.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Shia groups objected to the state imposing a Sunni interpretation; compulsory deduction seen as interference; protests by Shia groups in 1980; disagreement about the state's role in religion; some saw the measure as a political tool.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the economic growth and the sources of foreign money that Pakistan enjoyed during the 1980s.
parts.answer: Pakistan's economy grew at a relatively fast pace during the 1980s. Remittances from Pakistanis working in the Gulf states became a large source of foreign money, and US and Saudi aid linked to the Afghan war brought in further funds. Government spending increased, but borrowing also rose.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: relatively fast economic growth in the 1980s; remittances from Pakistani workers in the Gulf; US and Saudi aid linked to the Afghan war; rising government spending and borrowing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the economic growth of the 1980s was not fully sustainable.
parts.answer: Much of the growth was based on foreign money linked to the Afghan war and Gulf remittances, which could fall if the conditions changed. Borrowing rose and the budget deficit grew, which made the economy vulnerable to debt problems. Investment in industry and education was not enough to create long-term productivity.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: growth depended on temporary foreign money (Afghan war aid, Gulf remittances); rising borrowing and budget deficits; weak investment in industry and education; vulnerability to changes in world conditions; debt problems later.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the dismissal of Prime Minister Mohammad Khan Junejo by Zia-ul-Haq in May 1988.
parts.answer: On 29 May 1988 Zia-ul-Haq dismissed Junejo's government and dissolved the National Assembly, using his powers under the Eighth Amendment. He announced fresh elections for later in the year, and Junejo was later refused a chance to continue as Prime Minister.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: dismissal on 29 May 1988; government and National Assembly dissolved; use of the Eighth Amendment powers; fresh elections announced for later in the year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Zia-ul-Haq dismissed Junejo's government in 1988.
parts.answer: Junejo had begun to act more independently of Zia, including over the Geneva Accords on Afghanistan, which Zia had opposed. Junejo also tried to reduce the military's influence and to build his own base, so Zia saw him as a threat. The dismissal reasserted the President's control over the government and the army.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Junejo acted more independently, including on the Geneva Accords; tension over Afghan policy; Junejo's attempts to build an independent base and limit the military's influence; Zia's wish to keep control of the government through the President's powers; the Eighth Amendment allowed dismissal.

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's admission to the United Nations in 1947.
parts.answer: Pakistan became a member of the United Nations on 30 September 1947. Its admission was delayed by Afghanistan, which voted against it because of the dispute over the Pashtun border areas. Pakistan's membership gave it a platform to press its case over Kashmir.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: admitted on 30 September 1947; Afghanistan voted against admission; dispute over the Pashtun border areas; membership gave a platform to press its case over Kashmir.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Afghanistan opposed Pakistan's entry to the United Nations in 1947.
parts.answer: Afghanistan did not accept the Durand Line as its border with Pakistan, and it supported the demand for Pashtunistan. It feared that Pakistan would use its UN membership to strengthen its border claims. The Afghan government wanted the Pashtun question to be raised in international forums.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Afghanistan did not accept the Durand Line; support for Pashtunistan and the Pashtun areas; fear that Pakistan's membership would strengthen its border position; a wish to raise the Pashtun question internationally.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the UN resolutions on Kashmir passed in 1948 and 1949.
