parts.answer: In August 1948 the UN Commission for India and Pakistan passed a resolution calling for a ceasefire and a plebiscite on the future of Kashmir. In January 1949 a further resolution was passed for a plebiscite under UN supervision, and a ceasefire line was agreed.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: August 1948 resolution calling for a ceasefire; calls for a plebiscite on Kashmir's future; January 1949 resolution for a plebiscite under UN supervision; ceasefire line agreed in 1949.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the UN resolutions on Kashmir were never fully implemented.
parts.answer: The plebiscite required that Pakistan withdraw its forces first, and India insisted on its own conditions, so neither side would move first. The arrangements for demilitarisation were never agreed, and India later argued that Kashmir had joined India legally. Once the question became part of the Cold War, the UN could not force either side to comply.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: disagreement over the order of withdrawal and demilitarisation; India's claim that Kashmir had acceded legally; the UN lacked enforcement power; the Cold War made Security Council action difficult; both sides' conditions were incompatible.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the founding of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in 1969.
parts.answer: The OIC was founded in 1969 at a summit in Rabat, Morocco, after an arson attack on the Al-Aqsa mosque in Jerusalem. It was set up to promote the solidarity and interests of Muslim states, and it has been the main forum for Muslim countries since then.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: founded in 1969 at Rabat, Morocco; response to the arson attack on the Al-Aqsa mosque; purpose to promote solidarity and the interests of Muslim states; main forum for Muslim countries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan supported the OIC from its foundation.
parts.answer: Pakistan had a large Muslim population and wanted to build a strong Muslim voice in world affairs. The OIC was a way to secure support for the Kashmir cause and for Palestine, which Pakistan strongly backed. Membership also gave Pakistan links with Arab states that were important for trade and aid.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: a wish to build a strong Muslim voice; support for Kashmir at the OIC; solidarity with Palestine; links with Arab states for trade and aid; the OIC as an Islamic identity forum for Pakistan.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Islamic Summit held in Lahore in February 1974.
parts.answer: The second Islamic Summit was held in Lahore in February 1974 and brought together leaders of many Muslim countries. It was an important show of Muslim unity, and Pakistan used it to strengthen its ties with Arab states and to deal with the recognition of Bangladesh.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: held in Lahore in February 1974; attended by leaders of many Muslim countries; a show of Muslim unity; used to strengthen ties with Arab states; linked to the recognition of Bangladesh.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan wanted to host the Islamic Summit in 1974.
parts.answer: Pakistan wanted to demonstrate its place in the Muslim world after the loss of East Pakistan in 1971. It hoped that the summit would bring financial aid and political support from Arab countries. Bhutto also used the summit to improve Pakistan's standing with the Islamic states and to present his government as a leader of the Muslim world.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: to restore Pakistan's place in the Muslim world after 1971; to attract financial aid and political support from Arab states; Bhutto's wish to lead the Islamic world; to strengthen unity and relations with Muslim states; to support Palestine and the Muslim cause.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's support for the Palestinian cause at the United Nations and in the Muslim world.
parts.answer: Pakistan has consistently supported the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination and an independent state. It has refused to recognise Israel, and it has backed Palestinian causes in the UN and the OIC and in its statements at international meetings.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: consistent support for Palestinian self-determination; supports a Palestinian state; does not recognise Israel; backs Palestinian causes in the UN and the OIC.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Palestinian cause has been popular in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Many Pakistanis identify with the Palestinians as fellow Muslims who have suffered from the loss of their land. The issue has a strong religious significance because of Jerusalem. Pakistani politicians and religious parties have used the issue to show their commitment to the Muslim world, which makes it an easy issue to support.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Islamic solidarity and religious significance of Jerusalem; sympathy for a people seen as dispossessed; use by politicians and parties to show commitment to Islam; the issue fits a broader Muslim identity; the cause unites Pakistani public opinion.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the UN Security Council's response to the war of September 1965 between India and Pakistan.
parts.answer: In September 1965 the UN Security Council called for an immediate ceasefire and the withdrawal of forces. Both sides accepted the ceasefire after about seventeen days of fighting, and the UN monitored the ceasefire line in Kashmir.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Security Council called for an immediate ceasefire in September 1965; called for withdrawal of forces; both sides accepted the ceasefire; UN observers monitored the ceasefire line.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the UN was not able to end the 1965 war quickly.
parts.answer: The Security Council was divided by Cold War interests, and the USA and the Soviet Union had different positions. Neither India nor Pakistan wanted to accept a settlement that gave the other side advantages. The UN had no means to enforce its resolutions, so its authority depended on the goodwill of the parties.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Cold War divisions in the Security Council; neither side wished to accept a settlement that favoured the other; no enforcement power; the UN relied on the goodwill of the parties; the war was decided on the battlefield before a settlement.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Islamabad conference of Muslim foreign ministers held in January 1980.
parts.answer: The conference was held in Islamabad in January 1980 and was attended by the foreign ministers of many Muslim countries. It condemned the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and called for the withdrawal of Soviet forces. Pakistan used the conference to rally support for the Afghan resistance.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: held in Islamabad in January 1980; foreign ministers of many Muslim states attended; condemned the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan; called for Soviet withdrawal; Pakistan used it to rally support for the Afghan resistance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Islamabad conference was important for Pakistan's foreign policy under Zia-ul-Haq.
parts.answer: The conference gave Pakistan a leading role in Muslim diplomacy at a time when it was on the front line of the Afghan crisis. It helped Zia to present the war as a religious and moral struggle, and it brought diplomatic and financial support. The meeting also showed that Pakistan could influence the wider Muslim world.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: a leading role in Muslim diplomacy; presenting the Afghan war as a moral struggle; diplomatic and financial support from Muslim states; Pakistan on the front line of the crisis; the conference showed Pakistan's influence in the Muslim world.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three benefits that Pakistan gained from membership of the United Nations.
parts.answer: Membership gave Pakistan a voice in world affairs, a platform to present its case on Kashmir, and access to technical and development aid through UN agencies. Any three of these.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three: a voice in world affairs and a platform for diplomacy; a platform to press Kashmir before the Security Council; access to UN agencies and technical aid; peacekeeping roles that brought prestige and income; membership of world bodies such as UNESCO and the World Health Organisation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one problem that UN membership created for Pakistan.
parts.answer: Its disputes with India, especially Kashmir, were debated at the UN, which kept the issue in the public eye. Any reasoned answer.
parts.working: 1 mark for a problem and 1 for development: Kashmir debates were repeatedly raised without solution; UN resolutions remained unimplemented, causing frustration; Pakistan's criticism of the UN on Kashmir was often a source of diplomatic friction; obligations under UN sanctions regimes.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's membership of the Regional Co-operation for Development (RCD), founded in 1964.
parts.answer: The RCD was an organisation of Iran, Pakistan and Turkey, founded in 1964 to promote economic and technical co-operation among its members. It aimed to increase trade and joint projects, although its achievements were limited.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: founded in 1964; members Iran, Pakistan and Turkey; aim of economic and technical co-operation; joint projects and trade promotion; achievements limited.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the RCD achieved only limited success.
parts.answer: Economic links between the members were weak, and their trade was small compared with their trade with Western countries. Political rivalries and changes of government, including the Iranian revolution of 1979, reduced co-operation. The organisation lacked the funds and institutions needed for large joint projects.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: weak economic links and small trade; political changes, including the 1979 Iranian revolution; lack of funds and institutions for joint projects; competing priorities and rivalry; the wider Cold War alignment of members.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's contribution of UN peacekeepers to Bosnia in the 1990s.
parts.answer: In the 1990s Pakistan contributed troops to the United Nations Protection Force (UNPROFOR) in Bosnia. Pakistani soldiers served in the conflict zone as part of the UN mission, and the country was among the many contributors of peacekeepers to the region.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: troops contributed to UNPROFOR in Bosnia in the 1990s; served in the conflict zone; part of a UN mission; among the contributors of peacekeeping forces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan supported the Bosnian Muslims during the Bosnian war.
parts.answer: Bosnian Muslims were a religious community facing violence, and many Pakistanis saw the war as an attack on Muslims. Pakistan supported UN and OIC calls to protect the Bosnian people and to lift the arms embargo. The support also strengthened Pakistan's image as a champion of Muslims in the world.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: religious solidarity and public sympathy; OIC and UN calls to protect Bosnian Muslims; support for lifting the arms embargo; image of Pakistan as a champion of Muslims; humanitarian concern.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the idea of the "Muslim Ummah" as it was used in Pakistan's foreign policy after 1947.
parts.answer: Pakistan's leaders often described the Muslim world as a community of nations with shared faith and common interests. This idea was used to justify close relations with Muslim countries, support for Muslim causes and membership of Islamic organisations.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: idea of a shared community of Muslim nations (Ummah); used to justify relations with Muslim countries; support for Muslim causes such as Palestine and Kashmir; membership of Islamic organisations such as the OIC.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the idea of the Ummah was not always a reliable basis for Pakistan's foreign policy.
parts.answer: Muslim countries had different interests and rivalries, such as the conflicts in the Middle East and the rivalry between Iran and Saudi Arabia. Pakistan also needed the support of Western powers for its security and economy, so it could not give priority to the Muslim world alone. Shared religion did not always produce agreement on political issues.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Muslim states had different and conflicting interests; rivalry between Muslim powers (e.g. Iran and Saudi Arabia); Pakistan's dependence on Western support for security and the economy; religion did not always produce agreement; the Ummah idea was used to serve national interests.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's support for the Kashmir cause in the OIC in the 1990s.
parts.answer: In the 1990s Pakistan used the OIC to raise the Kashmir issue, with resolutions that called on India to respect the rights of Kashmiris and to allow a UN-supervised settlement. Pakistan argued that the Kashmir cause should be a priority for all Muslim countries, and the OIC supported its position in its statements.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Pakistan raised Kashmir in the OIC; resolutions calling on India to respect Kashmiri rights; support for a UN-supervised settlement; argument that Kashmir should be a priority for Muslim states.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "Pakistan's attempts to build unity in the Muslim world between 1947 and 1999 were largely successful." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: Pakistan helped to found and hosted key organisations (OIC, 1974 Summit, ECO/RCD), obtained support on Kashmir and Palestine, and gained influence in the Gulf and Afghan affairs. Points that disagree: Muslim states had rival interests and sometimes split (Iran–Saudi rivalry, Iraq–Iran war, Gulf disputes), Pakistan's own relations with some states were strained, and the unity was often rhetorical. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: UN, world organisations and the Muslim world

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's support for the Palestinian cause at the United Nations during the 1970s and 1980s.
parts.answer: Pakistan voted for UN resolutions recognising the rights of the Palestinian people, including their right to self-determination. It supported the Palestine Liberation Organisation as the representative of the Palestinians and opposed Israeli settlement policies in the occupied territories.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: voted for UN resolutions on Palestinian rights and self-determination; supported the PLO as the Palestinian representative; opposed Israeli occupation and settlements; backed Palestinian causes in the UN General Assembly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "Pakistan's support for the Palestinian cause at the United Nations was mainly symbolic." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: Pakistan had no military or economic power to affect the Israel–Palestine dispute; its statements and votes had little effect on the outcome; its interest was partly driven by domestic religious politics. Points that disagree: Pakistan's votes and diplomatic backing gave the Palestinian cause legitimacy in the Muslim world; it supported the OIC and aid for Palestinians; it helped keep the issue on the international agenda. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the provisions of the 1956 Constitution about the national language.
parts.answer: The 1956 Constitution recognised both Urdu and Bengali as the national languages of Pakistan. This was an important concession to East Pakistan, where Bengali was the language of the majority, and it was a result of the language movement and the demands of Bengali politicians.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Urdu and Bengali both recognised as national languages; important concession to East Pakistan; result of the language movement and Bengali demands; Bengali spoken by the majority of the population.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the recognition of Bengali as a national language mattered to the people of East Pakistan.
parts.answer: Bengali was the mother tongue of most people in East Pakistan, so its recognition was a sign that their culture was respected. It gave Bengali speakers equal status in government and education, and it was seen as a victory after the bloodshed of 1952. It also showed that the state could accept a federal and regional identity.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Bengali was the mother tongue of most East Pakistanis; recognition as respect for their culture and identity; equal status in government and education; a victory after the 1952 movement; sign that the state accepted regional identity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the provisions of Article 251 of the 1973 Constitution concerning the Urdu language.
parts.answer: Article 251 of the 1973 Constitution declared Urdu the national language of Pakistan. It required steps to be taken to make Urdu the official language, and it set a period of fifteen years for the change from English to Urdu in government business.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Urdu declared the national language; steps to make it the official language; fifteen-year period set for the change; English to be replaced in government business over time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three reasons why English remained the main language of government and higher education after 1973.
parts.answer: English was the language of elite education and of the legal system, and many officials had been trained in English. Few textbooks and technical terms existed in Urdu. Any three.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three: English dominant in elite and private education; legal system and courts used English; officials trained in English; limited technical vocabulary and textbooks in Urdu; resistance from some provinces and groups to a rapid change.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the launch of Pakistan Television in 1964.
parts.answer: Pakistan Television began broadcasting from Lahore in 1964 and was run by the state. It spread rapidly to other cities, and it gave the government a major means of reaching the public with news, drama and educational programmes.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: began broadcasting in 1964 from Lahore; state-run; expanded to other cities; news, drama and educational programmes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why television became an important means of building national identity in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Television brought the same programmes to people across different provinces, which helped to create shared experiences. Drama in Urdu and the regional languages showed many aspects of Pakistani life, and national events such as independence day broadcasts helped to unite viewers. The state used it to promote national values and national unity.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: shared programmes across provinces; Urdu and regional-language drama showing national life; national broadcasts on key events; promotion of national values by the state; reach to rural as well as urban areas over time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main proposals of the National Education Policy of 1970.
parts.answer: The National Education Policy of 1970 proposed the expansion of education at all levels, with a particular focus on primary schooling and on the teaching of science and technical subjects. It also set targets for literacy and for the training of teachers.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: expansion of education at all levels; priority on primary education; emphasis on science and technical education; targets for literacy and teacher training.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the National Education Policy of 1970 was not fully carried out.
parts.answer: The government had limited funds, and the money for education was often diverted to defence and other priorities. The political crisis of 1970–71 and the war in East Pakistan disrupted planning. Local shortages of teachers and buildings meant that targets were hard to reach in many areas.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: limited funds, with defence and other priorities taking money; the political crisis and war disrupted planning; shortages of teachers and buildings; difficulty of reaching rural areas; weak administration and changes of government.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes to the school curriculum made under Zia-ul-Haq's Islamisation programme.
parts.answer: Islamiat was made a compulsory subject for Muslim students in schools and colleges. Textbooks were revised to include more Islamic content, and religious education was given a larger place in the curriculum.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Islamiat made compulsory for Muslim students; textbooks revised with more Islamic content; religious education given a larger place; changes applied at school and college level.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Zia-ul-Haq wanted to change the school curriculum in this way.
parts.answer: Zia believed that education should reinforce the Islamic identity of the country and that it would help to strengthen the legitimacy of his government. Religious parties had long demanded such changes. The new curriculum was also a way to shape the values of the next generation and to support the Islamisation programme.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: belief that education should strengthen Islamic identity; legitimacy for the regime and support from religious groups; long-standing demands from religious parties; shaping the values of future citizens; part of a wider Islamisation programme.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the contribution of the poet Faiz Ahmed Faiz to Urdu literature and to political debate.
parts.answer: Faiz Ahmed Faiz was an Urdu poet whose verse expressed hope for social justice and opposition to oppression. He was imprisoned in 1951 after being implicated in a plot against the government, and he received the Lenin Peace Prize in 1962.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: major Urdu poet; verse on social justice and opposition to oppression; imprisoned in 1951 (Rawalpindi conspiracy case); awarded the Lenin Peace Prize in 1962.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the poetry of protest was popular with many Pakistanis.
parts.answer: Protest poetry gave voice to people who felt powerless under military or authoritarian governments. Its language was memorable and could be recited at gatherings, so it spread widely. It also expressed hope for social justice at times when open political opposition was dangerous.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: gave voice to people facing repression; memorable language recited and shared widely; expressed hope for justice when open debate was limited; connected with the wider Urdu literary tradition; made political ideas accessible to ordinary people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the founding of Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad.
parts.answer: Quaid-i-Azam University was founded in 1967 in Islamabad as a national university for research and advanced study. It was named after Muhammad Ali Jinnah, and it became one of the main centres of higher education in Pakistan.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: founded in 1967 in Islamabad; national university for research and advanced study; named after Jinnah; one of the main centres of higher education.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the growth of universities was important for Pakistan's development after 1947.
parts.answer: Universities trained teachers, engineers, doctors and officials that the country needed. They also produced research that could support industry and agriculture. Their graduates helped to build the civil service and the professions, and they contributed to national debate.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: training of skilled professionals; research for industry and agriculture; graduates for the civil service and professions; centres of national debate and ideas; reducing dependence on foreign expertise.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the adoption of the national anthem of Pakistan in 1954.
parts.answer: The national anthem was adopted in 1954. Its lyrics were written in Urdu by the poet Hafeez Jalandhari, and the music was composed by Ahmed Ghulamali Chagla. The anthem is played at official occasions and national events.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: adopted in 1954; lyrics in Urdu by Hafeez Jalandhari; music by Ahmed Ghulamali Chagla; played at official occasions and national events.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why national symbols such as the anthem help a country with many languages and regions to feel united.
parts.answer: Shared symbols give people a common identity that goes beyond language or region. An anthem sung at school and at national events builds a sense of belonging. Symbols allow citizens from different backgrounds to take part in the same national rituals and feel part of the same nation.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: shared symbols create a common identity beyond language or region; repeated use in schools and national events builds belonging; shared rituals bring citizens together; symbols represent the nation to others; they can be used to strengthen unity in times of crisis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Shaheed Minar (Martyrs' Monument) in Dhaka, built in 1963.
parts.answer: The Shaheed Minar in Dhaka was built in 1963 to commemorate the students and others killed in the language movement of 21 February 1952. It became a central symbol of Bengali identity and an important place for public gatherings.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: built in 1963 in Dhaka; commemorates those killed in the language movement of 21 February 1952; symbol of Bengali identity; place for public gatherings and commemoration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why 21 February became a symbol of Bengali identity and resistance after 1952.
parts.answer: Students who were killed by police in 1952 were seen as martyrs for the Bengali language. The day was marked each year and the memory spread among Bengalis at home and abroad. It became associated with the wider demand for Bengali cultural and political rights, which later fed into the movement for autonomy.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: students killed in 1952 seen as martyrs for the Bengali language; annual commemoration spread the memory; association with cultural and political rights; the day became a rallying point for autonomy; later linked to the 1971 independence movement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: "Language has been the most important factor in the unity of Pakistan since 1947." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: the 1952 language movement, the 1956 recognition of Bengali, and the 1972 Sindhi language bill all show language as a major source of conflict or unity; Urdu was the lingua franca for national communication. Points that disagree: the causes of separation of 1971 were mainly political and economic, and the state did not always handle language well, but regional languages and shared Islamic identity also contributed; provincial and political grievances mattered more than language alone. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways in which the state promoted a common national identity through school textbooks and the media after 1947.
parts.answer: Textbooks presented Pakistan's history from an Islamic and national viewpoint, the media broadcast national events and symbols, and the state celebrated national days. Any three.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three: textbooks presenting an Islamic and national history; state media broadcasting national events and symbols; national days and celebrations (Pakistan Day, Independence Day); national anthem and flag in schools; the promotion of Urdu as a common language.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why some groups felt that these national identity messages did not represent them.
parts.answer: Some groups, such as Bengalis and smaller provincial communities, felt their history and languages were not represented in textbooks and media. Any reasoned answer.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reason and 1 for development: Bengali and provincial histories left out; regional languages underused in state media; a sense that the national identity favoured one group; resentment at the promotion of one language or culture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the establishment of the Pakistan Academy of Letters in 1976.
parts.answer: The Pakistan Academy of Letters was set up in 1976 to promote literature in Pakistan's national and regional languages. It gave awards to writers, supported publications and organised literary events.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: established in 1976; promotes literature in national and regional languages; gives awards to writers; supports publications and literary events.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the state supported literature and the arts after 1947.
parts.answer: Literature and the arts helped to build national pride and a shared cultural identity. The state wanted to promote the national languages and to show Pakistan's achievements to the world. Support for writers and artists also gave the government a link to the intellectual community.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: build national pride and shared identity; promote national and regional languages; show Pakistan's cultural achievements abroad; link to the intellectual and artistic community; cultural diplomacy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Sindhi Language Bill of 1972 and the reaction to it.
parts.answer: In 1972 the Sindh provincial government passed a bill making Sindhi a compulsory subject in schools across Sindh. Urdu-speaking residents in Karachi and Hyderabad protested that the measure threatened their language and their rights, and violent clashes followed in July 1972.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: passed in 1972 by the Sindh government; made Sindhi compulsory in schools; Urdu-speaking residents protested; violent clashes in Karachi and Hyderabad in July 1972.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the Sindhi Language Bill caused unrest in 1972.
parts.answer: Urdu-speaking communities in Sindh feared that they would be treated as second-class citizens if Sindhi became the main language of administration. The bill was seen by Sindhi nationalists as correcting past neglect, but it was passed without enough consultation. Politicians exploited the fears on both sides, which led to violence.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Urdu speakers feared second-class status and loss of jobs; Sindhi nationalists saw it as correcting neglect; passed without consultation; politicians exploited fears on both sides; ethnic tension and violence in Karachi and Hyderabad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main aims of Ayub Khan's foreign policy between 1958 and 1969.
parts.answer: Ayub Khan aimed to keep close ties with the USA while also developing relations with China and the Soviet Union. He wanted to secure military and economic aid, to strengthen Pakistan's position against India and to build Pakistan's standing in the region.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: close ties with the USA for military and economic aid; developing relations with China; links with the Soviet Union; strengthening Pakistan's position against India; building Pakistan's regional standing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Ayub Khan moved closer to China after the Sino-Indian war of 1962.
parts.answer: The Sino-Indian war showed that India and China were rivals, so Pakistan saw an opportunity to gain a friendly power on its northern border. China also wanted to counter India, so both sides had common interests. The 1963 boundary agreement and growing trade confirmed the closer relationship.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: the Sino-Indian war made China a rival of India and a potential friend for Pakistan; shared interest in countering India; the 1963 boundary agreement; US reluctance to support Pakistan fully against India; trade and diplomatic contacts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the main aims of Liaquat Ali Khan's foreign policy between 1947 and 1951.
parts.answer: Liaquat Ali Khan aimed to secure Pakistan's place in the Commonwealth and in the UN, to build friendly relations with the USA and Britain, and to strengthen links with the Muslim world. He also sought to settle the Kashmir dispute and to protect Pakistan's share of assets from India.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Commonwealth and UN membership; friendly relations with the USA and Britain; links with the Muslim world; settlement of Kashmir and protection of assets.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan wanted to remain in the Commonwealth in 1947.
parts.answer: Membership gave Pakistan access to trade links and aid from Britain and other members. Commonwealth membership also gave Pakistan a recognised place in international affairs at a time when it needed to establish its legitimacy. Many Pakistani leaders had been educated under British institutions and valued these links.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: trade, aid and access to Commonwealth networks; international legitimacy for a new state; links to British institutions, the civil service and the army; the value of a recognised place in world affairs; continuity with the old British system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three aims of Pakistan's foreign policy that remained largely the same from 1947 to 1999.
parts.answer: Pakistan consistently sought security against India, support on Kashmir, and friendly relations with the Muslim world. Any three.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any three: security against India; support for the Kashmir cause; friendly relations with the Muslim world; alliances with major powers for security and aid; a balance between Western and Islamic partners.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why Pakistan's foreign policy remained focused on India throughout this period.
parts.answer: India was the main military threat, and the Kashmir dispute kept tension high. Any reasoned answer.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reason and 1 for development: India seen as the main military threat; Kashmir dispute kept tension high; the wars of 1947–48, 1965 and 1971; the size and power of India compared with Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of the Iranian Revolution of 1979 on Pakistan's relations with Iran during Zia-ul-Haq's rule.
parts.answer: The Iranian Revolution of 1979 brought Islamist leaders to power in Iran. In Pakistan the revolution stirred protests by Shia groups, including a demonstration that attacked the US consulate in Karachi in December 1979. Zia's government had to balance its relations with the new Iranian regime against its Islamic and Saudi ties.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Islamist government came to power in Iran in 1979; Shia protests in Pakistan, including attack on US consulate in Karachi (Dec 1979); Pakistan had to balance relations with Iran; relations with Saudi Arabia and Islamic ties.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Zia-ul-Haq's policies made relations with Iran difficult in the 1980s.
parts.answer: Zia's Islamisation policies, including the Zakat ordinance, were seen by many Shias in Pakistan as favouring Sunni interpretations and provoked protests. Iran's government also criticised Pakistan's close links with the USA and its support for the Afghan mujahideen. Saudi Arabia was an important ally of Pakistan, so Pakistan could not fully side with Iran in the Gulf rivalry.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: Zia's Islamisation and the Zakat ordinance angered Shia groups and created tension; Iranian criticism of Pakistan's US links and Afghan policy; Pakistan's alliance with Saudi Arabia limited its room for manoeuvre; sectarian tension in Pakistan affected relations with Iran.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the SAARC summit held in Islamabad in December 1988 during Benazir Bhutto's first government.
parts.answer: The summit was the first SAARC summit hosted by Pakistan, held in Islamabad in December 1988. Benazir Bhutto hosted the leaders of the South Asian countries, and the Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi attended, which was seen as a sign of improving relations.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: SAARC summit held in Islamabad in December 1988; hosted by Pakistan under Benazir Bhutto; attended by South Asian leaders including Rajiv Gandhi; seen as a sign of improving relations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Benazir Bhutto's government wanted better relations with India in 1988–1990.
parts.answer: Benazir wanted to end the tension of the Zia years and to show that the new civilian government could handle foreign policy. Better relations with India would help the economy and reduce military spending. She also wanted to show the West and the region that Pakistan was moving towards democracy and stability.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: to end the tension of the Zia period; to reduce military spending and help the economy; to show that civilian government could manage foreign policy; to win Western support for democracy; SAARC and trade as a way to build confidence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's policy towards Afghanistan after the fall of the Najibullah government in 1992.
parts.answer: After the fall of Najibullah's government in April 1992, Pakistan supported Afghan mujahideen groups in their struggle for power in Kabul. It hoped to secure a government friendly to Pakistan and to limit Indian influence in Afghanistan, and it gave support to factions such as the one led by Gulbuddin Hekmatyar.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Najibullah's government fell in April 1992; Pakistan supported mujahideen groups in the struggle for Kabul; aim of a friendly government in Afghanistan; aim to limit Indian influence; support for factions such as Hekmatyar.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan's Afghan policy created problems for Pakistan in the 1990s.
parts.answer: Support for rival factions led to a civil war in Afghanistan, which made the country unstable and increased refugee numbers. Pakistan was accused of interfering in Afghanistan's internal affairs. The fighting also encouraged militant groups and the drug trade, which affected Pakistan's own security.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: support for rival factions prolonged the civil war; instability and refugees affecting Pakistan; accusations of interference damaged relations with neighbours and the West; spread of militant groups and the drug trade; security costs for Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Benazir Bhutto's second government's support for the Taliban in Afghanistan.
parts.answer: Benazir Bhutto's second government (1993–1996) gave support to the Taliban, who emerged in 1994 in southern Afghanistan. Pakistan saw the Taliban as a means of bringing stability to Afghanistan and of securing trade routes to Central Asia.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: support for the Taliban during 1993–1996; Taliban emerged in 1994 in southern Afghanistan; aim of bringing stability to Afghanistan; aim of securing trade routes to Central Asia.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan supported the Taliban in the mid-1990s.
parts.answer: Pakistan wanted a government in Kabul that would be friendly and would end the civil war, which had made trade and refugee problems worse. The Taliban offered the prospect of a stable route to Central Asia. Pakistan also believed that a Pashtun-led government would keep Afghanistan away from Indian influence.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: a friendly government to end the civil war and refugee problems; a route to Central Asian trade; limit Indian influence in Afghanistan; a Pashtun-led government seen as stable; security concerns on the western border.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's policy of neutrality in the Iran–Iraq war of 1980–1988.
parts.answer: Pakistan declared itself neutral in the Iran–Iraq war, and it did not take sides in the fighting. It tried to mediate between the two countries and to protect its trade and its Shia and Sunni communities from the effects of the war.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: declared neutrality in the Iran–Iraq war; did not take sides in fighting; tried to mediate between the two countries; protected trade and its own communities from war effects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Zia-ul-Haq chose neutrality in the Iran–Iraq war.
parts.answer: Pakistan had close links with both Saudi Arabia and Iran, and it could not afford to offend either. The war threatened Pakistan's trade and security, and there was a large Shia community that might be affected by the conflict. Taking sides would have harmed Pakistan's support from Gulf states, which was important for its economy and the Afghan war.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: close links with both Iran and Saudi Arabia; the war threatened trade and security; sectarian sensitivity in Pakistan; support from Gulf states for the Afghan war and the economy was at stake; neutrality allowed Pakistan to mediate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Zia-ul-Haq's foreign policy towards Afghanistan, Iran and the Gulf in the 1980s.
parts.answer: Zia's government supported the Afghan mujahideen with US and Saudi aid, sheltered millions of Afghan refugees and developed close security links with Saudi Arabia. It also maintained neutrality in the Iran–Iraq war, while avoiding confrontation with Iran.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: support for the Afghan mujahideen with US and Saudi aid; sheltering of Afghan refugees; close security links with Saudi Arabia; neutrality in the Iran–Iraq war; careful management of relations with Iran.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "Zia-ul-Haq's foreign policy made Pakistan more secure than it had been before 1977." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: Zia secured large US and Saudi aid, built up the army, and gained influence in the Gulf and in Afghan affairs; the Soviet threat was countered through the mujahideen and no Soviet advance into Pakistan occurred. Points that disagree: the Afghan war brought refugees, arms, drugs and militancy into Pakistan; sectarian tension rose; relations with India and Iran were strained; the security gains were partly temporary and were paid for in internal instability. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the foreign policy of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto as Foreign Minister under Ayub Khan between 1963 and 1966.
parts.answer: Bhutto as Foreign Minister sought to strengthen Pakistan's ties with China and the Soviet Union while keeping relations with the USA. He negotiated the boundary agreement with China in 1963 and promoted an independent foreign policy, which he later presented as an alternative to dependence on the USA.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: Foreign Minister from 1963 to 1966; strengthened ties with China; negotiated the 1963 boundary agreement with China; promoted a more independent foreign policy; kept links with the USA.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Bhutto wanted Pakistan to become less dependent on the USA in the mid-1960s.
parts.answer: The USA had suspended arms supplies to Pakistan in 1965, which showed the risks of depending on a single ally. Bhutto believed that Pakistan should have a more independent role and that its interests were not always matched by the USA. Close relations with China and the Soviet Union gave Pakistan other options, and the Tashkent talks showed Soviet willingness to mediate.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: the US arms embargo of 1965 exposed the risks of dependence; belief that US and Pakistani interests diverged; alternative partners in China and the Soviet Union; a wish for an independent foreign policy and national pride; the Tashkent talks showed Soviet role.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the signing of the Geneva Accords in April 1988 and Pakistan's part in them.
parts.answer: The Geneva Accords were signed in April 1988 by Pakistan, Afghanistan, the Soviet Union and the USA, under UN supervision. Pakistan signed as one of the parties. The agreement provided for the withdrawal of Soviet troops from Afghanistan, which was completed in February 1989.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: signed in April 1988; signed by Pakistan, Afghanistan, the USSR and the USA; UN supervision; provided for withdrawal of Soviet troops, completed in February 1989.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan's government under Junejo signing the Geneva Accords caused controversy.
parts.answer: Some army officers and Zia-ul-Haq were unhappy with the terms, which they felt did not protect the mujahideen or Pakistan's interests. The agreement seemed to end Pakistan's role as the centre of the war, and it did not guarantee a government friendly to Pakistan in Kabul. The disagreement helped lead to the dismissal of Junejo's government in May 1988.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: army and Zia unhappy with terms that did not protect the mujahideen or Pakistan; no guarantee of a friendly government in Kabul; agreement seemed to end Pakistan's central role; the dispute contributed to Junejo's dismissal in May 1988; a conflict between the civilian government and the military establishment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's links with Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states in the 1980s.
parts.answer: Pakistan's links with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states grew in the 1980s. Saudi Arabia gave financial support for the Afghan war and for Pakistan's development. Large numbers of Pakistani workers went to the Gulf, and their remittances became a major source of foreign money.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: growth of links with Saudi Arabia and the Gulf in the 1980s; Saudi financial support for the Afghan war and Pakistan; large numbers of Pakistani workers in the Gulf; remittances as a major source of foreign money.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Pakistan's relations with the Gulf states were important for its economy and security in the 1980s.
parts.answer: Remittances from workers in the Gulf helped to pay for imports and support families, which boosted the economy. Saudi aid helped Pakistan to fund the Afghan war effort and to build its armed forces. Pakistan also saw the Gulf states as partners in the Muslim world, and they provided diplomatic support on Kashmir.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: remittances helped pay for imports and support families; Saudi aid for the Afghan war and the armed forces; diplomatic support from the Gulf states on Kashmir; a source of jobs for Pakistani workers; Islamic solidarity and a shared security outlook.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the foreign policy of Benazir Bhutto's governments towards the USA between 1988 and 1996.
parts.answer: Benazir Bhutto's governments sought good relations with the USA, which was important for aid and trade. They faced problems over Pakistan's nuclear programme, and the US Pressler Amendment restricted aid. Relations were also affected by Pakistan's role in Afghanistan.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: sought good relations with the USA for aid and trade; problems over the nuclear programme; Pressler Amendment restricted aid; Pakistan's role in Afghanistan affected relations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: "Benazir Bhutto's foreign policy was more successful than her domestic policy between 1988 and 1996." How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Level-marked: any well-supported balanced answer that reaches a clear judgement. See working for content.
parts.working: Level marking. Points that agree: the SAARC summit of 1988, the return to the Commonwealth in 1989 and efforts to improve relations with India and the West were real achievements; her domestic record was marked by corruption charges and economic problems. Points that disagree: the Pressler sanctions and the Afghan policy caused lasting problems; the India relationship did not improve much and Kashmir became more violent; the foreign gains did not translate into lasting stability. Level 4–5 (11–14): balanced, supported, with a clear judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe Pakistan's recognition of the Taliban government in Afghanistan in 1997.
parts.answer: In 1997 the Pakistan government recognised the Taliban government in Kabul, after the Taliban had captured most of Afghanistan. Pakistan was among the few countries to give official recognition, and it saw the Taliban as a friendly force on its western border.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 4: recognition in 1997; Taliban had captured most of Afghanistan; Pakistan one of very few countries to recognise the regime; seen as a friendly force on the western border.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the recognition of the Taliban damaged Pakistan's relations with the West and with the wider world.
parts.answer: The Taliban's treatment of women and minorities, and their harbouring of militant groups, were widely condemned. Western governments saw recognition as support for a regime that broke human rights norms, and this made relations with Western countries harder. It also raised concerns that Pakistan was supporting extremism and reduced its image as a moderate state.
parts.working: Level marking. L3 (5–7): two reasons explained: the Taliban's treatment of women and minorities was condemned; recognition seen as support for a regime that broke human rights norms; harboured militant groups, raising concerns about extremism; reduced Pakistan's image as a moderate state; difficult relations with Western governments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'load factor' as used by an airline.
parts.answer: The percentage of the available seats on a flight that are filled by passengers (passengers carried ÷ seats available × 100).
parts.working: 1 mark for 'seats/places filled by passengers'; 1 mark for the percentage calculation or ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A domestic route is flown 3 times a day by an aircraft with 180 seats. The average load factor is 85%. Calculate the total number of passengers carried on this route in one day.
parts.answer: 459 passengers
parts.working: M1 seats filled per flight = 180 × 0.85 = 153; M1 × 3 flights = 459; A1 459 passengers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why air freight is used to send fresh exports such as cut flowers and fresh mangoes.
parts.answer: Speed: the produce reaches distant buyers within hours, so it arrives fresh and can be sold at a good price. Access: it allows exporters to reach distant or high-price markets before the produce spoils. Less handling and damage than a long road journey. (Any two developed reasons.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed reason (e.g. shorter transit time means less spoilage and better quality); 1 mark for a simple reason stated without development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A flight covers 1,200 km at an average speed of 720 km/h. Calculate the flight time in minutes.
parts.answer: 100 minutes (1 h 40 min)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why the actual time from leaving the departure gate to reaching the arrival gate may be longer than the flight time calculated in (a).
parts.answer: Taxiing and queuing for take-off; holding or waiting for air-traffic clearance; climbing and descent procedures; weather delays; boarding and disembarking. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct reason, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two roles of air traffic control at an airport.
parts.answer: Air traffic control keeps aircraft safely separated in the air and on the runway; it gives take-off and landing clearances in the right order; it guides aircraft on the taxiways; it passes on weather and hazard warnings to pilots.
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed role (e.g. 'gives take-off and landing clearances so that aircraft do not collide'); 1 mark for a role named only in outline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A regional airport recorded 48,000 domestic passengers in 2020 and 61,440 in 2025 (illustrative figures). Calculate the percentage increase in domestic passengers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason for the increase in passengers.
parts.answer: New or more frequent flights on the route; rising incomes so more people can afford air travel; growth of business or tourism in the area; better road links to the airport.
parts.working: 2 marks for one developed suggestion linked to the data; 1 mark for a suggestion without link.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two environmental problems caused by a large airport built close to a city.
parts.answer: Noise from aircraft takeoffs and landings disturbs sleep, schools and hospitals; air pollution from aircraft engines and extra road traffic to the airport; loss of farmland, trees or wildlife habitat; surface water drainage changed. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed problem (cause and effect); 1 mark for a problem named but not developed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 'hub airport' is a major airport where many routes meet. Define the term 'hub airport'.
parts.answer: A large airport where airlines connect passengers or cargo between many domestic and international routes.
parts.working: 1 mark for 'large airport'; 1 mark for 'connects passengers or cargo between many routes'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a hub airport can benefit the national economy.
parts.answer: It attracts airline and business investment and creates jobs in airport services, catering and logistics; it gives exporters quick access to world markets; transit passengers spend money in the country; it supports tourism and business travel.
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed benefit; 1 mark for a benefit named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which new airports and air routes are more important than roads for connecting the remote northern areas of Pakistan with the rest of the country.
parts.answer: For air: fast access for emergency patients, tourists and officials; air is the only quick link when roads are blocked by snow, landslides or floods; perishable goods can be flown. Against: flights are expensive and have few seats, they are disrupted by weather, and most people and freight depend on roads for daily movement; roads are cheaper to build and use. Judgement: air is vital for speed and emergencies, but roads are more important for everyday movement of people and goods.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about air or roads. Level 2 (3–4): developed points for one side and some for the other. Level 3 (5–6): balanced, developed evaluation of both with a supported judgement that refers to the remote northern areas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features that distinguish a motorway from a national highway.
parts.answer: A motorway has limited access (only at junctions, no pedestrians or slow vehicles); it has separate carriageways for each direction with a central divider; it allows higher speeds; it has grade-separated junctions. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct feature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the term 'metalled road'.
parts.answer: A road surfaced with tar or asphalt (or concrete) which can be used in all weathers.
parts.working: 1 mark for a surface such as tar, asphalt or concrete; 1 mark for 'usable in all weathers' or 'all-year use'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three problems that farmers face when rural roads are unmetalled (not surfaced) during the monsoon season.
parts.answer: Crops cannot reach the market in time and perishable produce spoils; vehicles get stuck in mud or ruts; transport costs rise; children cannot reach school and sick people cannot reach a clinic. (Any three.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct problem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bus travels 360 km on a motorway at an average speed of 90 km/h. Calculate the driving time in hours.
parts.answer: 4 hours

parts.label: b
parts.text: The bus leaves at 07:30 and makes two rest stops of 15 minutes each. Calculate the arrival time on the 24-hour clock.
parts.working: M1 total time = 4 h 30 min (4 h driving + 30 min stops); A1 07:30 + 4 h 30 min = 12:00.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a toll system works on a motorway and state one reason why some road users dislike it.
parts.answer: Vehicles pay a fee at toll plazas, usually based on vehicle type or distance, before or after using the road; the money is used to build and maintain the road. Reason for dislike: the fee adds to the cost of travel, which is hard for poorer drivers, daily commuters and lorry operators; or there is no free alternative.
parts.working: 1 mark for describing payment at a toll plaza; 1 mark for the purpose (maintenance or recovering costs); 1 mark for a reason for dislike.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the function of a bypass road for a large city such as Lahore.
parts.answer: A bypass takes through-traffic, especially heavy lorries, around the city centre, reducing congestion and pollution inside the city; it shortens journeys between places on either side of the city; it reduces accidents in crowded streets; it gives access to industrial estates on the edge of the city.
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed function; 1 mark for a function named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In one district, 1,680 road casualties were recorded in 2024 and 1,428 in 2025 (illustrative figures). Calculate the percentage fall in casualties.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two measures that could reduce road casualties in the district.
parts.answer: Repairing potholes and marking lanes; enforcing speed limits with cameras or checkpoints; compulsory helmets for motorcyclists; better street lighting and road signs; driver training. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each sensible measure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which poor road maintenance, such as potholes and overloaded lorries, increases the cost of transporting goods.
parts.answer: Potholes damage tyres, suspensions and axles, so repair and replacement costs rise; vehicles must travel more slowly, so journeys take longer and drivers and fuel cost more; overloading wears the road surface faster and causes breakdowns, which means lost trips and delayed deliveries.
parts.working: 2 marks for each explained cause and effect on transport cost; 1 mark for a cause stated without explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which road transport is more suitable than rail for moving perishable food, such as milk and vegetables, from the farms of Sindh to the markets of Punjab.
parts.answer: For road: door-to-door delivery, flexible routes and timing, refrigerated lorries, speed over medium distances. Against road: higher cost per tonne-km, fuel use, congestion and accidents, overloading. For rail: cheaper for bulk and long distances, less fuel and pollution. Against rail: slower, fixed timetables, few refrigerated wagons, transfers needed at both ends. Judgement: road is usually more suitable for perishables over this distance unless rail offers reliable refrigerated wagons and timetables.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about road or rail. Level 2 (3–4): developed points for road and rail. Level 3 (5–6): balanced evaluation of both, referring to perishability and distance, with a supported judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two services that mobile phone companies provide other than voice calls.
parts.answer: Text messaging (SMS); mobile internet and data; mobile money or digital payments; video calls. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct service.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'broadband' and state one advantage of broadband over an older dial-up connection.
parts.answer: Broadband is a high-speed, always-on internet connection that can carry large amounts of data at once. Advantage: faster downloads, smooth video streaming and video calls, and no need to dial in before each session.
parts.working: 1 mark for a definition that includes 'high-speed' or 'large amounts of data'; 1 mark for one valid advantage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A district had 240,000 mobile phone subscribers in 2020 and 300,000 in 2025 (illustrative figures). Calculate the percentage increase in subscribers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why mobile phone coverage is often weaker in the mountainous northern districts than in the plains.
parts.answer: Mountains block and reflect radio signals, so valley villages may not receive a signal; masts are harder to build and power on steep, remote slopes, so companies are reluctant to install them; a small population means less income for the company, so coverage is not profitable. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed explanation; 1 mark for a simple point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a 'fibre-optic cable' and give one advantage of it over a copper cable.
parts.answer: A cable made of thin glass or plastic strands that carries signals as pulses of light. Advantage: much greater data capacity and speed, less signal loss over long distances, and not affected by electrical interference. (Any one.)
parts.working: 1 mark for a definition (strands, light pulses); 1 mark for one valid advantage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A digital payment service charges 1.5% of the amount sent. Calculate the fee for sending Rs 4,000.
parts.answer: Rs 60

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the internet has changed how Pakistani farmers get information about market prices and weather.
parts.answer: Farmers can check crop prices in several towns before selling, so they can bargain for a better price or choose the best market; weather forecasts and pest or fertiliser advice can be received by phone, so farmers can plan sowing and spraying; farmers can contact buyers directly, reducing the role of middlemen. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed explanation; 1 mark for a change named without explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two social or cultural effects of the growth of social media among young people in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Young people can stay in touch with family abroad and share ideas, which widens their awareness of the world; but false news and rumours can spread quickly; pressure about appearance and comparison with others can harm self-confidence and mental health; time spent online can reduce study and sleep. (Any two developed effects, positive or negative.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed effect; 1 mark for an effect named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the digital divide between urban and rural areas limits the education of rural students.
parts.answer: Many rural homes and schools have no reliable internet or electricity, so students cannot use online lessons or research; fewer computers and devices are available; teachers may have little training in digital tools; weak mobile coverage means students cannot access online learning materials. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed point (cause and effect on learning); 1 mark for a point not developed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which improvements in telecommunications have helped disaster warning and relief in Pakistan.
parts.answer: For: mobile alerts and radio and television warnings reach people quickly before floods or earthquakes; relief agencies co-ordinate by phone and satellite; families can report needs and trace relatives. Against: power cuts and damaged masts stop communications exactly when they are needed; many remote areas have no coverage; false information spreads on social media. Judgement: telecommunications helps warning and relief greatly, but its value depends on reliable power and networks that survive disasters.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about warnings or communications. Level 2 (3–4): developed points for and against. Level 3 (5–6): balanced evaluation reaching a supported judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two types of freight carried by Pakistan Railways.
parts.answer: Coal; cement; fertiliser; grain. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct type of freight.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages of rail over road for carrying heavy bulk goods over long distances.
parts.answer: A train carries a very large load in one journey, so the cost per tonne-kilometre is lower; it uses less fuel per tonne-kilometre and so causes less air pollution; it takes lorries off the roads and reduces road damage. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct advantage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A train has 12 coaches with 60 seats each. On one journey 75% of the seats are occupied. Calculate the number of passengers on the train.
parts.answer: 540 passengers

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why many people choose buses rather than trains for short journeys.
parts.answer: Buses pick people up and drop them near home and work, so there is no need to travel to a station; buses leave more often and at more times of day; fares for short trips are often lower; trains can be delayed or fully booked. (Any two developed reasons.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed reason; 1 mark for a simple reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two safety measures used at railway level crossings.
parts.answer: Barriers or gates that close to road traffic when a train approaches; warning lights, bells and signs; staff or a gatekeeper at the crossing; drivers must stop and check before crossing. (Any two developed measures.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each measure described with its purpose; 1 mark for a measure named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two benefits of electrifying a railway line.
parts.answer: Electric trains accelerate faster and can run more frequently, so the line carries more passengers or freight; electric traction costs less to run than diesel and produces no exhaust fumes; the journey is quieter and smoother. (Any two developed benefits.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed benefit; 1 mark for a benefit named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A train leaves Lahore at 14:20 and the journey takes 4 hours 35 minutes. Calculate the arrival time on the 24-hour clock.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A freight train covers 1,000 km in 12 hours 30 minutes, including stops. Calculate its average speed in km/h.
parts.answer: 80 km/h

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a freight train often travels more slowly than a passenger train on the same line.
parts.answer: Freight trains are heavy and long, so they accelerate and brake slowly and need a longer distance to stop; they often wait on sidings to let passenger trains pass; on single-track lines they may have lower priority; the track may be restricted to lower speeds for heavy loads. (Any two developed reasons.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed reason; 1 mark for a reason named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which rail freight could reduce road damage and carbon emissions in Pakistan.
parts.answer: For: one freight train can replace many lorries, reducing wear on roads and fuel use per tonne-km; rail produces fewer emissions per tonne moved. Against: rail is slower, the track and wagons are old, many factories and farms have no rail connection, so lorries are still needed at both ends, and transfers add cost. Judgement: rail freight helps greatly on main corridors for bulk goods, but its benefit is limited where last-mile delivery by road is needed.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about rail or roads. Level 2 (3–4): developed points on both. Level 3 (5–6): balanced evaluation of road damage and emissions with a supported judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'rolling stock'.
parts.answer: The vehicles that run on a railway, such as locomotives, coaches and wagons.
parts.working: 1 mark for 'vehicles/locomotives/wagons/coaches'; 1 mark for 'that run on the railway'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two types of cargo handled at a seaport.
parts.answer: Containers; bulk goods such as coal, grain or cement; petroleum products; vehicles. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct type.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'deep-water port' and why large ships prefer to use one.
parts.answer: A port where the water is deep enough for large ships to enter and berth without constant dredging of the channel. Large ships carry more cargo per voyage, which lowers the cost per tonne, so shipping lines prefer such ports.
parts.working: 1 mark for 'water deep enough for large ships'; 2 marks for an explanation of why large ships prefer it (lower cost per tonne, more cargo, no waiting for the tide).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the province in which Gwadar Port is located.
parts.answer: Balochistan
parts.working: 1 mark for Balochistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A port handles 3,600,000 tonnes of cargo in a year of 365 days. Calculate the average tonnes handled per day, giving your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 9,860 tonnes per day

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a dry port helps to reduce congestion at a busy seaport.
parts.answer: Containers can be unloaded at an inland dry port and customs checks can be done there, rather than all cargo staying in the seaport yard; cargo is then moved by rail or road from the dry port, so ships are unloaded faster and seaport yards are less crowded; factories near the dry port get goods without waiting at the sea terminal. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed point (cause and effect); 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages to an exporter of having a dry port close to the factory.
parts.answer: A shorter road journey to the dry port reduces transport costs; containers can be prepared and cleared near the factory, which saves time at the seaport; delays at the seaport affect the exporter less; goods can be booked and tracked closer to home. (Any two developed advantages.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed advantage; 1 mark for an advantage named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A country's three seaports handle 20.0 million tonnes of cargo in total. Port X handles 6.4 million tonnes. Calculate Port X's percentage share of the total cargo.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two environmental impacts of dredging a shipping channel in a port.
parts.answer: Dredging stirs up sediment, which cuts light and harms seagrass, corals and fish eggs; dumped spoil can smother seabed life; the work can disturb mangroves and coastal habitats; changes to tides and currents can increase coastal erosion. (Any two developed impacts.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed impact; 1 mark for an impact named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a landlocked country such as Afghanistan depends on access to seaports in neighbouring countries for its trade.
parts.answer: Afghanistan has no coastline, so its sea trade must pass through the ports of another country; goods must travel long distances by road or rail across other countries, which is slow and expensive; seaports give access to world shipping routes for both imports and exports. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed point; 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which customs procedures can delay cargo in a port.
parts.answer: Shipping documents such as invoices and permits must be checked, and errors must be corrected, which takes time; containers may be physically inspected, which causes queues; there may be too few officers at busy times; while waiting, cargo stays in the yard and storage charges rise. (Any two developed ways.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed way (cause and effect on cargo); 1 mark for a way named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which new deep-sea ports such as Gwadar will boost Pakistan's economy more than improving existing roads and railways.
parts.answer: For ports: a deep-sea port handles large container ships, cuts shipping costs, attracts investment and industry, and links the country to world trade routes. Against: a port is only useful if roads and rail connect it to producers and markets; it may be under-used; the investment is large and slow to repay; roads and rail help trade across the whole country. Judgement: ports are important, but their value depends on good land links to the rest of the economy.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about ports, roads or rail. Level 2 (3–4): developed points on both. Level 3 (5–6): balanced evaluation reaching a supported judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three problems that a poor road network causes for rural hospitals and clinics.
parts.answer: Ambulances and patients are delayed, so emergencies may become fatal; medicines, vaccines and blood cannot be delivered reliably, so stocks run short or spoil; doctors and nurses find it hard to reach or stay at remote posts; patients cannot reach the clinic when roads are cut by floods. (Any three.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct problem, up to 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'infrastructure' as used in economic development.
parts.answer: The basic facilities a country needs for its economy to work, such as roads, railways, ports, power supply and communications.
parts.working: 1 mark for 'basic facilities or structures'; 1 mark for examples or the purpose for the economy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how transport costs can influence where a factory is located.
parts.answer: Factories are placed where total transport costs are lowest: near raw materials if these are heavy or bulky and lose weight in processing; near markets if the product is fragile, perishable or bulky to move; good transport allows an industry to locate further from its markets because deliveries remain cheap. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed point; 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two effects of traffic congestion on businesses in Karachi.
parts.answer: Deliveries arrive late, so businesses must hold more stock and pay more storage costs; workers arrive late or tired, reducing productivity; fuel and vehicle running costs rise; customers may avoid shops that are hard to reach. (Any two developed effects.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed effect; 1 mark for an effect named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The transport cost of a product is 18% of its price. The price is Rs 2,500. Calculate the transport cost.
parts.answer: Rs 450

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before a new road opened, a 540 km truck journey took 9 hours. After the road opened, the same journey took 6 hours. Calculate the percentage increase in average speed.
parts.working: M1 average speed before = 540 ÷ 9 = 60 km/h; after = 540 ÷ 6 = 90 km/h; A1 (90 − 60) ÷ 60 × 100 = 50%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which better transport can reduce regional inequality within Pakistan.
parts.answer: Remote areas gain access to markets and jobs, so incomes rise; children and patients can reach schools and hospitals more easily; tourism brings income to poorer areas; migrants can travel to better-paid work and send money home. (Any two developed ways.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed way; 1 mark for a way named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which a poor transport network can lead to food being wasted.
parts.answer: Perishable produce such as milk, fruit and vegetables spoils while stuck on bad roads or waiting for transport; long delays at markets lower quality, so the produce is thrown away or sold cheaply; farmers cannot reach buyers and leave crops unharvested. (Any two developed ways.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed way; 1 mark for a way named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how an improved road into a mountain valley can increase tourism and local incomes.
parts.answer: More visitors arrive by car and bus, so hotels, guest houses and restaurants earn more; local people sell handicrafts and food; guides and drivers find work; the road also makes it possible to bring building materials and supplies for new businesses. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed point; 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A trucking firm runs 25 trucks. Each truck makes 2 return trips per week on a route that is 1,200 km one way. Calculate the total distance driven by all trucks in one week, in km.
parts.working: M1 one return trip = 2,400 km; each truck does 2 return trips = 4,800 km; A1 25 × 4,800 = 120,000 km.

parts.label: a
