parts.text: Evaluate the view that spending a large sum on a new motorway would do more for Pakistan's economy than spending the same sum on rural roads that link farms to markets.
parts.answer: For the motorway: faster movement of freight and passengers between the main cities and ports; attracts investment and factories along the route; lowers transport costs for large volumes of trade. Against: rural roads link farms and villages that have no other route to markets, so they cut post-harvest losses and help more poor families; a motorway is very costly and mainly benefits areas that are already developed; rural roads are cheaper per kilometre and raise incomes quickly. Judgement: the motorway may add more to total trade, but rural roads usually do more to reduce poverty, so the answer depends on the government's aim.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about motorways or rural roads. Level 2 (3–4): developed points for and against. Level 3 (5–6): balanced evaluation of growth against poverty reduction, with a supported judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a flood that closes a major highway could affect exports from the agricultural areas of Sindh.
parts.answer: Lorries cannot reach the port or factory, so shipments are delayed and buyers may cancel orders; fresh produce spoils while it waits; alternative routes are longer and more costly; farmers' incomes fall because they cannot sell their crops on time. (Any two developed effects.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed effect; 1 mark for an effect named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the river that flows past the city of Lahore.
parts.answer: Ravi
parts.working: 1 mark for Ravi.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which farmers in Punjab use river water.
parts.answer: Water is taken through canals and distributaries to irrigate crops such as wheat, rice and sugarcane.
parts.working: 1 mark for 'irrigation' or 'canals'; 1 mark for a named crop or development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the flow of Pakistan's rivers changes between winter and summer, and explain why.
parts.answer: Flow is low in winter because snow and ice in the mountains are frozen and rainfall is light; flow is high in summer because snow and glacier ice melt and the monsoon brings heavy rain, which is why most floods come in summer.
parts.working: 1 mark for low winter flow; 1 mark for high summer flow; 1 mark for an explanation (melting snow and glaciers, monsoon rain).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A river channel is 250 m wide and 4 m deep on average. The water flows at an average speed of 1.5 m/s. Calculate the discharge of the river in m³/s (cross-sectional area × velocity). Use illustrative values only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two benefits to farmers of the seasonal flooding of land beside the Indus in Sindh.
parts.answer: Flood water leaves fertile silt on the fields, which improves soil fertility without much fertiliser; flood water soaks into the land so crops can be grown in dry months; wetlands and flooded land support fish and provide grazing for livestock. (Any two developed benefits.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed benefit; 1 mark for a benefit named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which dams and barrages on the Indus have reduced flood risk for people in Punjab and Sindh.
parts.answer: For: dams and reservoirs store flood water and release it gradually, reducing peak floods; barrages regulate the river and divert its water into canals, which spreads the supply through the year; both store water for irrigation and generate power. Against: they cannot control very large floods or heavy rain on tributaries; silt builds up behind dams, reducing storage; the flood deposits on fields that once fertilised the land are lost; some floods still cause damage; flood defences need maintenance. Judgement: dams and barrages reduce some risk, but cannot remove it on their own.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about dams or floods. Level 2 (3–4): developed points for and against. Level 3 (5–6): balanced evaluation for both provinces with a supported judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Thal Desert is in Punjab. State two features of this desert.
parts.answer: Sandy or loamy soil; very low rainfall; very hot summers; scrub vegetation (thorny bushes and grasses); dunes in parts. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct feature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the sandy soil of the Thal Desert holds very little water.
parts.answer: Sand has large gaps between the grains, so water drains away quickly; sandy soil has little clay or humus to hold water.
parts.working: 1 mark for 'large spaces between grains, so water drains through'; 1 mark for 'little clay or humus to hold water'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A desert area has an average annual rainfall of 100 mm and a potential evaporation of 2,400 mm per year (illustrative figures). Calculate how many times greater the evaporation is than the rainfall.
parts.answer: 24 times

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which people in desert areas obtain water for drinking and farming.
parts.answer: Hand-dug wells or tubewells draw water from underground; karez underground channels bring water from springs or aquifers to the surface in Balochistan; canals bring river water from the Indus; rainwater is collected in tobas (ponds) after rain. (Any two developed ways.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed way; 1 mark for a way named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why sand dunes in desert areas of Pakistan can move and bury roads, fields and villages.
parts.answer: Strong winds blow loose sand up the windward slope and drop it on the lee side, so each dune moves slowly downwind; sand is deposited across roads and fields and buries them; moving dunes can cover farmland and houses, forcing families to move away. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed explanation (cause and effect); 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two adaptations of desert plants that help them survive dry conditions.
parts.answer: Thick waxy or waterproof stems or leaves that reduce water loss; deep roots to reach groundwater; small or spiny leaves that reduce transpiration; storage of water in stems. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each adaptation with its effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sand dune in an illustrative desert moves about 8 m each year. Calculate how many years it would take the dune to move 1 km. Give your answer to the nearest year.
parts.answer: 125 years

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which the desert areas of Pakistan, such as Cholistan and Thar, can be developed for farming.
parts.answer: For: canal water, groundwater from tubewells, solar-powered pumps and drip irrigation can support crops and livestock; government schemes and new varieties of drought-tolerant crops help. Against: rainfall is very low and evaporation is very high; sandy soils hold little water and are often saline; there are few roads, schools and services; groundwater can be over-pumped and become salty; drought risk remains. Judgement: development is possible with reliable water and careful management, but the cost and environmental risks are high.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about deserts or farming. Level 2 (3–4): developed points for and against. Level 3 (5–6): balanced evaluation of the water, soil and cost issues with a supported judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two mountain ranges found in the north of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Karakoram; Himalayas; Hindu Kush. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct range.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A road climbs from 1,200 m to 3,300 m above sea level over a horizontal distance of 35 km. Calculate the average gradient of the road in metres per kilometre.
parts.answer: 60 m per km

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name a mountain pass in the north-west that is used for trade between Pakistan and Afghanistan.
parts.answer: Khyber Pass (Torkham is the border crossing on the pass).
parts.working: 1 mark for Khyber Pass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which mountains affect the climate of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Mountains force moist air to rise and cool, so rain and snow fall on the windward slopes and the north receives heavy snow; the high mountains keep the north cool and block cold winds from Central Asia, so the plains are warmer in winter; areas behind the mountains lie in a rain shadow and are very dry. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed explanation; 1 mark for a simple effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how melting glaciers in the Karakoram and Himalayas supply water to the Indus.
parts.answer: Glacier ice melts in spring and summer as temperatures rise, and the meltwater flows into streams that join the Indus and its tributaries such as the Jhelum and Chenab; this keeps river flow high in the hot, dry months when lowland rain is scarce. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed point; 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems faced by people living in high mountain villages in northern Pakistan.
parts.answer: Heavy snow and landslides cut off roads, so food, medicine and fuel are hard to bring in; the short growing season and steep slopes limit how much food can be grown; earthquakes and avalanches can destroy homes and fields; children may miss school when roads are closed. (Any two developed problems.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed problem; 1 mark for a problem named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Karakoram and Himalayas have been a barrier to movement and trade in the past.
parts.answer: The high peaks and steep valleys make travel slow and dangerous; many passes are closed by snow for much of the year; trade had to use a few narrow routes, such as the passes into Central Asia and China; roads have been difficult and costly to build. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed point; 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which tourism can develop the mountain areas of Pakistan without damaging the environment.
parts.answer: For: income from hotels, guides, porters and handicrafts; new roads and services; cultural exchange and pride in local heritage. Against: litter and sewage in lakes and rivers; cutting of forests for wood and building; road cutting that causes landslides; overcrowding in fragile valleys; loss of local farmland to hotels. Judgement: tourism can help mountain communities if it is limited and managed, with waste disposal, controlled building and local employment.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about tourism or the environment. Level 2 (3–4): developed points for and against. Level 3 (5–6): balanced evaluation of economic and environmental effects with a supported judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two countries that share land borders with Pakistan on its western side.
parts.answer: Afghanistan (north-west); Iran (south-west). Either order.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct country.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Four administrative units have these areas (illustrative figures): Unit A 300,000 km²; Unit B 205,000 km²; Unit C 78,000 km²; Unit D 27,000 km². Calculate the total area of the four units.
parts.working: M1 adding the four areas; A1 610,000 km².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate Unit A's share of the total area, as a percentage correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A map has a scale of 1:2,000,000. Two towns are 7.5 cm apart on the map. Calculate the real distance between them in km.
parts.answer: 150 km

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether Pakistan lies north or south of the Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N). Explain your answer in one sentence.
parts.answer: North: all of Pakistan lies north of 23.5°N, so the whole country is outside the tropics.
parts.working: 1 mark for 'north'; 1 mark for a reason linked to the latitude of the Tropic of Cancer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the sea that lies to the south of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Arabian Sea
parts.working: 1 mark for Arabian Sea.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two physical features of Pakistan's coastline that make ports possible.
parts.answer: Sheltered bays and natural harbours (such as the bay at Karachi); deep water close to the shore at Gwadar; flat coastal land behind the coast for port terminals, container yards and warehouses. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct feature.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which Pakistan's location at the meeting point of South Asia, Central Asia and the Middle East is an advantage.
parts.answer: It lies on land routes between Central Asia and the Arabian Sea, so it can be a trade and transit route for goods; it is close to the Gulf states, which are major markets and sources of oil and labour; it offers cultural and economic links with many regions. (Any two developed advantages.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed advantage; 1 mark for an advantage named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the importance of the Khyber Pass and the Bolan Pass for trade.
parts.answer: The Khyber Pass links Peshawar with Afghanistan and Central Asia and has carried trade for centuries; the Bolan Pass links the Balochistan plateau with the Sindh plain and routes towards Afghanistan; both passes give land access through the mountains so goods can move between regions. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed point; 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the capital city of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the capital city of Balochistan.
parts.answer: Peshawar (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa); Quetta (Balochistan).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct city.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that Pakistan's location gives it more advantages than disadvantages.
parts.answer: Advantages: sea access on the Arabian Sea; land routes to Central Asia, China and Iran; close to the Gulf markets; a wide range of climates and resources. Disadvantages: long borders that need defence; instability in neighbouring Afghanistan can disrupt trade and security; border disputes and tensions with India; trade routes can be closed by conflict or floods. Judgement: the location brings many advantages if the country can keep its borders secure and stable and build good transport links.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about advantages or disadvantages. Level 2 (3–4): developed points on both sides. Level 3 (5–6): balanced evaluation with a supported judgement.

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two causes of soil erosion on farmland in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Heavy monsoon rain washing away topsoil; strong winds blowing dry, bare soil; overgrazing that removes plant cover; cutting down trees and hedges; ploughing up and down slopes. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct cause.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output

parts.label: a
parts.text: A wheat farmer's costs are Rs 45,000 per acre. The farm yields 28 maunds per acre (illustrative figures), and the price is Rs 3,200 per maund. Calculate the profit per acre.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which low prices for crops can increase debt for farmers.
parts.answer: Income falls below the cost of seed, fertiliser, water and labour, so the farmer must borrow to continue; borrowing from money-lenders at high interest makes the debt grow each season; if the debt cannot be repaid, the farmer may have to sell land or accept bonded labour. (Any two developed ways.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed way (cause and effect); 1 mark for a way named only.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'fragmentation of land' as a problem for farmers.
parts.answer: The division of a farm among heirs over generations into many small, scattered plots, which makes farming less efficient.
parts.working: 1 mark for 'division into small plots'; 1 mark for 'less efficient or harder to farm'.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Agricultural problems, land reform and output

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which mechanisation has solved the problem of low yields for small farmers in Pakistan.
parts.answer: For: tractors, tubewells and combine harvesters speed up ploughing, sowing and harvesting; they reduce losses and allow more than one crop per year. Against: machines suit large fields, not small scattered plots; they are costly to buy or hire and need fuel and skills; many small farmers cannot afford them; yields also depend on water, seed, fertiliser and pest control. Judgement: mechanisation helps, mostly larger farmers, but it does not solve low yields alone.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about machines or yields. Level 2 (3–4): developed points for and against. Level 3 (5–6): balanced evaluation for small farmers with a supported judgement.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name a crop grown in Punjab from whose seeds edible oil is extracted, and state whether it is a kharif or a rabi crop.
parts.answer: Mustard (rapeseed); it is a rabi crop, sown in autumn and harvested in spring.
parts.working: 1 mark for mustard or rapeseed; 1 mark for rabi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three districts have wheat areas of 45,000 ha, 62,500 ha and 38,750 ha (illustrative figures). Calculate the total wheat area of these three districts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The total wheat area of the province is 1,000,000 ha (illustrative figure). Calculate the percentage of the province's wheat area that these three districts make up.
parts.answer: 14.6% (to 1 decimal place)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the conditions needed for growing maize.
parts.answer: Warm temperatures during the growing season; a moderate rainfall of around 500 mm or more, or reliable irrigation; well-drained, fertile loam soil; sown in the spring or early summer (kharif) season. (Any three.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct condition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why cotton output has fallen in some years in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Pest attacks such as whitefly and pink bollworm destroy the bolls and reduce yields; heavy rain or floods during sowing and picking damage the crop; poor-quality or unapproved seed gives weak plants; low prices lead farmers to switch to other crops; shortages of irrigation water in the sowing season. (Any two developed reasons.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed reason; 1 mark for a reason named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two uses of sugarcane.
parts.answer: Making white sugar; making gur (unrefined jaggery); producing molasses for ethanol or animal feed; drinking as cane juice. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farmer plans to sow 15 hectares of wheat. The seed rate is 40 kg per hectare and the seed costs Rs 180 per kg. Calculate the total cost of the seed.

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the difference between commercial farming and subsistence farming.
parts.answer: Commercial farming produces crops or animals mainly to sell for profit; subsistence farming produces food mainly for the farmer's own family, with little or no surplus to sell.
parts.working: 1 mark for commercial = sell for profit; 1 mark for subsistence = mainly to feed own family.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe mixed farming in the Punjab plains.
parts.answer: Farmers grow crops such as wheat, cotton and sugarcane and also keep livestock such as cattle, buffaloes and poultry on the same farm; livestock supply milk, manure and draught power; crop residues are used as animal fodder.
parts.working: 1 mark for crops and livestock on the same farm; 1 mark for an example of each; 1 mark for a linked benefit (manure, fodder, draught power).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'intensive farming'.
parts.answer: Farming a small area with high inputs of labour, fertiliser, water or capital in order to obtain a high output per hectare.
parts.working: 1 mark for 'small area with high inputs'; 1 mark for 'high output per hectare'.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the Indus Basin Irrigation System, naming two of its main parts.
parts.answer: The Indus Basin Irrigation System is one of the largest canal networks in the world. River water is diverted at barrages (for example Taunsa, Guddu and Sukkur) into main canals, which feed distributaries and then watercourses that reach the fields. Link canals move water between rivers. It supplies most of the irrigated land of Punjab and Sindh. Named parts (any two): barrage, main canal, distributary, watercourse, link canal.
parts.working: 1 mark for describing the network; 1 mark for each correctly named part (up to 2); 1 mark for its purpose (irrigating Punjab and Sindh).

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages and one disadvantage of tubewell irrigation for farmers in Punjab.
parts.answer: Advantages: water can be pumped when canal supply is short, so farmers can irrigate in dry spells and grow more crops; in waterlogged areas, pumping lowers the water table and improves drainage. Disadvantage: pumping costs for fuel or electricity are high; over-pumping can lower the groundwater and draw in salty water in some areas.
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed advantage; 1 mark for the disadvantage.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: A village has 240 families who share 1,200 hectares of farmland. Calculate the average area of farmland per family in hectares.
parts.answer: 5 hectares
parts.working: M1 1,200 ÷ 240; A1 5 hectares.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why drip irrigation may be useful for farmers in Balochistan.
parts.answer: Water is scarce, and drip irrigation delivers it slowly to the roots of each plant, so little is lost to evaporation or runoff; this saves water so that more land can be watered from the same source; less weed growth and less labour are needed; fertiliser can be dissolved in the water and applied directly. (Any two developed reasons.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed reason; 1 mark for a reason named only.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name a fruit that grows well in the valleys of Gilgit-Baltistan.
parts.answer: Apricot (apples and walnuts are also acceptable).
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct fruit.

author: HomiLabs

subtopic: Types of farming and farming systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that subsistence farming will disappear from Pakistan within the next 20 years.
parts.answer: For: population growth and migration to towns leave fewer people on the land; commercial farms and markets offer higher incomes; land is split into ever smaller plots that cannot support a family; young people prefer other work. Against: millions of small farmers and landless families still depend on it for food; it gives security when prices or jobs fail; credit, water and markets are not available to everyone, so change is slow; family and cultural ties keep people on the land. Judgement: subsistence farming will shrink, but it is unlikely to disappear completely within 20 years.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about subsistence farming. Level 2 (3–4): developed points for and against. Level 3 (5–6): balanced evaluation with a supported judgement about the time-scale.

author: HomiLabs

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two products obtained from goats.
parts.answer: Meat; milk; wool or hair (from some breeds); skins or hides; manure. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A poultry farm has 4,000 hens. On a typical day, 85% of the hens each lay one egg. Calculate the number of eggs collected in one week (7 days).
parts.answer: 23,800 eggs

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two diseases that can affect cattle and buffaloes.
parts.answer: Foot-and-mouth disease; mastitis (infection of the udder); anthrax. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct disease.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of livestock in providing income for landless families in rural Pakistan.
parts.answer: A few cows, buffaloes or goats give milk that can be sold each day, giving a regular cash income; animals can be sold in an emergency or to pay for weddings or medicine; manure can be used on family plots or sold; women and children often do the milking and herding, so the whole family earns. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed point; 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why the grazing land available to herders is shrinking in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Rangeland is ploughed up or built on as the population grows; forest and scrub are cut for fuel and timber; canals, roads and fences take land; overgrazing and drought reduce the grass that grows. (Any two developed reasons.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed reason; 1 mark for a reason named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by 'artificial insemination' in cattle breeding and give one benefit to farmers.
parts.answer: Sperm from a selected male animal is placed into the female's reproductive tract without mating; benefit: offspring inherit high milk yield or good body features from a chosen sire; the spread of disease through mating is reduced. (Any one benefit.)
parts.working: 1 mark for sperm from a selected male placed into the female; 1 mark for 'without mating'; 1 mark for a valid benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways in which the livestock sector contributes to Pakistan's economy.
parts.answer: Milk and meat form a large part of agricultural output and food supply; hides and skins support the leather trade and its exports; it gives employment to herders, transporters and processors; animals provide draught power and manure for crops. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed point; 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A dairy farm produces 240 litres of milk per day at a feed cost of Rs 2,700 per day. Calculate the feed cost per litre of milk, correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: Rs 11.25 per litre
parts.working: M1 2,700 ÷ 240; A1 Rs 11.25 per litre.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a shortage of fodder can affect animal health and milk output.
parts.answer: Animals lose body weight and become weak, so their resistance to disease falls; pregnant animals may give birth to weak calves; milk yield falls; farmers may have to sell animals early at low prices to cut losses. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed link; 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which large intensive poultry and dairy farms are better than traditional herding for Pakistan's food security.
parts.answer: For: large farms produce more eggs, meat and milk at lower cost per unit, supply cities reliably, and can use vaccination and hygiene. Against: they depend on imported feed and medicines and are hit hard by disease outbreaks; they can pollute water and air; herding families who lose their livelihood may lose food security; traditional herding uses rangeland that cannot be farmed intensively and supports poorer families. Judgement: intensive farms add to supply, but food security for the poor depends on keeping small and herding producers too.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about farming types. Level 2 (3–4): developed points for and against. Level 3 (5–6): balanced evaluation linked to food security with a supported judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two uses of fish meal.
parts.answer: Animal feed for poultry and livestock; feed for farmed fish; fertiliser. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pakistan's total annual catch is 600,000 tonnes and inland fisheries provide 14,000 tonnes (illustrative figures). Calculate the percentage of the total catch that comes from inland fisheries, correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two measures that a government can use to limit overfishing.
parts.answer: A closed season when fish breed, so stocks can recover; a minimum mesh size so that young fish can escape; licences that limit the number of boats; catch quotas or bans on damaging gear such as bottom trawls in coastal waters. (Any two developed measures.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each measure with its purpose; 1 mark for a measure named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why fish stocks in the Arabian Sea may decline.
parts.answer: Overfishing, including trawling that catches young fish and damages the seabed; pollution from sewage, oil and plastic; warming sea or changes in upwelling that move fish away from the coast; destruction of mangroves and breeding grounds. (Any two developed reasons.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed reason; 1 mark for a reason named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term 'mesh size' as applied to a fishing net.
parts.answer: The size of the openings (holes) in the net.
parts.working: 1 mark for 'size of the openings or holes'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a larger mesh size can help to protect young fish.
parts.answer: Small and young fish can swim through the larger openings and escape, so they survive to grow and breed.
parts.working: 1 mark for 'young fish escape'; 1 mark for 'so the stock can recover or breed'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fishing cooperative sells 3,600 kg of fish at Rs 450 per kg. Calculate the total value of the sale.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the extent to which fish farming (aquaculture) can reduce the pressure on wild fish stocks in Pakistan.
parts.answer: For: ponds and cages produce fish all year with controlled feeding and disease control, so less fish is taken from the sea and rivers; it creates jobs in inland areas where there is no sea fishing; it can produce fish close to markets. Against: farmed fish often need feed made from fish meal, which is caught from wild stocks; ponds need water and land and can pollute rivers; disease can spread to wild fish; starting a farm needs capital that small fishermen lack. Judgement: aquaculture can reduce pressure on wild fish if feed is sustainable and farms are well managed.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about fish farming or wild stocks. Level 2 (3–4): developed points for and against. Level 3 (5–6): balanced evaluation of feed, pollution and livelihoods with a supported judgement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two problems caused by plastic waste in the sea for fish and for fishing.
parts.answer: Fish, turtles and seabirds eat or become tangled in plastic, which injures or kills them so catches fall; plastic gets caught in nets and propellers, increasing repair costs and lost fishing time; tiny plastic fragments enter the food chain and may reach people who eat fish. (Any two developed problems.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed problem; 1 mark for a problem named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which the mangroves of the Indus Delta help to protect the coast.
parts.answer: They slow down waves and storm surges, so less land is flooded by the sea; their roots bind the mud and reduce coastal erosion. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two types of vessel used for fishing in Pakistan's coastal waters.
parts.answer: Small motorised fibreglass or wooden boats for inshore fishing; mechanised trawlers for deeper water; traditional wooden boats. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each type of vessel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how fish can be dried, and state why drying preserves fish.
parts.answer: The fish is cleaned, split if needed, and laid out in the sun or wind (often after salting) until it is dry; the water is removed so bacteria and moulds cannot grow.
parts.working: 1 mark for cleaning and laying out in sun or wind; 1 mark for drying until dry or salted; 1 mark for 'removes water so bacteria cannot grow'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A boat lands 2,500 kg of fish. 12% of the catch spoils before it reaches the market. Calculate the weight of fish that remains to be sold.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two benefits of a cold-storage facility at a fish harbour.
parts.answer: Fish stays fresh for longer, so it can be sold at a better price; fish can be stored when supply is high and sold when prices are better; spoilage and waste are reduced; cold storage helps exporters meet hygiene and cold-chain standards. (Any two developed benefits.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed benefit; 1 mark for a benefit named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a purse seine net is used to catch fish.
parts.answer: The net is set in a large circle around a shoal of fish; the bottom edge is drawn in (pursed) like a drawstring so the fish are trapped; the net is then hauled aboard and the catch is taken out.
parts.working: 1 mark for setting the net around a shoal; 1 mark for closing the bottom of the net; 1 mark for hauling in the catch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why fish sold in local markets may spoil more quickly than frozen fish sent for export.
parts.answer: Local markets often lack refrigeration, so fish is exposed to heat and bacteria; fish may be left for a long time between catch and sale; hygiene may be poor. Export fish is chilled or frozen quickly and kept in a cold chain, so spoilage is slower. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed explanation; 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fish processor packs fish into boxes that each hold 20 kg. Calculate the number of boxes needed for 1,650 kg of fish.
parts.answer: 83 boxes
parts.working: M1 1,650 ÷ 20 = 82.5; A1 83 boxes (a part-full box is still needed).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a fishing village may need a landing jetty or fish harbour to develop its fishing industry.
parts.answer: Boats can tie up and unload safely in all weather and at all tides; the catch can be sorted, auctioned and processed in one place; ice and fuel can be stored and sold there; traders and buyers gather, creating jobs and a steady market. (Any two developed reasons.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed reason; 1 mark for a reason named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two hook-based fishing methods.
parts.answer: Hand line; long line (a main line with many baited hooks). (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name a freshwater fish found in the Indus river system, other than the palla.
parts.answer: Mahseer, rohu or catfish (any one correct freshwater species).
parts.working: 1 mark for a correct freshwater species found in the Indus system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A pie chart shows the annual catch of three species: tuna 40 tonnes, sardines 25 tonnes and shrimp 35 tonnes (illustrative figures). Calculate the angle of the sector for sardines.
parts.working: M1 total = 100 tonnes, so sardines = 25 ÷ 100 of the circle; A1 25/100 × 360 = 90°.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two crustaceans that are caught commercially off Pakistan's coast.
parts.answer: Shrimp (prawns); crabs. (Any two.)
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct crustacean.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sardine landings fell from 1,200 tonnes in one year to 960 tonnes in the next (illustrative figures). Calculate the percentage fall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Indus dolphin is a conservation concern.
parts.answer: It is a rare freshwater species found only in the Indus river system; it is accidentally caught in gill nets; dams and barrages divide its habitat into separate stretches and reduce the water it needs; pollution reduces the fish it feeds on. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed point; 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Annual tuna catches over five years were 4,200, 3,900, 4,500, 4,100 and 3,800 tonnes (illustrative figures). Calculate the average annual tuna catch.
parts.answer: 4,100 tonnes
parts.working: M1 total = 20,500 tonnes; A1 20,500 ÷ 5 = 4,100 tonnes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one difference between marine fish and freshwater fish.
parts.answer: Marine fish live in salt water in the sea; freshwater fish live in rivers, lakes or ponds with fresh water and must control the salt in their bodies in a different way.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming the habitat difference (salt sea versus fresh water); 1 mark for a valid biological or habitat detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why shrimp earns a higher value per kilogram in the market than sardines.
parts.answer: Shrimp is a high-value species in demand from export buyers and restaurants, and it must be handled carefully and kept cold; sardines are a low-cost food for local people and are sold in large volumes at low prices. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed point (demand, handling, price); 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A catch of 320 tonnes is sold at Rs 1,400 per kg. Calculate the value of the catch in rupees.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why marine fish catches can vary greatly from one year to the next.
parts.answer: Changes in sea temperature or currents move fish away from the usual fishing grounds; the strength of upwelling and the monsoon winds vary from year to year; overfishing reduces stocks so catches fall; storms and fishing bans stop boats from fishing. (Any two developed reasons.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed reason; 1 mark for a reason named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the Indus Delta is important as a nursery ground for fish.
parts.answer: Mangrove creeks and mud flats give shelter and food for young fish and shrimp; fresh water from the river mixes with sea water and brings nutrients that feed plankton; young fish can grow in these sheltered waters before moving to the open sea and joining the catch. (Any two developed points.)
parts.working: 2 marks for each developed point; 1 mark for a point named only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the view that the best way to increase Pakistan's fish catch is to buy more trawlers.
parts.answer: For: more boats can fish further offshore and land more fish, creating jobs and income. Against: more trawlers increase overfishing and catch young fish (by-catch), use more fuel and damage the seabed, so catches may fall; better management such as mesh-size rules, closed seasons, harbours, cold storage and aquaculture may give a more sustainable increase. Judgement: more trawlers may add catch in the short term, but management and infrastructure are likely to give a lasting increase.
parts.working: Level 1 (1–2): simple statements about trawlers or catches. Level 2 (3–4): developed points for and against. Level 3 (5–6): balanced evaluation, including sustainability, with a supported judgement.
